Constitutional law --
Charter of Rights
-- Application -- Regulation
providing for religious education in public schools -- Parties attacking
curriculum of school board because of predominantly Christian nature of
teaching -- Curriculum subject to Charter scrutiny --
Constitution Act, 1982,
s. 52
-- Education Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, ss. 10(1), para. 18, 50 -- R.R.O.
1980, Reg. 262, s. 28.

The applicants, the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and parents of
children enrolled in or previously enrolled in schools of the respondent board
of education, brought an application for judicial review to challenge the
constitutional validity of s. 28 of R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262, and the curriculum
of religious studies of the board. Section 28(4) of the regulation requires two
periods of religious education each week. Pursuant to s. 28(6), instruction
shall be given by the teacher, and issues of a controversial or sectarian
nature shall be avoided. Section 28(7) permits a board to allow clergy or lay
people to give religious instruction in lieu of teachers. Parents of a child
can apply to have a child exempted from religious education pursuant to s.
28(10). A teacher may also claim exemption from teaching religious education.
Section 50 of the Education Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, provides that each pupil
shall receive religious instruction only as his or her parent or guardian
desires or, where the pupil is an adult, as he or she desires, while s. 10(1),
para. 18 permits the Lieutenant-Governor in Council to make regulations respecting
religious education.

At the time the application commenced, religious instruction was offered
only by members of a county Bible association, and the instruction was largely
from a fundamentalist Christian perspective. In 1986-1987, there were curriculum
changes to add references to other faiths. The board resolved, after this
litigation commenced, that in 1987-1988, class-room teachers, rather than lay
volunteers, would provide elementary religious education. The population of the
county is overwhelmingly Christian and largely Protestant.

The applicant parents all object to the sectarian nature of the religious
instruction, although two families chose not to exempt their children from
religious instruction, because they feared that the child would be ostracized
or subject to stigma.

On an application for judicial review held, Austin J. dissenting, the
regulation was valid.

Per Watt J., McKeown J. concurring: Neither the purpose nor effects of s. 28
of the regulation violate freedom of religion in
s. 2(a)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. The purpose of s. 28, especially when viewed in
the context of its enabling authority in
ss. 10(1)
, para. 18 and 50 of the
Education Act, is to make available for public elementary school pupils instruction
in religious education as part of the curriculum in schools. Its provision is
part of the over-all purpose of the public school system to provide systematic
training of the young. Instruction in religious education is made available to
students to instil a sense of morality. The individual applicants conceded that
such instruction is constitutionally permissible and desirable.

The purpose of s. 28 is not to indoctrinate pupils in majoritarian Christian
religious beliefs. The enabling legislation was enacted for a constitutionally
permissible purpose, that is, the secular purpose of introducing a moral
element into the education of public elementary school pupils whereby, together
with intellectual instruction, they may become adequately equipped to function
in life. Nothing in the language of the enabling authority nor in the
provision- exemption dichotomy there enacted evinces a sectarian purpose of
religious indoctrination in majoritarian Christian precepts. Neither the
structure nor language of the regulation converts the constitutionally
permissible purpose underlying the enabling authority to that which is
constitutionally infirm on account of
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. The fact of
exemption shows that the purpose is not indoctrination. As well, the
subject-matter of religious education is drained of sectarian content by s.
28(6). Generally, a teacher gives the instruction, which indicates a secular
purpose.

The effects of s. 28 do not prevent individual pupils from entertaining or
manifesting religious beliefs. The unqualified nature of the exemption
underscores that the provisions seek to ensure self-determination of religious
beliefs. The effect does not coerce individuals to affirm a specific religious
belief nor to act contrary to their beliefs. The legislation does not proclaim
the standards of any faith. The provisions preserve and enhance the
multicultural heritage of Canadians, rather than impair religious freedom. The
applicants have failed to discharge the burden of persuasion to show that there
is psychological pressure on children to conform, rendering illusory the right
to claim an exemption. However, even if the evidence does support the
applicants, the effects do not violate
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

There is no denial of equality rights. There are two classes of pupils,
those who entertain Christian religious beliefs and those who do not, who are
similarly situated, as they are all pupils in the public elementary school
system. There is no violation of
s. 15(1)
, as any disadvantage inherent in
exemption from religious education is chosen by the pupil. The treatment is not
irrational or unfair, as it arises from the pupil's act. The exemption
mechanism facilitates individual self-determination and exemplifies fairness.
It is a right available to all, regardless of religious beliefs. There is
neither inherent disadvantage to the non-Christian pupil nor irrational and
unfair treatment based on religious belief.

The board's curriculum is law, subject to scrutiny under
s. 52(1)
of the

Constitution Act, 1982
, as the school board's authority to provide religious
education is furnished by s. 50 of the Education Act and s. 28 of the
regulation. The curriculum, as presently taught, does not violate
s. 2(a)
of
the Charter. The proposed curriculum does not, in purpose or effect, prevent
individuals from entertaining religious beliefs. Pupils, their parents and
guardians are fully informed of the exemption process and exemptions are
granted on request. The fact that discussion of Christian religious beliefs
dominates the curriculum, thereby reproducing a mirror image of the county in
which instruction is given, does not force pupils to act contrary to their
religious beliefs. The Charter does not guarantee that equal time in religious
instruction must be afforded to every religion. Moreover, the curriculum will
include a discussion of religions other than Christianity and will be taught by
board teachers.

The curriculum does not deny equality rights by conferring a benefit on the
Christian religion. The curriculum does not exclude the tenets of non-Christian
religions, although the Christian religion dominates. Public meetings have
solicited the views of constituents, and there is no evidence of the board's
failure to include material on any religion upon request therefor. Moreover,
the curriculum does not provide instruction to pupils of Christian religious
belief and exemptions for others, as anyone, regardless of belief, can claim
exemption.

Per Austin J. dissenting: The purpose of s. 28(4) of the regulation was to
permit the indoctrination of school children in Ontario in the Christian faith,
and it is being used in the county, at least, for the purpose of indoctrination
of a fundamentalist, evangelical Christian nature at the present time. There is
evidence from the parents and experts that there is an appreciable degree of
coercion or pressure on the personal applicants in this case. There is an
inequality of situation by virtue of the nature of this programme. The
exemption provisions do not constitute an answer to the suggestion of
inequality or coercion. Therefore, s. 28(4) is a denial of freedom of religion
and an inequality within
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Charter
.

The respondents have not demonstrated that the law is a reasonable limit
under s. 1. Interference with the religious rights of a minority is not
justifiable to satisfy the religious requirements of the majority. Moreover, if
school should teach moral values, they can do so without religious instruction.

Even if s. 28(4) of the regulation is valid, the curriculum, as it existed
in 1983 through 1987, violates
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Charter
.

Reg. 262, as amended, violates inter alia
ss. 2(a)

WATT J.:-- This is an application for judicial review whereby it is sought:

(a) to declare s. 28 of R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262, as amended, to be of no force or
effect in consequence of its alleged infringement or denial of certain rights
or freedoms guaranteed by the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms

("the Charter");

(b) to declare the curriculum of religious studies prescribed by the
respondent, the Elgin County Board of Education, to be a denial of certain
rights or freedoms guaranteed by the Charter, and

(c) to enjoin the respondent, the Elgin County Board of Education, from
continuing to require or permit its curriculum of religious studies to be
offered in its schools.

I INTRODUCTION

1. THE PROCEDURAL HISTORY

(
1
) Introduction

It will be helpful at the outset to rehearse briefly the procedural history
of the present application, to describe the parties thereto and to set out
thereafter the statutory provisions which are here impugned or said to
constitute the basis of the constitutional infirmity here asserted.

(
2
) The parties

(a) The Corporation of the Canadian Civil
Liberties Association

The corporate applicant, the Corporation of the Canadian Civil Liberties
Association, is a non-profit corporation, the objects of which are identical to
those of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association ("C.C.L.A."). The
C.C.L.A., a national organization created in 1964, actively promotes respect
for and the observance of fundamental human rights and civil liberties. It has,
for some two decades, asserted the existence of violations of religious freedom
in the public school system in this province. The association has made
representations and presented briefs to Royal Commissions as well as to various
Ministers of the Crown in support of its position.

(b) James and Nancy Millington

James and Nancy Millington were formerly residents of Elgin County with
children in the public school system administered by the respondent, the Elgin
County Board of Education. They are members of the Baha'i faith and have
determined to raise their children in accordance with its precepts which
include tolerance of and respect for the religious beliefs of others. Whilst
resident in Elgin County, the Millingtons approached the respondent board and
its representatives concerning the programme of religious studies then being
offered in its schools. It was the wish of Mr. and Mrs. Millington that their
children, as pupils in the board's school, be apprised of the various religions
of the world, their moral teachings and precepts, rather than be restricted to
instruction in Christian and fundamentalist doctrine.

In the ultimate result, the Millingtons, apparently dissatisfied with the
nature and extent of the board's response to their request, sought to be joined
as applicants in the present proceedings initiated by the C.C.L.A. On September
15, 1986, Griffiths J. ordered that the Millingtons be added as
parties-applicant in these proceedings.

James and Nancy Millington moved out of Elgin County in March, 1987.

(c) Edith Louise Hough

Edith Louise Hough, apparently a lifelong resident of Elgin County, has two
children in public schools administered by the respondent board. Mrs. Hough,
herself educated in the public schools of Elgin County, takes objection to the
nature of religious education offered in the board's schools. It is her
position that the board's programme in religious education is, as it ought not
to be, restricted to the teaching of Christian dogma rather than the
dissemination of information about the organized religions of the world. She
asserts that the board and its agents have demonstrated little or no tolerance
for thinking on religion that does not mirror their own (Christian) conventions
and beliefs.

By notice of motion dated June 2, 1987, and returnable before the court on
the hearing of the application for judicial review, Mrs. Hough sought to be
added as a party-applicant in the present proceedings. The respondents neither
consented to nor opposed her application. It has been established to my satisfaction
that Mrs. Hough ought to be added as a party- applicant in the present
proceedings. Her interest in the subject-matter of the dispute, as well as her
entitlement to the relief afforded by the
Charter
in the event of adequate
demonstration of infringement or denial of a right or freedom enshrined
therein, is sufficient to sustain her joinder as a party-applicant.

(d) Elizabeth C. Sebestyen

Mrs. Elizabeth C. Sebestyen, a resident of Elgin County since 1979,
currently has two children enrolled in public schools administered by the
respondent board. She first became aware of the nature of the programme in
religious education in 1979 and was concerned that it did not extend beyond
Christian teachings. Mrs. Sebestyen has no objection to the teaching of a
programme in world religious studies in the public schools of Elgin County
provided the classes are taught in a general and objective manner by the
home-room teacher as one of the subjects in the curriculum.

By notice of motion dated June 2, 1987, and returnable before the court on
the hearing of the application for judicial review, Mrs. Sebestyen sought to be
added as a party-applicant in the present proceedings. The respondents neither
consented to nor opposed her application. It has been established to my
satisfaction that Mrs. Sebestyen ought to be added as a party- applicant in the
present proceedings. In my respectful view, her asserted interest in the
subject-matter of the dispute, as well as her entitlement to the
Charter
relief
here claimed, upon adequate proof of infringement or denial of an enumerated
right or freedom, is sufficient to warrant her joinder as a party-applicant.

(e) The Minister of Education

The Minister of Education ("the Minister"), a member of the
Executive Council of the Government of Ontario, is the Minister responsible for
the administration of the Education Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, as amended, and
the regulations enacted pursuant thereto. Regulation 262, is but one of the
regulations which falls within the responsibility of the Minister. It is s. 28,
and more particularly s-s. (4) of that regulation, which is here said to be
constitutionally infirm on account of its infringement or denial of certain
rights or freedoms enumerated in the
Charter
. Under s. 28(15) of the impugned
regulation, the Minister may grant to a board exemption from the teaching of
religious education in any class-room or school if the board requests in
writing the exemption and submits reasons for its request.

(f) The Elgin County Board of Education

The Elgin County Board of Education ("the Board") operates the
public school system in Elgin County. In accordance with the provisions of s.
50(1) of the Education Act, the Board has offered and continues to offer pupils
enrolled in its schools a programme in religious instruction. The curriculum in
religious instruction approved by the Board for use in its schools is
challenged in the present application upon the basis that it infringes or
denies certain enumerated rights and freedoms under the
Charter
. There is no
record of any application by the Board for exemption from the teaching of
religious education in any of its class-rooms or schools.

2. THE STATUTORY PROVISIONS

(1) Introduction

The basis upon which the present application is founded engages a consideration
of the enabling provincial statute, the Education Act, as amended, regulations
passed pursuant thereto, in particular s. 28 of Reg. 262, as amended, entitled
"Religious Exercises and Religious Education in the Public Schools",
as well as certain provisions of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
.
It will be convenient to here set out the relevant provisions.

(2) The Education Act

It is s. 50 of the Education Act, as amended ("the Act"), which
permits religious instruction to be given in the public schools of Ontario. The
section, entitled "Religious Instruction", appears in Part III of the
Act "Public and Secondary Schools", and enacts, as follows:

50(1) Subject to the regulations, a pupil shall
be allowed to receive such religious instruction as his parent or guardian
desires or, where the pupil is an adult, as he desires.

(2) No pupil in a public school shall be required
to read or study in or from a religious book, or to join in an exercise of
devotion or religion, objected to by his parent or guardian, or by the pupil,
where he is an adult.

Section 50(1) of the Act allows pupils to receive religious instruction in
the schools governed by this part. It does not, in terms, require such instruction
to be given nor the pupil to receive it. Whether such instruction is received
by the pupil is dependent upon the desires of the pupil's parent or guardian
or, where the pupil is an adult, of the pupil him- or herself. The receipt of
religious instruction is also expressly made subject to the regulations under
the Act.

Section 50(2) makes it plain that no pupil in a public school is required to
read or study in or from a religious book nor to join in an exercise of
devotion or religion where objection is taken thereto by the parent, guardian
or pupil, if an adult.

The effect of s. 50 of the Act would appear to be at least three-fold. In
the first place, the section merely allows a public school pupil to receive
religious instruction. It would seem to follow that a board is permitted to
extend such instruction to its pupil. The pupil is not required to receive nor
the board compelled to provide religious instruction. Secondly, the receipt by
the pupil of religious instruction is expressly made dependent upon the desires
of the parent, guardian or pupil, if an adult. It would seem logically to
follow that no pupil in the public schools is to receive religious instruction
to any greater extent, if at all, than that desired by the pupil's parent, guardian
or the pupil him- or herself, if an adult. The same result obtains in respect
of religious exercises. Finally, the receipt of religious instruction under s.
50(1) is expressly made subject to the regulations passed under the Act.

It is not here alleged that s. 50 of the Act is constitutionally infirm on
account of any infringement upon or denial of any right or freedom enumerated
in the
Charter
.

The authority to make regulations in respect of schools or classes
established under the Act or any predecessor statute is given to the Minister
of Education, subject to the approval of the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, by
s. 10 of the Act. In particular, s. 10(1), para. 18 provides the following:

10(1) Subject to the approval of the Lieutenant
Governor in Council, the Minister may make regulations in respect of schools or
classes established under this Act, or any predecessor of this Act, and with
respect to all other schools supported in whole or in part by public money,

. . . . .

18. governing the provision of religious
exercises and religious education in public and secondary schools and providing
for the exemption of pupils from participating in such exercises and education
and of a teacher from teaching, and a public school board or a secondary school
board from providing, religious education in any school or class;

It may be observed that in the excerpted paragraph the ministerial authority
to make regulations extends concurrently to the provision of religious
education and exercises and exemptions therefrom. The exemptions are not
limited, as would arise, for example, under s. 50 of the Act, to pupils in the
public and secondary school system. The regulation-making authority conferred
by s. 10(1), para. 18 of the Act expressly contemplates that exemption from
religious exercises and education be available equally to pupils, teachers and
boards. No distinction is drawn amongst those entitled to such exemption nor is
there specified any basis upon which such relief may be given.

(
3
) The Regulation

In accordance with the enabling authority of s. 10(1), para. 18 of the Act,
the Lieutenant-Governor in Council has made s. 28 of Reg. 262 ("the
Regulation"), respecting religious exercises and education in the public
schools. The section, as amended by s. 21 of O. Reg. 617/81, in its entirety,
provides, as follows:

28(1) A public school shall be opened or closed
each school day with religious exercises consisting of the reading of
Scriptures or other suitable readings and the repeating of the Lord's Prayer or
other suitable prayers.

(2) The readings and prayers that form part of
the religious exercises referred to in subsection (1) shall be chosen from a
list of selections approved for such purpose by the board that operates the
school where the board approves such a list and, where the board does not
approve such a list, the principal of the school shall select the readings and
prayers after notifying the board of the principal's intention to do so, but
this selection is subject to revision by the board at any time.

(3) The religious exercises under subsection (1)
may include the singing of one or more hymns.

(4) Two periods per week of one-half hour each,
in addition to the time assigned to religious exercises at the opening or
closing of a public school, shall be devoted to religious education.

(5) Religious education shall be given
immediately after the opening of a public school or immediately before the
closing of school in either the morning or the afternoon session.

(6) Instruction in religious education shall be
given by the teacher and issues of controversial or sectarian nature shall be
avoided.

(7) By resolution of a board, a clergyman or
clergymen of any denomination, or a lay person or lay persons selected by the
clergyman or clergymen, may give religious instruction in a school of the board
in lieu of a teacher or teachers.

(8) Where two or more clergymen of different
denominations, or lay persons selected by the clergymen, upon written
application to the board, secure permission under subsection

(7) to give religious instruction in the same school, the principal of the
school, by resolution of the board, shall arrange for such accommodation within
the school and such times within the periods referred to in subsection (5) as
are agreeable to both the principal and the clergymen or the lay persons
selected by the clergymen.

(9) Where the number of rooms in a public school
is insufficient to meet the needs of the groups organized for religious
instruction under subsection (7) or (8), the principal of the school, by
resolution of the board, may arrange for additional accommodation elsewhere.

(10) No pupil shall be required to take part in
any religious exercises or be subject to any instruction in religious education
where a parent of the pupil, or the pupil where the pupil is an adult, applies
to the principal of the school that the pupil attends for exemption of the
pupil therefrom.

(11) In public schools without suitable waiting
rooms or other similar accommodation, if the parent of a pupil or, where the
pupil is an adult, the pupil applies to the principal of the school for the
exemption of the pupil from attendance while religious exercises are being held
or religious education given, such request shall be granted.

(12) Where a parent of a pupil, or the pupil
where the pupil is an adult, objects to the pupil's taking part in religious
exercises or being subject to instruction in religious education, but requests
that the pupil remain in the classroom during the time devoted to religious exercises
or instruction in religious education, the principal of the school that the
pupil attends shall permit the pupil to do so, if the pupil maintains decorous
behaviour.

(13) If, because of the right to be absent from
religious exercises or instruction in religious education, any pupil is not
present in the classroom during the periods specified for religious exercises
or instruction in religious education, the absence shall not be considered a
contravention of the rules of the school.

(14) A teacher claiming exemption from the
teaching of religious education as prescribed by this section shall notify the
board to that effect in writing, and the board shall make such other provisions
as is necessary to implement this section with respect to the teaching of
religious education.

(15) The Minister may grant to a board exemption
from the teaching of religious education in any classroom or school if the
board requests in writing the exemption and submits reasons for its request.

(16) The appropriate supervisory officer shall
each year bring the provisions of this section to the attention of the board or
boards in respect of which such officer has jurisdiction.

It will suffice for present purposes to here record a brief description of
the scheme of religious education apparently contemplated by the Regulation.
Section 28(4) of the Regulation requires that in each week, two one-half hour
periods be devoted to religious education. These periods of religious education
are expressly said to be in addition to the opening or closing religious
exercises for which provision has been made in s. 28(1) to (3), inclusive.
Religious education, in accordance with s. 28(5), is to be given immediately
after the opening of a public school or immediately before the closing of the
morning or afternoon session of the school.

The Regulation not only makes twice weekly religious education mandatory in
the public school system and enacts when it shall be given, but it further
makes express provision for who shall give it. Section 28(6) at once identifies
the primary source of such instruction as "the teacher" and is
limitative of the nature of issues which may be discussed. The injunction
against discussion of issues of controversial or sectarian nature would appear
to be the only aspect of the regulation which is directed to the content of
religious education, that is to say, what is to be taught. The injunction there
contained is limitative of the subject-matter of religious education to be
taught in the public schools. There is no provision elsewhere in the section,
so far as I am able to determine, to relieve against this mandatory injunction
in respect of course content. Provision is made, however, in s. 28(7) and (8)
for lay persons or members of the clergy to give religious instruction in the
public schools in lieu of a teacher or teachers. Teacher substitution is only
permitted, however, by resolution of the board of education in whose schools
the instruction is to be given. It is not suggested that the content of the
instruction in religious education given by the board-authorized surrogates is
otherwise than as circumscribed by s. 28(5). Put shortly, the regulation
authorizes substitution of who shall instruct not what shall be taught.

One further feature of the regulation requires especial mention at this
preliminary stage. It will be recalled that s. 28(4) of the Regulation makes it
mandatory that two periods per week of one-half hour each be devoted to
religious education. Subsection (4) does not, however, stand alone. The section
elsewhere provides exemption from the teaching of religious education to
pupils, teachers and boards of education.

The pupillary exemption for which provision is made in s. 28(10) becomes
engaged upon application by the parent of a pupil or the pupil, if an adult, to
the principal of the school for exemption. It would appear that nothing is
required beyond the mere fact of application by the parent or adult pupil. The
subsection does not expressly require that reasons be given for the application
for exemption. It also seems to follow from the simple fact of application
being made to and by an authorized person that the pupil is thereby not subject
to any instruction in religious education. An exempt pupil will either be suitably
accommodated elsewhere in the school or, at his or her option and upon
condition of maintaining decorous behaviour, remain in the class-room during
the time devoted to instruction in religious education. Absence from the
class-room under such circumstances is not considered a contravention of the
rules of the school.

The teacher exemption for which provision is made in s. 28(14) equally
becomes engaged upon the simple fact of notice to the governing board. The
notice need only be in writing and assert a claim to exemption from the
teaching of religious education as prescribed in s. 28. Upon receipt of the
notice claiming exemption, the board becomes obliged to make such other
provision as is necessary to implement the instruction in religious education
mandate of the section.

A board of education may also seek exemption from the teaching of religious
education. The request for exemption may be made in respect of any class-room
or school within the board's jurisdiction. The request must be directed to the
Minister of Education, be in writing and contain the reasons therefor. The
Minister, upon application, is given a discretion to grant the exemption sought
by the board. Section 28(15) is silent in respect of the basis upon which the
ministerial discretion may be exercised.

In summary, the regulation provides for specified periods of instruction in
religious education each week in the public school system. The instruction is
to be given by teachers or board-approved surrogates. It would seem to follow
that, prima facie, pupils are required to receive such instruction as is given.
Exemption from such instruction is given to pupils upon application therefor to
the school principal by the parent or pupil, if adult. The statute does not
require the articulation of grounds. In other words, pupils are required to
take instruction in religious education offered by a board through its teachers
or approved surrogates unless exempted therefrom. In light of what appears to
be the prima facie rule, the onus is on the pupil or his or her parents to
initiate, by application, the exemption procedure provided for in the
regulation. Equally, the statutory requirement that instruction in religious
education be given by the teacher would appear to impose upon each teacher the
correlative obligation or duty to give such instruction. Exemption is provided
upon notice therefore given by the teacher to the board. To put the matter
somewhat differently, teachers are required to give instruction in religious
education unless exempted therefrom. Finally, it would appear to be the prima
facie obligation of a board to provide, through its teachers or approved
surrogates, the requisite periods of instruction in religious education to its
non-exempt pupils. The board may only be relieved of its statutory obligation
by ministerial exemption initiated by the board's own request.

II THE APPLICATION

1. INTRODUCTION

It will be recalled that by this application for judicial review the several
applicants seek declaratory and injunctive relief. It is not asserted that the
enabling legislation, ss. 50(1) and 10(1), para. 18 of the Education Act, are
constitutionally infirm. It is submitted, however, that s. 28 of Reg. 262, as
amended, as well as the curriculum adopted by the respondent Board in the
discharge of its responsibilities in accordance therewith, are not
constitutionally sustainable on account of their infringement or denial of
rights and freedoms enshrined in the
Charter
. It is, accordingly, essential to
first examine the legislative background of the impugned Regulation and the
substance of the curriculum offered by the respondent Board thereunder.

2. THE LEGISLATIVE BACKGROUND

(1) Introduction

A description of the legislative background of the impugned Regulation
requires a brief historical review of the enabling legislation as well as a
consideration of predecessor regulations.

(2) Early legislation and regulations

(a) The Act

The first statutory reference to religious instruction in the public schools
in what is now Ontario appeared in the School Act of 1843 ("Act for the
establishment and maintenance of Common Schools in Upper Canada", S.C.
1843, c. 29). Section 54 of the Act, a statute of the then Province of Canada,
provided as follows:

54. And be it enacted, that in the Common Schools
or Town or City Schools, established under this Act, no child shall be required
to read or study in or from any Religious Book, or to join in any exercise of
Devotion or Religion, which shall be objected to by his or her Parents or
Guardians.

It may be observed that the reference there contained is enacted as a
statutory exemption. The section exempts school children upon the basis of
parental objection from what would apparently be otherwise required of them,
namely, that they "read or study in or from any Religious Book, or ...
join in any exercise of Devotion or Religion". Neither "religious
education" nor "instruction in religious education" is mentioned
in the section, but the very fact of the exemption, as well as its nature,
conduces to no rational conclusion other than that some form of religious
education or instruction was included in the school curriculum.

It would appear that by 1850 provincial legislation expressly recognized the
right of pupils to receive religious instruction in the schools. By s. 14 of
"Act for the better establishment and maintenance of Common Schools in Upper
Canada", S.C. 1850, c. 48, it was enacted as follows:

14. ... nor shall any pupil in any such School be
required to read or study in or from any religious book, or join in any
exercise of devotion or religion, which shall be objected to by his or her parents
or guardians: Provided always, that within this limitation, pupils shall be
allowed to receive such religious instruction as their parents and guardians
shall desire, according to the general regulations which shall be provided
according to law.

It may be observed that irrespective of whether the legislation explicitly
recognized the right of pupils in the public schools to receive religious
instruction, exemption from such instruction or exercises was always available
upon parental objection. It would seem to follow that, absent objection and,
thereby, exemption, pupils would be allowed to receive and, in every event, be
given religious instruction.

The absence of any attack upon the constitutional integrity of the
provisions of ss. 50 and 10(1), para. 18 of the Education Act, renders it
unnecessary to trace the intervening statutory history of the present
provisions. It will suffice to here record that the present provisions, enacted
by S.O. 1974, c. 109, fairly represent the approach of the legislature to
religious instruction in the public schools. The Act allows religious
instruction to be given to such extent as the parent, guardian or adult pupil
desires. It is only to such extent that pupils shall receive religious
instruction. The manner in which the instruction is to be given, including what
shall be taught, by whom and when, is left to regulations passed pursuant to s.
10(1), para. 18 of the Act. The regulations also provide for exemptions for
pupils, teachers and boards from obligations otherwise imposed under the Act or
regulations passed pursuant thereto.

(b) The regulations

The legislative background of the regulations respecting religious exercises
and instruction in the province may conveniently commence with a reference to
s. 13 of the General Regulations, Public and Separate Schools, issued by the
Minister of Education in 1924. In addition to opening and closing religious
exercises, the regulations made express provision for religious instruction to
be given by members of the clergy. Section 13(3) provided as follows:

13(3)(a)(i) A clergyman of any denomination shall
have the right, and it shall be lawful for the Board to allow him, to give
religious instruction to the pupils of his own denomination, in each school
house, at least once a week, before the hour of opening the school in the
morning or after the hour of closing the school in the afternoon as the Board
may determine.

(ii) Under the same conditions, a clergyman,
selected by the clergymen of any number of denominations, shall also have the
right to give religious instruction to the pupils belonging to such
denominations.

(b) If the clergyman of more than one
denomination apply to give religious instruction in the same school-house where
the number of classrooms is insufficient for all at the same time, the Board
shall decide on what day of the week a class room shall be at the disposal of
each, at the time above stated.

A clear distinction appears to have been drawn in the regulation between
religious exercises and religious instruction. In respect of religious
exercises, the following provisions of s. 13(1) are apposite:

13(1)(a) Every Public School shall be opened with
the reading of the Scriptures and the repeating of the Lord's Prayer, and shall
be closed with the Lord's Prayer or the prayer authorized by the Department;
but no pupil shall be required to take part in any religious exercises objected
to by his parent or guardian.

(b) (i) In schools without suitable waiting-rooms
or other similar accommodation, if the parent or guardian demands the
withdrawal of a pupil while the religious exercises are being held, such demand
shall be complied with, and the reading of the Scriptures shall be deferred in
inclement weather until the closing.

(ii) To secure the observance of this regulation,
the teacher, before commencing a religious exercise, shall allow the necessary
interval to elapse, during which the children or wards of those who have
signified their objection thereto may retire.

(c) If the parent or guardian objects to his
child or ward taking part in the religious exercises, but directs that he shall
remain in the schoolroom during these religious exercises, the teacher shall
permit him to do so, provided that he maintains decorous behaviour during the
exercises.

(d) If, in virtue of his right to be absent from
the religious services, any pupil does not enter the schoolroom in the morning
till the close of the time allowed for religious exercises, such absence shall
not be treated as an offence against the rules of the school.

It should be here observed that under the regulation religious exercises
would appear to be mandatory but subject to exemption of the pupil and teacher.
Such exercises were to take place at the opening or closing of classes and were
generally to be conducted by the teacher. Religious instruction, on the other
hand, was to be given by a member of the clergy to pupils of his own
denomination or, by special designation, to those of other denominations,
outside regular school hours. Religious instruction was neither mandatory nor
given within regular school hours. It was given by a member of the clergy, not
by a teacher. No limitation was placed upon the content. The permissive nature
of the instruction rendered exemptions wholly superfluous. It would seem clear
that its purpose was purely sectarian.

It was not until 1944 that any material change occurred in the regulations
governing religious exercises and instruction in the public schools of Ontario.
In February, 1944, it was announced in the Speech from the Throne that
religious education would be offered in the province's public elementary and
secondary schools. In August of 1944, s. 13 of General Regulations, Public and
Separate Schools, 1939, was revoked and O. Reg. 30/44, substituted therefor.
The new regulation entitled, Religious Exercises and Religious Education in the
Public Schools, provided, as follows:

13(1)(a) Every public school shall be opened each
school day with religious exercises consisting of the reading of the Scriptures
and the repeating of the Lord's Prayer or other prayers approved for use in
schools.

(b) The Scripture passages, forming a part of the
religious exercises referred to in 1 (a), shall be read daily and
systematically at the opening of school and may be chosen from any list of
selections adopted by the Department for use in schools, or from any other list
approved by the Minister, as the Board by resolution may direct.

(c) If the Board does not pass the resolution
provided for in 1 (b) above, the principal shall make the selection after duly
notifying the Board of his intention, but such selection shall be subject to
revision by the Board at any time.

(d) The religious exercises held at the daily
opening of school may include the singing of one or more hymns authorized for
use in schools.

(2)(a) Subject to the regulations, two periods
per week of one-half hour each, in addition to the time assigned to religious
exercises at the opening of school, shall be devoted to Religious Education.

(b) Religious Education shall be given
immediately after the opening of school or immediately before the closing of
school in either the morning or the afternoon session.

(c) Instruction in Religious Education shall be
given by the teacher in accordance with the course of study authorized for that
purpose by the Department, and issues of a controversial or sectarian nature
shall be avoided.

(d) By resolution of the School Board, a
clergyman or clergymen of any denomination, or a lay person or lay persons selected
by the clergyman or clergymen, shall have the right, subject to the
regulations, to give Religious Instruction, in lieu of a teacher or teachers.

(e) If two or more clergymen of different
denominations, upon written application to the Board, secure permission to give
Religious Instruction, the principal of the School, by resolution of the Board,
shall arrange for such accommodation within the school and at such prescribed
times within the periods denoted above as shall be agreeable to both the principal
and the clergymen concerned.

(f) Where the number of rooms in the school is
insufficient to meet the needs of the groups organized for Religious
Instruction under 2 (d) and (e) above, the principal of the school, by
resolution of the Board, may arrange for additional accommodation elsewhere.

(3)(a) No pupil shall be required to take part in
any religious exercises or be subject to any instruction in Religious Education
to which objection is raised by his parent or guardian.

(b) In schools without suitable waiting-rooms or
other similar accommodation, if the parent or guardian applies to the principal
for the exemption of his child or ward from attendance while religious
exercises are being held or Religious Education given, such request shall be granted.

(c) If the parent or guardian objects to his
child or ward taking part in religious exercises or being subject to
instruction in Religious Education, but requests that he shall remain in the
schoolroom during the time devoted to such education, the teacher shall permit
him to do so provided he maintains decorous behaviour.

(d) If by virtue of his right to be absent from
religious exercises or instruction in Religious Education, any pupil is not
present in the classroom during such specified periods, his absence shall not
be considered a violation of the rules of the school.

(4) A teacher claiming exemption from the
teaching of Religious Education as prescribed by the regulations, shall notify
the Board to that effect in writing; and it shall then be the duty of the Board
to make such other provisions as may be necessary to implement the regulations
with respect to the teaching of the subject.

(5) The Minister may grant to a Board exemption
from the teaching of Religious Education in any classroom or school provided
the Board shall request in writing such exemption and shall submit reasons
therefor.

(6) The inspector shall each year bring to the
attention of the boards of trustees of his inspectorate the foregoing
regulations relating to religious exercises and Religious Education.

A number of significant changes were effected by the enactment of this
regulation. In the first place, it was provided by cl. 13(2)(a) that religious
education would be given in the public schools. It had earlier been provided in
the General Regulations, Public and Separate Schools, that religious exercises
were to be held at the opening and closing of school. Members of the clergy
were permitted to give religious instruction to pupils of their own or, by
designation, other denominations, but outside regular school hours. There had
not earlier been any general provision regarding religious education. Secondly,
the new regulation, to the extent there provided, made religious education
mandatory, viz., "subject to the regulations, two periods per week of one-
half hour each ... shall be devoted to Religious Education". The
antecedent regulations, as earlier observed, had made no reference to religious
education, a fortiori, to mandatory religious education. In addition, the mandatory
religious education introduced by O. Reg. 30/44, was to be taught twice weekly
during school hours in defined periods of time. The earlier religious
instruction by members of the clergy was only offered to actual or designated
constituents outside regular school hours. Fourthly, the new regulation
required that instruction in religious education be given by the teacher. It
had, of course, earlier been provided that religious instruction be given by
the clergy to their adherents.

The new regulation, to some extent at least, designated the subject-matter
of religious education. The content of the course of study was as
"authorized for that purpose by the Department". It was further made
mandatory that "issues of a controversial or sectarian nature shall be
avoided". By comparison, it may be recalled that under the predecessor
General Regulations, there was neither a prescribed course of study nor
injunction against discussion of controversial or sectarian issues. It would
seem to follow that under O. Reg. 30/44, and more particularly cl. 13(2)(c)
thereof, what was to be given as religious education was a prescribed course of
study which avoided issues of a sectarian or controversial nature.

It will be recalled that under the General Regulations in force prior to the
proclamation of O. Reg. 30/44, it was permissible for pupils, as well as
teachers, to seek exemption from participation in religious exercises. In each
case the fact of objection determined the issue: the pupil or the teacher, upon
objection, was not obliged to participate. O. Reg. 30/44 not only retained the
rights of pupils and teachers to claim and be granted exemption from
participation in religious exercises, but expanded or enlarged such rights to
include exemption from the newly mandated religious education. Further, it was
provided that a ministerial exemption from the teaching of religious education
in any class-room or school could be given upon application in writing therefor
by a board accompanied by supporting reasons. It would seem logically to follow
that a ministerial exemption from the teaching of religious education could
extend to each and every school administered by any local or county board.

Two final observations are appropriate concerning the obligation of a board in
the event of a teacher claiming an exemption from the teaching of religious
education and its authority to have persons other than teachers give
"religious instruction". Upon receipt of a claim for exemption by a
teacher, a board is obliged by the regulation to "make such other
provision as may be necessary to implement the Regulations with respect to the
teaching of the subject [religious education]". It would appear, for
example, to be permissible for a board to engage the services of another
teacher for such purpose. Further, it would appear equally open to a board, by
resolution, to engage a member of the clergy or lay person selected by such a
member "to give Religious Instruction, in lieu of a teacher or
teachers". It will be observed that cl. 13(2)(d) refers to "Religious
Instruction" rather than "Religious Education" or
"Instruction in Religious Education" as used elsewhere in the
regulation. A review of the whole of the regulation satisfies me, however, that
what is there described as "Religious Instruction" is the self-same
subject as "Instruction in Religious Education" and "Religious
Education" as used elsewhere in the regulation. It should also be pointed
out that the instruction given by the surrogates is expressly made
"subject to the regulations". In my respectful view, such requirement
imposes an obligation upon the surrogates equally to avoid issues of a
controversial or sectarian nature and to instruct in accordance with the
authorized course of study.

In summary, O. Reg. 30/44, for the first time, made instruction in religious
education a part of the public school curriculum in Ontario. As a general rule,
it was the obligation of a board to provide for, a teacher to give, and a
public school pupil to receive, instruction in religious education. Any or all
of the participants, upon objection, would or, in the case of a board, could be
exempted from their obligations under the regulation. The course of study was
as authorized by the Department of Education. Excluded from the course of study,
however, were issues of controversial or sectarian nature.

Instruction in the authorized course of study was assisted by the production
of a series of guides for teacher use in Grades I to VI. The guides, a revision
for use in Ontario of a series of guide books successfully used in England and
known as the Surrey Guides, were recommended to the department by the Inter-
Church Committee on Weekday Religious Education. Before publication the revised
guides were submitted to the committee and representatives of other religious
bodies.

(3) The intervening years

(a) Introduction

Since the proclamation of O. Reg. 30/44, there have been at least two
occasions upon which a commission or committee has reported to the Government
of Ontario concerning the state of religious education in the province's public
schools. It is appropriate at this juncture briefly to recall the observations
and recommendations of those bodies.

(b) The Royal Commission on Education in Ontario

By Order in Council under date of March 21, 1945, a number of commissioners
were appointed

... to inquire into and report upon the
provincial education system and, without derogating from the generality
thereof, including courses of study, text books, examinations, financing, and
the general system and scheme of elementary and secondary schools involving
public schools, separate schools, continuation schools, high schools,
collegiate institutes, vocational schools, schools for the training of teachers
and all other schools under the jurisdiction of the Department of Education, as
well as the selection and training of teachers, inspectors, and other officials
of such schools, and the system of provincial and local school administration.

The commission is generally described as the Royal Commission on Education
or, as it shall be here designated, "the Hope Commission" after its
chairman, the Honourable Mr. Justice Hope.

On December 15, 1950, the Hope Commission submitted its report to the
Lieutenant-Governor. In its chapter on "Aims of Education", the
Commission recorded the following views about "cardinal virtues":

15. There are two virtues about which there can
be no question -- honesty, and Christian love. They reflect the intellectual
and religious heritage of Western Civilization. Honesty means truthfulness and
fair dealing, which are the very foundations of freedom. Christian love means
kindness and consideration for others, which are mandatory by the Golden Rule.
Honesty and love must be taught by precept and even more by example, as
absolute rights, or eternal verities, which everyone must accept, defend, and
strive to practise. To insist on their acceptance will do no violence to the
conscience of any child or parent. No earnest Christian or Jew, or sincere
adherent of any other enduring faith or philosophy of intelligence and good
will, could have conscientious scruples regarding these two virtues. They may
be taught whole-heartedly and without reservation.

16. Without honesty, society disintegrates. Fair
dealing is the indispensable basis of community life. Truthfulness and respect
for truth, no less than free access to truth, are essential to the operation of
democracy and to the safeguarding of democracy against false doctrines which
may threaten to overthrow it. Without love of our fellow-men life is not worth
living. There is need for more consideration toward those with whom we come
into immediate contact, and need for more consideration towards those who will
be affected less directly but no less surely by our beliefs and our practices. There
is a warning to the world in the recent spread of ideologies under which
kindness is weakness and pity is evidence of guilt. For the preservation of our
society the school must teach honesty and Christian love.

17. But the school must not be content with
theory. It must teach honesty and love in practice, and thus educate for
service to one's fellow-men, to one's country, and to God. As the pupil
recognizes the obligation to be honest, he must give value in his work and in
every transaction. Because he recognizes the obligation of love, he must seek
to translate it into action. Whether in relation to one other person, to
several persons, or to all -- whether at home, at school, in business, or as a
citizen -- he must fulfil this dual obligation to the best of his ability. In
his education, the school must help him not only to understand and to accept
these obligations, but also to acquire the disposition, the will, and the
ability, to live daily by the application of this divine precept.

18. In teaching these universal values the school
cannot work alone. The enemy of honesty and love in action is the ubiquitous
demon named selfishness. The church, in particular, must build and continuously
strengthen the spiritual foundations of the basic virtues. The home must
provide security for their growth in understanding and practice. School, home,
and church should stand together to counteract more effectively those
influences in society which offer rewards for selfishness. Gradually, the whole
social environment of future generations may then, perceptibly improve as an
educative agency [pp. 27-28].

. . . . .

19. Honesty and Christian love are the absolutes
of a free society. They may therefore be taught by the strongest means at the
school's command -- an explicit acceptance that they are right. If this be
indoctrination we accept the stricture [p. 29].

The Commission then articulated certain aims for the schools of Ontario:

40. In the light of all this discussion, we may
now, as promised earlier in the chapter, set forth certain specific aims for
our schools. These are not separate and distinct, but interrelated. Our
introductory discussion is a necessary prelude to them because we believe that
no question relating to the aims of education admits of an answer without a
reference to ultimate convictions about human nature and human destiny, and
about society and the individual and the fundamental relationship between the
two. We believe the aims of education should include the following:

A. To develop capacity to apprehend and practise
basic virtues.

B. To develop the power to think clearly,
independently, and courageously.

C. To develop talent to understand the views of
others and to express one's views effectively.

D. To develop competence for a suitable occupation.

E. To develop good health.

F. To develop aptitudes for recreation.

G. To develop characteristics for happy family relations.

H. To develop good citizenship.

I. To develop the concept that education is a continuing
process beyond the school.

The report described in greater detail its aim of development in pupils of a
capacity to apprehend and practise basic virtues:

41. We reiterate that the two essential allies of
the school in this regard are the home and the church. By precept and by
example gifted teachers can engender in their pupils certain immutable values
accepted, and indeed won, by mankind as the expression of his highest ideals in
terms of beauty, truth, and goodness. Mankind has found in the practice of
these ideals the deepest satisfaction as he seeks to serve his fellow-men, his
country, and his God. The importance of the individual and the significance of
his obligations, which form part of our spiritual heritage, are the foundations
of our democratic society. The meaning of life is made manifest in adherence
and obedience to ideals that lie outside oneself and that transcend one's
personal interests. Inspiration and aspiration are never self-centred. Without
proclaiming any creed or doctrine we know that in our democracy the Christian
ideals personified and exemplified by Jesus have an appeal to all persons of
good will, and are the surest common ground for an educational programme
related to the pupil as a person. The attitude of Jesus toward children, His
understanding of human nature and behaviour, His charity and loving kindness
toward all men, form a perfect model for a true democracy in the classroom, the
community, and the nation [p. 37].

A chapter of the report of the Hope Commission specifically examined the
"social, spiritual and other aspects of education". The Commission
observed that there had been relatively little change take place over the past
century in the statutes or regulations relating to religious instruction in the
public schools of the province. In respect of the then recent proclamation of
O. Reg. 30/44, the Commission observed:

4. It is evident that the spirit of the original
statutes still pervades the Acts and regulations regarding religious
instruction in our schools. In September, 1944, revised regulations made
provision for religious education as a subject of instruction in public
elementary schools, and the following excerpts from these indicate the policy
of the Department of Education. They ensure:

(1) That the programme of studies in religious
education for public elementary schools will be non-sectarian and
undenominational:

Instruction in Religious Education shall be given
by the teacher in accordance with the course of study authorized for that
purpose by the Department, and issues of a controversial or sectarian nature
shall be avoided.

(2) That religious freedom of the individual will
be guaranteed:

No pupil shall be required to take part in any
religious exercises or be subject to any instruction in Religious Education to
which objection is raised by his parent or guardian.

A teacher claiming exemption from the teaching of
Religious Education as prescribed by the regulations, shall notify the Board to
that effect in writing; and it shall then be the duty of the Board to make such
other provision as may be necessary to implement the regulation with respect to
the teaching of the subject.

The Minister may grant to a Board exemption from
the teaching of Religious Education in any classroom or school provided the
Board shall request in writing such exemption and shall submit reasons therefor
[p. 124].

The changes effected by the regulations were described as "... fewer
... than is commonly supposed":

7. ... The major changes were brought about by
the provisions for specific instructions in religious education during school
hours and for affording the clergy an opportunity to give instruction in
religious education at such time [p. 125].

The report concluded upon this aspect of the matter with a description of
the then existing state of religious education and its recommendations for
future religious instruction in the public schools:

8. The prescribed course of study for religious
education has met with general acceptance, although strong objections were
raised by certain Presbyterian ministers, certain Baptist ministers, and some
members of the Jewish faith. The objections, in the main, centred around the
possibility of interference by the state in matters of conscience.

9. The Bible is the only textbook for the subject
of religious education. There are strong reasons for valuing the authorized
version, based on tradition and literary appreciation, but it is written in
sixteenth-century English and the language is a serious obstacle to
understanding on the part of pupils in the elementary school.

10. The course in religious education is designed
to ensure that all children will have an opportunity to receive religious
instruction and become more familiar with the Scriptures. But pupils may be
exempted from such instruction if objections are raised by a parent or
guardian, or by the board of trustees as representatives of the community. In
the school year 1944-45, with 5,405 public school boards of trustees operating
in the province, only 63 requested exemption from the teaching of religious
education in classes or schools under their jurisdiction. The figures for the
three following years were as follows: 1945-46, 37; 1946-47, 35; 1947-48, 46.
Of the 46 boards of trustees which asked for exemption in 1947-48, 7 were urban
with jurisdiction over 143 classes and 4,094 pupils, and 39 were rural with
jurisdiction over 199 public school classes and 5,273 pupils. The schools
concerned were widely distributed over the province. In 40 of the 46 cases the
request originated in centres having several religious denominations, including
Roman Catholic. In one case, reference was made to a "large number of
Jewish children". In 21 of the 46 cases exemption had been claimed in the
preceding school year.

11. Evidence submitted to us has demonstrated
that, if our aims in education are to be achieved, religious education should
be included as a subject of study in the curriculum of the proposed public
elementary schools. The present regulations relating to religious education in
public schools seem to be eminently satisfactory. Accordingly we recommend

(a) that religious exercises continue to be
conducted and religious education continue to be a subject of instruction in
public elementary schools;

(b) that the present regulations relating to
religious exercises and religious education in public schools be continued;

(c) that in any revision of the guide books in
religious education careful consideration be given to specific items raised by
the Canadian Jewish Congress in Brief 46, Appendix I;

(d) that consideration be given to the advisability
of granting approval for the use of children's Bible stories containing such
parts of the Scriptures as may be especially suitable for elementary school
pupils;

(e) that the Department of Education seek the
co-operation of The Inter-Church Committee on Weekday Religious Education in
the preparation of a list of daily Scripture readings, based directly on the
course of study for religious education, or use in the senior division of the elementary
school;

(f) that provision be made in the programmes of
junior colleges of education and in the elementary school option of the Ontario
College of Education for instruction in methods of conducting religious
exercises and of teaching religious education in public elementary schools [pp.
125-27].

The Commission recommended that the injunction against the display of
religious emblems of a denominational nature be continued in secondary schools
and expanded to include elementary schools. In this respect, the report
concluded:

15. Section 24 of the Regulations for High
Schools and Collegiate Institutes reads as follows: "No religious emblem
of a denominational nature shall be exhibited in a high school during school
hours." Similar regulations are in effect for other secondary schools,
and, up to 1944, were effective for public schools. In our opinion, some
regulation of this kind is essential in all publicly supported schools. We
therefore recommend

that regulations be drafted to ensure

(i) that religious emblems of a denominational
nature be not exhibited in any public elementary school, secondary school,
junior college, or provincial educational institution during school hours,
except in a room used for religious instruction by a clergyman, or a
representative designated by him, to adherents of his own denomination, and
then only during the periods alloted to such instructions;

(ii) that a religious habit be not permitted to
be worn by a teacher employed in any public elementary school, secondary
school, junior college, or provincial educational institution while discharging
his official duties, except by a teacher in training while engaged in his
programme of training [pp. 128-9].

(c) The committee on religious education in the
public schools

It would appear that there continued to be some opposition to the programme
in religious education in the public schools of Ontario. By Order in Council
dated January 27, 1966, which recited a need for evaluation of the programme of
religious education in the public schools in light of experience and then
present requirements, a committee on religious education in the public schools
was appointed:

... to examine and evaluate the present program;
to receive representations from all interested bodies about the effectiveness
and desirability of the program; to consider suggestions for changes and
improvement; to study means by which character building, ethics, social
attitudes and moral values and principles may best be instilled in the young;
to consider the responsibility of the Public Schools in these matters; and to
make recommendations thereon for the information and consideration of the
Minister [of Education].

On February 3, 1969, the committee, chaired by the Honourable J. Keiller
Mackay (the Mackay Committee), submitted its report to the then Minister of
Education, the Honourable William G. Davis.

The Committee presaged its discussion of the historical background of
religious instruction in Ontario with the following observation:

It is possible to say with some truth that
religious instruction has always been present in the public schools of Ontario
and also that it had not been present until 1944. So ambiguous has the
situation been that any statement about it depends on definition of terms and
on the speaker's angle of vision. To one shade of opinion the schools may
appear always to have been steeped in religious feeling and to another to have
been unswervingly secular throughout their history.

Again, it is often said that in the early years
of the province school populations were homogeneous in character and therefore
no conflict over religious matters occurred. In fact, this was never the case,
for from the beginning the Church of England aspirations of many settlers from
the United Kingdom conflicted with the Methodist ideas of many settlers from
the United States.

In its appraisal of the then existing course in religious education offered
in Ontario's public schools, the Mackay Committee concluded:

This material, much of which is definitely
Christian and Protestant in content, is in our opinion a vehicle leading to
religious commitment rather than to true education. The Regulations and
Programme clearly states "that 'the schools of Ontario exist for the
purpose of preparing children to live in a democratic society which bases its
way of life upon the Christian ideal,' and further, that 'the school must seek
to lead the child to choose and accept as his own those ideals of conduct and
endeavour which a Christian and democratic society approves.' The teacher is
then counselled 'to bring home to the pupils as far as their capacity allows,
the fundamental principles of Christianity and their bearing on human life and
thought.' "

In accordance with these instructions, the
children of Ontario are exposed to Christian indoctrination throughout the
elementary grades. This indoctrination begins in the kindergarten where the
teacher finds readily available Christian Bible stories, hymns, and busy-work
materials adapted to young children, and it continues with more or less
intensity into the higher grades. The pressure becomes stonger at the Christmas
and Easter seasons, sometimes resulting in serious conflict in the minds of
children. The views expressed in their homes on religious matters may differ
from those stated by the teacher. To the youthful mind the authority of the
teacher is usually beyond question. Where does this leave the authority of the
parents? Confusion and distress is thus created in the minds of young children
loyal to both teacher and parents.

Christian doctrines are not only inculcated by
the present course, but it is implied that these truths are exclusive to
Christianity. The introduction to the Programme of Studies for Grades I to VI
states:

Religious teaching cannot be confined to separate
periods on the timetable. It will affect the teaching of all subjects, and the
wise teacher will be anxious, in the various departments of school activity, to
bring home to the pupils, as far as their capacity allows, the fundamental truths
of Christianity and their bearing on human life and thought.

Accordingly, pupils may be taught that all of the
high principles of morals and ethics on which our society is founded are
exclusive to Christianity. It is quite conceivable, therefore, that children
might leave grade 8 with the impression that the Ten Commandments and the
Golden Rule, for example, are solely Christian doctrines. This misapprehension
will not be discouarged in those schools where the classes are conducted by
some Protestant clergymen, or by teachers employed through Christian Bible
clubs.

Organized religions other than Christian are made
to appear alien and inferior in our present course of studies [pp. 21-2].

The Committee appreciated that some general knowledge of religion was
necessary to the development of a well-educated person:

We do, of course, recognize that a general
knowledge of religion is necessary to form a well-educated person. This,
however, does not mean that religious indoctrination should take place in the
public schools. We must distinguish between religion as a subject for study and
religion as a manifestation of faith. As a subject for study it will be
encountered naturally in all areas of the curriculum. When taught in a period
specifically set aside to achieve the aims of the present course, it is much
too likely to become an exercise in religious commitment.

Most children who enter the public schools of
Ontario have had some religious indoctrination, in the home, the church, the
temple, or synagogue. That indoctrination must be respected throughout their
public school careers. Some children have not been brought into touch with
religion in any form, in some cases through misfortune or neglect, but in
others by the deliberate choice of their parents. The public school system has
neither the obligation nor the right to try to inculcate religious faith in the
latter, nor has it the obligation or right to proselytize the former. The
rights of individual conscience must be respected. While obedience to the principles
of education requires the school to present for study by all of the children
the significant ideas, events, and personalities of different religions, this
need not become indoctrination [pp. 23-4].

The Mackay Committee also considered the role of exemptions as a means
whereby perceived indoctrination might be avoided. It concluded:

It has been suggested to the Committee by several
briefs that although the present course of study may appear to leave children
open to Protestant religious indoctrination, the provisions for exemption of
those whose parents object to the teaching offset the exposure. It is our view,
and we are supported by a number of other briefs, that this special treatment
is in itself discriminatory and should as far as possible be eliminated from
the public school system. Discrimination through exemption is felt equally by
those who find the course too secular to accord with their religious ideas and
by those who find it too sectarian. It is unfair, also, to teachers who are
unable to teach the course conscientiously and are accordingly either
embarrassed by having to secure exemption or are pressured into hypocritical
conformity. It is important to see clearly where the responsibility in this
situation lies: contrary to popular belief, discrimination is not the problem
of those who are discriminated against, but of the "smug majority"
who permit the practice, and who alone have the power to end it. The public
schools must surely be kept free of prejudices if society as a whole is to advance
towards their elimination. Every course or program in the public school should
be designed to be acceptable to all reasonable persons and, consequently, leave
no justification for requiring discriminatory exemptions [p. 24].

The Committee recommended that the then present course of study in religious
education be discontinued. It concluded as follows:

It is the conclusion of this Committee that the
present course of study in religious education in the elementary schools of
Ontario should be discontinued, and that the aims as set out in related
legislation, programs of studies, regulations, and guide books, should be
abandoned.

We take the view, notwithstanding, that it is an
essential function of the educational system to instil knowledge about religion,
as well as to develop the ideals, attitudes, and values derived from our
heritage, of which religion forms so great a part. The cultural advantages of
the study of world religions are self-evident. The Scriptures are the world's
great literary treasure. History, literature, art, and music cannot be
understood or appreciated without an adequate background of religious
knowledge. Equally important are the ethical values inherited from religion.

The present course of studies in religious
education has failed in its first obligation, teaching, because it is not
designed in accordance with modern principles of education. It does not provide
for the objective examination of evidence, nor stimulate the inquiring mind; it
does not teach children to think for themselves either about the facts of
religion or about ethical matters. Instead, it presents Bible stories and
religious ideas which may have little relation to the daily life of children,
and it sometimes does so in terms that are offensive to many.

We believe that it is possible to build a sound
program which will furnish young people with adequate knowledge of world
religions. In the course of this program, they can be made aware, for example,
that most people in our society believe in a religious interpretation of life
which involves the existence of God as a transcendental power. At the same
time, they may recognize, without prejudice, that there are people for whom
this interpretation is not valid. And we believe that there are ways of
encouraging the development in young people in public schools of high standards
of character, ethical ideals, and an understanding of moral values, without
trespassing on the personal religious beliefs which they have learned at home
or in their separate places of worship [pp. 27-8].

It is common ground that the recommendations of the Mackay Committee were
not adopted by the Government of Ontario.
