3. THE CURRICULUM OF THE RESPONDENT BOARD

(1) Introduction

The public school system administered by the respondent Board operates 25
elementary schools whose 8,100 pupils are drawn from the nearly 70,000
inhabitants of the county. According to the 1981 Canadian census, in excess of
90% of Elgin County's residents are of Christian background.

It is common ground that for many years the respondent Board has offered
instruction in religious education in the class- rooms of its elementary
schools. It is further acknowledged by the respondent Board that, at least
until recently, its curriculum in religious education was exclusively Christian
in focus, thereby a reflection of the high proportion of Christian residents
within the county in which the schools are located. The impeachment by the
present application of the curriculum of the respondent Board necessitates a
brief examination of the applicable curriculum, as well as its antecedents.

(2) The early curriculum: 1974-1978

In 1974 the respondent Board approved the continuation of a religious
education programme in its elementary schools. The curriculum was prepared by
the Board's committee on religious education which consisted of three board
trustees, representatives of the local ministerial association, the Elgin
County Bible Club, the elementary principals' association and the
Superintendent of Education. It would appear that between 1974 and 1978 two
subcommittees of the religious education committee, the theological and
pedagogical committees, developed a comprehensive religious education
curriculum for use in all grades of the elementary schools. The lessons
developed for each grade, from kindergarten to grade eight, were based upon
passages from the Old and New Testament of the Bible. The programme was
designed to provide pupils with a context, primarily Christian, within which to
develop appropriate responses to life's situations. Board policy authorized
class-room teachers, ordained ministers of any denomination, and teachers
assigned by the Elgin County Bible Club to teach religious education in the
Board's schools, subject to the approval of the principal and the respective
Superintendent of Education. It would appear, however, that such instruction
was, in fact, given by lay volunteers, members of the Elgin County Bible Club.
The policy also permitted exemption of a pupil from religious education classes
upon the written request of a parent. The respondent Board approved this
curriculum for its elementary schools in 1978.

(3) The curriculum revisions: 1983-1987

It would appear that in 1983 the then Superintendent of Education for the
respondent Board set up a committee to undertake a revision of the Board's
curriculum in religious education. In the fall of 1984, the theological
committee of the ministerial association of Elgin County and a pedagogical
committee of interested teachers from the staffs of the Elgin County elementary
schools commenced to rewrite the curriculum in religious education to be used
in the elementary schools operated by the respondent Board. The objectives for
the teaching of religious education were described by the joint committee, as
follows:

The objective of the religious education program
in the schools of Elgin County would be to provide pupils with a religious
context, primarily Christian in which to develop appropriate responses to
life's situations.

It should not be assumed by a statement of this
objective that other religious bodies and even non-religious interests are to
be ignored. Rather, it is hoped that moral, ethical, and religious concerns
which they hold in common with Christianity will be the primary content of any
religious education program in the public schools. As such groups become more
numerous in proportion to the population, this objective should be reviewed in
the light of their concerns.

Amongst the criteria for the teaching of religious education in the
elementary schools of Elgin County, the joint committee included the following:

(2) An open approach should be used in
controversial areas, as recommended by the Theological Committee.

(3) The approach should recognize the
possibilities and values of other beliefs, respecting as well the concerns of
agnostic pupils.

(4) Every attempt should be made to correlate
concepts presented in religious education classes with the other subjects of
the curriculum.

By the fall of 1985 a revised curriculum in religious education in the
primary and junior grades of the public elementary schools in Elgin County had
been prepared and awaited Board approval. A new board of trustees elected in
November, 1985, determined, however, that a more extensive review of the religious
education programme should be undertaken. This review, which encompassed
consideration of the obligations cast upon the Board under the Education Act,
the composition of the voluntary teaching staff, the curriculum in religious
education followed in neighbouring counties and the revisions proposed in Board
policy, commenced in early 1986. The review process was suspended when the
C.C.L.A. commenced the present proceedings.

In June, 1986, the respondent Board, by resolution, determined to continue
to offer religious education in its elementary schools. It decided to establish
a special committee which would invite written submissions and briefs and could
receive oral representations from interested individuals and groups concerning
the development of a revised policy on religious education in the Board's
schools. The new policy was to reflect the social and cultural nature of the
county. The committee undertook to recommend its revised religious education
policy to the Board by the end of 1986.

In accordance with the mandate given it by the respondent Board, the special
committee directed the Superintendent of Education, Sandra Westaway, to
develop, plan and prepare material for the teaching of religious education
during the 1986-87 academic year. In the summer of 1986, Mrs. Westaway
commenced preparation of materials and the development of a plan for
instruction in religious education for the following year. She drew heavily
upon materials prepared by the Quebec Ministry of Education and edited lessons
prepared by the Board's own revision committee between 1984 and 1986. The
respondent Board, by the placement of advertisements in local newspapers,
itself solicited submissions on revisions to the religious education programme.
Several thousand residents responded. Forty-five persons forwarded extensive
written submissions. Only three of the written submissions criticized the Board
or opposed its then existing programme. The authors of written briefs or

5. THE EXEMPTIONS

(1) Introduction

A critical aspect of the present application fastens upon the effect of the
exemption clause of s. 28(10) of Reg. 262, as amended. The subsection, it may
be recalled, provides, as follows:

28(10) No pupil shall be required to take part in
any religious exercises or be subject to any instruction in religious education
where a parent of the pupil, or the pupil where the pupil is an adult, applies
to the principal of the school that the pupil attends for exemption of the
pupil therefrom.

Not only the respondents, but equally, the applicants, attach especial
significance to the exemption in their submissions in support of or in
opposition to the constitutionality of the Regulation. It is necessary to
briefly review the evidence bearing upon the impact or perceived impact of the
exemption.

(2) The applicants' perception

James and Nancy Millington carefully considered invoking the exemption
mechanism of the Regulation and discussed its operation with their daughter,
Andrea. The pupil was already very sensitive about the fact that her religious
beliefs differed from those of her teacher and class-mates. The Millingtons
felt that exemption would ostracize Andrea and embarrass her with her
class-mates. Andrea herself was worried about teasing from her peers and became
upset at the suggestion of the exemption. She said, "Please don't make me
sit in the hall." Mr. and Mrs. Millington, accordingly, resolved not to
seek an exemption for Andrea. Andrea also demurred to the suggestion that she
speak out in class, thereby disclosing her own ideas to her class-mates. She
was concerned that her teacher, Mr. Plum, would become angry and fellow
students would tease her.

Elizabeth Sebestyen found the option of requesting an exemption equally
unacceptable on account of her fear that her children would be socially ostracized
by their class-mates. The Sebestyen family lives in a small, rural community
where, it is said, the children have few opportunities outside school to
establish social relationships. She wished her children to have the opportunity
in the primary grades to learn to get along and feel compatible with their
peers. It was the opinion of Mrs. Sebestyen that there was a stigma attached to
exclusion from the class-room, namely, punishment. Despite her misgivings as to
the nature and content of the curriculum, Mrs. Sebestyen did not request
exemption. She determined to explain her own religious beliefs, to teach morals
and to describe the basic teachings of the other religions of the world at
home.

(3) The Board's position

The respondent Board has plainly recognized that, in accordance with s.
50(2) of the Act and s. 28(10) of the Regulation, parents are entitled to
request exemption for their children from the religious education programme. In
the 1986-87 school year 124 pupils were exempted from the programme. No request
for exemption has been refused by the Board. It will be recalled that there are
8,100 public elementary school pupils in the county.

It is the present practice of the Board to inform parents in the parents'
handbook of the right to seek exemption by notice in writing to the school
principal. Pupils exempted from instruction in religious education are
accommodated under supervision in the school library or, occasionally, in the
office. Upon parental request, a pupil may remain in the class- room engaged in
other lessons whilst instruction is given in religious education.

The excusal of students from the class-room for non- disciplinary purposes
is by no means indigenous to those who seek exemption from instruction in
religious education. In all but two of the Board's schools resource withdrawal
services are offered. Gifted, as well as educationally retarded children, leave
their class-room, singly or in small groups, to receive special education in
other parts of the school for periods of one-half to one hour per day.
Approximately 715 pupils, slightly fewer than six times the number exempted
from religious education classes, participate in resource withdrawal services.
Other children leave the class-room for matters such as speech pathology,
instruction in English as a second language, and, discussion of behavioural or
family problems with social workers.

(4) The expert evidence

(a) Introduction

The applicants and respondent Board have each filed the affidavit of a
psychologist. Each affiant there proferred his opinion of the effect, if any,
of exemption from instruction in religious education upon the pupil in respect
of whom such exemption is exercised. The opinions, as it might reasonably be
anticipated, differ.

(b) Dr. Jonathan Lewis Freedman

The applicants place reliance upon the opinions expressed in the affidavit
of Dr. Jonathan Lewis Freedman, a professor of psychology at the University of
Toronto. Dr. Freedman, whose academic qualifications and achievements are
impressive, expressed the opinion that children in whose public elementary
school class instruction in religious education is offered, are under great
pressure to remain in the class-room during such instruction. The pressure,
which is not alleviated by merely advising the children or their parents that
they are free to leave or not to participate, derives principally from two
sources, namely:

(i) the authority of the teacher and the school in which the instruction is
given, and

(ii) the rest of the class of which the pupil is a member.

It is the opinion of Dr. Freedman that, especially when the religion taught
is apparently that of the majority of members of the class, a child whose
religious beliefs differ will perceive school and teacher approval of the
instruction given and thereby find it difficult to resist the influence, hence
teachings, of this combined authority. No relief from the pressure thus
perceived is achieved upon telling the child of the exemption privilege as it
appears to the child that the authorities would plainly prefer him or her to
remain in the class-room. Some children may be sufficiently strong to resist
the pressure, but many will be unable to do so. Children in such circumstances
will suffer considerable conflict and stress. Some, if not most, will succumb
to the pressure to remain, notwithstanding their disagreement with the content
of the class and preference to be absent. The majority will recognize that the
authorities prefer participation rather than absence and fear characterization
as deviant for non- compliance. Participation offends either their own beliefs
or those of their parents. Non-participation incurs a risk of offence to the
teacher and perception as deviant by their peers. In Dr. Freedman's opinion, a
child who endures religious instruction against parental wishes or his or her
own inclination may, in fact, be more likely to be influenced by the teaching
than if not given the illusion of choice ab initio. Dr. Freedman concluded:

19. People who freely participate in an activity
or expose themselves to information that is discrepant from their own opinions,
tend to be affected more than those who did not think that they were free to
choose.

. . . . .

21. In summary, it is my opinion that children
whose religion is different from that being taught in the classroom are faced
with the following situation. They are told that they are free not to
participate. However, they feel pressure to conform and may experience conflict
and stress in connection with the decision. If they decide not to participate,
they feel deviant and worry about the consequences. If they decide to
participate, they feel conflict with their own religion and with the wishes of
their parents and this also causes stress and discomfort. Participation may, in
these circumstances, make them especially likely to be influenced by what they
hear.

(c) Dr. Donald Robert Kennedy

The respondent Board places reliance upon the opinion of Dr. Donald Robert
Kennedy, a registered psychologist and practitioner of educational, clinical
and consulting psychology. Dr. Kennedy's practical experience in education at
both the elementary and secondary school level is as impressive as are Dr.
Freedman's academic credentials. Dr. Kennedy does not share the view of Dr.
Freedman that pupils of a public elementary school class in which instruction
in religious education is given are under great pressure to remain in the
class-room during such instruction. According to Dr. Kennedy, individualized
student instruction, with its concomitant of pupil excusal from class, has
become a commonplace in the Ontario public school system. He exemplifies such
absence by reference to instruction in French immersion, enrichment or heritage
language programmes. Remedial instructions, speech lessons or psychological
consultation afford further instances of pupil excusal. A school day, of
necessity, entails student movement to and amongst various class settings. The
pressure to remain in a particular class-room for any given activity is largely
absent. Exemptions create no expectation of participation. Attendance for one
activity is expected of some, absence and participation of others.

Dr. Kennedy concluded, as follows:

15. In my experience, children in Ontario schools
do not perceive the choices of remaining in or leaving a classroom in the way
that Dr. Freedman suggests. First, the usual instruction to and the normal
practice of teachers in public schools is to mimimize the singling out of any
student, especially in a negative manner. Second, it is common practice in
schools to separate children for participation in different activities, as I
have noted above. These alternative activities are sometimes associated with
specific difficulties, sometimes with enrichment and sometimes simply as an
alternative for the students involved. Although any such exemption could be
construed negatively by an individual school staff member or by some children,
alternative activities in Ontario schools in themselves are the norm and are
not at all unusual. Specific exemptions, even in core subjects, are not
uncommon. There should be therefore little pressure to conform with respect to
any school activity that has not been assigned to a student involved. Within
individual children there could be some feelings of conflict around participation
in religious instruction classes just as there could be in connection to the
many other school activities in which they do or do not participate. In other
children, there would be no conflict at all.

16. Dr. Freedman, in paragraph 14 of his Affidavit,
suggests that children faced with an exemption from religious education class
"will suffer considerable conflict and stress". As indicated above, I
am of the opinion that the creation of peer pressure is not a normal or usual
result of exemption from any school activity. Nor, in my opinion, should
"peer pressure" or "conflict" be considered harmful except
in very extreme situations. Moderate levels of "pressure to conform"
and ''conflict" are part of the normal developmental process in children,
as well as in adults. In normal children such pressures or conflicts are most
likely to increase the child's arousal level and thereby strengthen the child's
learning process. In the context of participation or exemption from religious
education classes, in the normal child the result of such pressures or conflict
would be a strengthening of genuinely held convictions. In the abnormal child
problems could occur in relation to this or in relation to any other school or
non-school activity.

The practitioner added that the strengthening effect of peer pressure was
likely to be maximized with support for the pupil's own belief system amongst
his or her family, friends or class-mates. He pointed out that in modern
society some religious and cultural groups differentiate themselves and/or
their children, as for example by modes of dress, from the majority, thereby
encouraging and perpetuating their distinctive identities.

III THE CONSTITUTIONAL ISSUE

1. INTRODUCTION

The constitutional issues raised by the present application concern the
validity of s. 28 of Reg. 262, as amended, and the curriculum of the respondent
Board in accordance with which instruction in religious education is given to
public elementary school pupils in Elgin County. Each is said to be
constitutionally infirm, thereby inoperative, upon the same basis.

The issues which arise in respect of the constitutionality of the Regulation
may be separated out in the following manner, namely:

(a) Is s. 28 of Reg. 262, as amended, unconstitutional in whole or in part in
that in purpose or effect it infringes or denies the individual applicants
freedom of religion as guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
?

(b) Is s. 28 of Reg. 262, as amended, unconstitutional in whole or in part
in that in purpose or effect it infringes or denies the individual applicant's
right to the equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination
based upon religion as guaranteed by
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
?

(c) If the answer to either (a) or (b), supra, is in the affirmative, does
the infringement or denial constitute a reasonable limit prescribed by law of
such a nature as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society
and is it, accordingly, saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
?

(d) If the answer to (c), supra, is in the negative, what remedy is
appropriate and just in the circumstances?

Similar issues are raised in respect of the constitutionality of the
curriculum of the respondent Board, though their determination is overlaid by a

the words "any law" as they appear in
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution
Act, 1982
, such that it may be declared of no force or effect to the extent of
its inconsistency with the Charter.

(a)

(4) The position of the respondent Minister

. It follows, in the submission of Mr. Wright, that the impugned section

We recommend that the high duty of public

administered incidentally throughout the whole school spectrum. It will have as
its focus character building, ethics, social attitudes, and moral values and
principles.

We recommend that the acquisition of information
about and respect for all religions be recognized as an essential objective of
the educational system from kindergarten to grade 13. This should be achieved
by a program of incidental teaching and study, not through a formal syllabus.

optional courses in grades 11 and 12 in the secondary schools. Instruction in

On the other hand, it is the submission of the individual applicants that

the guise of religious education is, in fact, but indoctrination in
majoritarian Christian religious beliefs. The individual applicants actively
support the dissemination of information concerning the religions of the world
as an integral part of a course of study in religious education in the public
elementary shcools. What they find offensive and constitutionally impermissible

Religious education is at once constitutionally permissible and desirable for
the moral development of the child. Indoctrination in majoritarian Christian

3. THE APPROACH

(1) Introduction

It will be helpful at the outset to recall briefly the approach to be taken
when a law is impugned as being constitutionally infirm under the
Charter
.

It will be recalled that in Hunter v. Southam Inc.,
1984 CanLII 33 (SCC)
, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 145, 11
D.L.R. (4th) 641, 14 C.C.C. (3d) 97, 2 C.P.R. (3d) 1, Dickson J., as he then
was, emphasized on behalf of the court that the proper approach to the
interpretation of the
Charter
is a purposive one. Such a broad purposive
analysis interprets specific provisions of a constitutional document which
enumerate fundamental rights and freedoms in light of the larger objects of the
Constitution.

In R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321, 18
C.C.C. (3d) 385, Dickson J., as he then was (Beetz, McIntyre, Chouinard and
Lamer JJ. concurring), considered that both purpose and effect are relevant in
determining constitutionality. He held, as follows, at pp. 331-2 S.C.R., p. 350
D.L.R.:

In my view, both purpose and effect are relevant
in determining constitutionality; either an unconstitutional purpose or an unconstitutional
effect can invalidate legislation. All legislation is animated by an object the
Legislature intends to achieve. This object is realized through the impact
produced by the operation and application of the legislation. Purpose and
effect respectively, in the sense of the legislations' object and its ultimate
impact, are clearly linked, if not indivisible. Intended and actual effects
have often been looked to for guidance in assessing the legislation's object
and thus, its validity.

Moreover, consideration of the object of
legislation is vital if rights are to be fully protected. The assessment by the
courts of legislative purpose focuses scrutiny upon the aims and objectives of
the Legislature and ensures they are consonant with the guarantees enshrined in
the
Charter
. The declaration that certain objects lie outside the Legislature's
power checks governmental action at the first stage of unconstitutional
conduct. Further, it will provide more ready and more vigorous protection of
constitutional rights by obviating the individual litigant's need to prove
effects violative of Charter rights. It will also allow courts to dispose of
cases where the object is clearly improper, without inquiring into the
legislation's actual impact.

His Lordship added, at p. 334 S.C.R., pp. 351-2 D.L.R.:

In short, I agree with the respondent that the
legislation's purpose is the initial test of constitutional validity and its
effects are to be considered when the law under review has passed or, at least,
has purportedly passed the purpose test. If the legislation fails the purpose
test, there is no need to consider further its effects, since it has already
been demonstrated to be invalid. Thus, if a law with a valid purpose interferes
by its impact, with rights or freedoms, a litigant could still argue the
effects of the legislation as a means to defeat its applicability and possibly
its validity. In short, the effects test will only be necessary to defeat
legislation with a valid purpose; effects can never be relied upon to save
legislation with an invalid purpose.

The Supreme Court of Canada has, accordingly, laid it down that the test of
constitutional validity to be applied under the
Charter
engages a
consideration, not only of the legislative purpose which underlies the
enactment of a statute or regulation, but also of the effect or actual impact
of the law in respect of which the challenge is made. It is plain that either
an unconstitutional purpose or an unconstitutional effect may invalidate
legislation under the Charter.

In connection with legislative purpose as a determinant of
constitutionality, it is as well to here recall that legislative purpose is a
function of the intent of those who draught and enact the legislation, at the
time of its enactment, not at the time of the constitutional challenge or
impeachment. To state the matter in somewhat different language, legislative
purpose is a constant fixed upon enactment and ascertained by reference to
factors operative at that time. It is not a variable nor a chameleon, whose
purpose shifts or is transformed over time by changing social conditions.
Indeed, to so hold would render pronouncements upon constitutionality of the
quintessence of ephemerality and but encourage relitigation upon the slightest
scent of social change: see R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra, at pp. 334-6
S.C.R., pp. 352-3 D.L.R., per Dickson J.

It is self-evident that to be successful any allegation of constitutional
infringment must initially identify an enumerated
Charter
right or freedom said
to be and, thereafter, demonstrate the extent of its impairment or denial by
the legislation whose constitutionality is challenged. The content of the
enumerated Charter right or freedom becomes the standard against which the
constitutionality of the enactment is adjudged. In the case at bar, it will be
recalled, it is said that s. 28(4) to (16) of Reg. 262, as amended, and,
further, the curriculum of the respondent Board deny or infringe the individual
applicant's freedom of religion under
s. 2
(a), as well as their equality under
the law, and their right to the equal protection and benefit of the law without
discrimination based on religion under
s. 15(1)
of the Charter. It becomes
necessary at this juncture to ascertain the content and reach of the freedom
and right which are said to be here infringed.

(2) Freedom of religion

(a) Introduction

Section 2
of the
Charter
constitutes a guarantee to "every one" of
the "fundamental freedoms" therein enumerated, including freedom of
religion.

The "fundamental freedoms" enshrined in s. 2, however, like the
rights guaranteed elsewhere in the
Charter
, are not wholly without limitation
or qualification. Although the language in which the guarantee of freedom of
religion is expressed is itself unqualified, the provision is none the less
subject to the limitative effect placed upon all rights and freedoms by
s. 1
.
Any law which limits a
s. 2
fundamental freedom, as for example freedom of
religion, will none the less be valid under
s. 1
in the event that it constitutes
a reasonable limit which can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic
society. Further, the fundamental freedoms guaranteed under
s. 2
, including
freedom of religion, are expressly subject to the override clause,
s. 33
, of
the Charter.

It will be of assistance at this juncture to briefly examine the substance
or content of freedom of religion guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
whereby
to set the standard against which the constitutionality of the Regulation here
impugned may be adjudged.

(b) The substance of the guarantee

The decision in R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra, shall serve as a
convenient point of origin for discussion of the substance of the freedom of
religion guarantee enshrined in
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

Big M Drug Mart Ltd. was charged with unlawfully carrying on the sale of
goods contrary to s. 4 of the Lord's Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13. The accused
challenged the constitutionality of the Lord's Day Act, not only upon what
might be termed traditional division of power grounds, but also on account of
its alleged denial or infringement of the guarantee of freedom of conscience
and religion enacted by
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

At trial, the accused was acquitted on two grounds, that is to say,

(i) that the Lord's Day Act could no longer be constitutionally justified
upon the basis of the exercise of Parliament's criminal law power under Head 27
of
s. 91
of the
Constitution Act, 1867
; and,

(ii) that the Lord's Day Act infringed freedom of religion guaranteed by
s.
2(a)
of the
Charter
.

The Attorney-General of Alberta appealed the acquittal of Big M by way of
stated case to the Alberta Court of Appeal [
1983 CanLII 3630 (AB PC)
, [1983] 4 W.W.R. 54, 25 Alta. L.R.
(2d) 195, 5 C.R.R. 281]. The Alberta Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal
1983 ABCA 268 (CanLII)
, 5
D.L.R. (4d) 121, 9 C.C.C. (3d) 310, [1984] 1 W.W.R. 625.

The Attorney-General of Alberta took a further appeal to the Supreme Court
of Canada. In the constitutional questions stated by the court was the
following:

1. Does the Lord's Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13
and especially s. 4 thereof infringe upon the freedom of conscience and
religion guaranteed in
s. 2(a)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
?

The judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada was delivered by Dickson J., as
he then was. In prefatory remarks concerning freedom of religion, the present
Chief Justice observed, at pp. 336-7 S.C.R., pp. 353-4 D.L.R.:

A truly free society is one which can accommodate
a wide variety of beliefs, diversity of tastes and pursuits, customs and codes
of conduct. A free society is one which aims at equality with respect to the
enjoyment of fundamental freedoms and I say this without any reliance upon
s.
15
of the
Charter
. Freedom must surely be founded in respect for the inherent
dignity and the inviolable rights of the human person. The essence of the
concept of freedom of religion is the right to entertain such religious beliefs
as a person chooses, the right to declare religious beliefs openly and without
fear of hindrance or reprisal, and the right to manifest belief by worship and
practice or by teaching and dissemination. But the concept means more than
that.

Freedom can primarily be characterized by the
absence of coercion or constraint. If a person is compelled by the state or the
will of another to a course of action or inaction which he would not otherwise
have chosen, he is not acting of his own volition and he cannot be said to be
truly free. One of the major purposes of the
Charter
is to protect, within
reason, from compulsion or restraint. Coercion includes not only such blatant
forms of compulsion as direct commands to act or refrain from acting on pain of
sanction, coercion includes indirect forms of control which determine or limit
alternative courses of conduct available to others. Freedom in a broad sense
embraces both the absence of coercion and constraint, and the right to manifest
beliefs and practices. Freedom means that, subject to such limitations as are
necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals or the fundamental
rights and freedoms of others, no one is to be forced to act in a way contrary
to his beliefs or his conscience.

What may appear good and true to a majoritarian
religious group, or the state acting at their behest, may not, for religious
reasons, be imposed upon citizens who take a contrary view. The
Charter

safeguards religious minorities from the threat of "the tyranny of the
majority".

After concluding that the meaning of the concept of freedom of conscience
and religion could not be determined solely by the degree to which it was
enjoyed by Canadians prior to the proclamation of the
Charter
and, in
particular, under the Canadian Bill of Rights, Dickson J., as he then was, set
out the approach to be taken in defining the rights and freedoms governed by
the Charter. He wrote in this respect, at p. 344 S.C.R., pp. 359-60 D.L.R.:

This Court has already, in some measure, set out
the basic approach to be taken in interpreting the
Charter
. In Hunter et al. v.
Southam Inc. (decision rendered September 17, 1984) [since reported
1984 CanLII 33 (SCC)
, 14 C.C.C.
(3d) 97, 11 D.L.R. (4th) 641, [1984] 2 S.C.R. 145] this Court expressed the
view that the proper approach to the definition of the rights and freedoms
guaranteed by the Charter was a purposive one. The meaning of a right or
freedom guaranteed by the Charter was to be ascertained by an analysis of the
purpose of such a guarantee; it was to be understood, in other words, in the
light of the interests it was meant to protect.

In my view, this analysis is to be undertaken,
and the purpose of the right or freedom in question is to be sought by
reference to the character and the larger objects of the
Charter
itself, to the
language chosen to articulate the specific right or freedom, to the historical
origins of the concepts enshrined, and where applicable, to the meaning and
purpose of the other specific rights and freedoms with which it is associated
within the text of the Charter. The interpretation should be, as the judgment
in Southam emphasizes, a generous rather than a legalistic one, aimed at fulfilling
the purpose of the guarantee and securing for individuals the full benefit of
the Charter's protection. At the same time it is important not to overshoot the
actual purpose of the right or freedom in question, but to recall that the
Charter was not enacted in a vacuum, and must therefore, as this Court's
decision in Law Society of Upper Canada v. Skapinker (1984),
1984 CanLII 3 (SCC)
, 11 C.C.C. (3d)
481, 9 D.L.R.(4th) 161, [1984] 1 S.C.R. 357, illustrates, be placed in its
proper linguistic, philosophic and historical contexts.

The court next underscored the centrality of individual conscience and
judgment to our democratic political tradition and concluded, at pp. 346-7
S.C.R, pp. 361-2 D.L.R.:

Viewed in this context, the purpose of freedom of
conscience and religion becomes clear. The values that underlie our political
and philosophic traditions demand that every individual be free to hold and to
manifest whatever beliefs and opinions his or her conscience dictates,
provided, inter alia, only that such manifestations do not injure his or her
neighbours or their parallel rights to hold and manifest beliefs and opinions
of their own. Religious belief and practice are historically prototypical and,
in many ways, paradigmatic of conscientiously-held beliefs and manifestations
and are therefore protected by the
Charter
. Equally protected, and for the same
reasons, are expressions and manifestations of religious non-belief and
refusals to participate in religious practice. It may perhaps be that freedom
of conscience and religion extends beyond these principles to prohibit other
sorts of governmental involvement in matters having to do with religion. For
the present case it is sufficient in my opinion to say that whatever else
freedom of conscience and religion may mean, it must at the very least mean
this: government may not coerce individuals to affirm a specific religious
belief or to manifest a specific religious practice for a sectarian purpose. I
leave to another case the degree, if any, to which the government may, to
achieve a vital interest or objective, engage in coercive action which
s. 2
(a)
might otherwise prohibit.

There are but two further passages in the reasons of the present Chief
Justice that, for present purposes, it is necessary to excerpt. He observed, at
p. 347 S.C.R., p.362 D.L.R.:

The equality necessary to support religious
freedom does not require identical treatment of all religions. In fact, the
interests of true equality may well require differentiation in treatment.

At p. 349 S.C.R., pp. 363-4 D.L.R., Dickson J.concluded:

With the entrenchment of the
Charter
the
definition of freedom of conscience and religion is no longer vulnerable to
legislative incursion. I conclude therefore that a definition of freedom of
conscience and religion incorporating freedom from compulsory religious
observance is not only in accord with the purposes and traditions underlying
the Charter; it is also in line with the definition of that concept as found in
the Canadian jurisprudence.

The court held that the Lord's Day Act and, in particular, s. 4 thereof
infringed
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
in a manner which could not be demonstrably
justified in a free and democratic society under
s. 1
. The Act, to such an
extent, was declared to be of no force or effect.

In Jones v. The Queen,
1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 284, 31 D.L.R. (4th) 569, 28 C.C.C.
(3d) 513, the accused was charged with three counts of truancy on the part of
his three children, contrary to
s. 180(1)
of the
School Act, R.S.A. 1980, c.
S-3
. It was the position of the accused that the requirement that his children
attend public school, as well as the requirement that he apply for their
exemption therefrom, as provided for in the Act, contravened his freedom of
religion and deprived him of his liberty otherwise than in acccordance with the
principles of fundamental justice, contrary to
s. 2(a)
and
7
of the
Charter
.

At trial, the accused was acquitted upon the basis that a provision of the
Act, which required that proof of efficient instruction at home or elsewhere,
an excuse for non-attendance in the public schools, could only be established
by means of a certificate issued by an employee of the board, the Minister or
his designate, denied the accused the right to make full answer and defence
and, accordingly, was inimical to the principles of fundamental justice
guaranteed under
s. 7
of the
Charter
. The argument, based on an alleged
infringement of the accused's freedom of religion, failed. The Alberta Court of
Appeal entered convictions against the accused on all counts [
1984 ABCA 207 (CanLII)
, 10 D.L.R. (4th)
765, 13 C.C.C. (3d) 261, 57 A.R. 266]. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of
Canada was granted upon a single constitutional question, namely, at p. 324
S.C.R., pp. 586-7 D.L.R.:

Whether Sections 142, 143 and 180 of the School
Act,
R.S.A. 1980, c. 3
are inconsistent with
Section 2(a)
or
Section 7
of the

Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
and therefore of no force or effect to
the extent of the inconsistencies pursuant to
Section 52(1)
of the Constitution
Act, 1982?

The appeal was dismissed by a majority of the court (Dickson C.J.C., Beetz,
McIntyre, Le Dain and La Forest JJ.). Wilson J. dissented upon the basis that
s. 143(1) of the School Act violated the accused's right to liberty under
s. 7

of the
Charter
to such an extent that could not be preserved by
s. 1
.

It may be recalled that in Jones, supra, the relevant provisions of the
Alberta school legislation were impeached under both
ss. 2(a)
and
7
of the

Charter
. In respect of the constitutional challenge under
s. 2
(a), the majority
opinion was that of Wilson J., who dissented in respect of constitutionality
under
s. 7
. She was joined in her reasons in connection with freedom of
religion by Beetz, McIntyre and Le Dain JJ. The minority view upon the
constitutional impeachment under
s. 2
(a) was that of La Forest J., with whom
Dickson C.J.C. and Lamer J. concurred.

On behalf of the majority on the
s. 2
(a), freedom of religion, issue, Wilson
J. held that the compulsory attendance provisions of the School Act, taken as a
whole, do not infringe the appellant's freedom of conscience and religion. In
respect of the purpose of the legislation, Wilson J. observed at p. 313 S.C.R.,
p. 578, D.L.R.:

The purpose of the legislation, in my view, is to
ensure that children receive an adequate education, a purpose with which I
believe the appellant is in full agreement. There is surely no inherent
incompatibility between religious instruction and efficient instruction in
secular subjects.

A critical feature of the appellant's position that the legislation was
constitutionally defective on account of its infringement of the freedom of
religion guarantee of s. 2(a), was the submission that it placed an onus upon
him to seek an exemption for his children in order that they may be educated elsewhere
than in the public school system. Upon this issue Wilson J. reasoned, at pp.
313-4 S.C.R., p. 578 D.L.R.:

The appellant's real complaint, it seems to me,
is effects- based rather than purpose-based. It is the effect of the statutory
machinery for certification on his religious beliefs that he is concerned about
and he points to this court's decision in R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra, at
pp. 413-4 C.C.C., pp. 349-50 D.L.R., p. 331 S.C.R., as authority for the
proposition that legislation may be invalidated if its effect is to violate a
constitutional guarantee. However, even assuming that this legislation does
affect the appellant's beliefs, which for the reasons given I doubt, not every
effect of legislation on religious beliefs or practices is offensive to the
constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion.
Section 2
(a) does not require
the Legislature to refrain from imposing any burdens on the practice of
religion. Legislative or administrative action whose effect on religion is
trivial or insubstantial is not, in my view, a breach of freedom of religion. I
believe that this conclusion necessarily follows from the adoption of an
effects-based approach to the
Charter
.

She concluded, at
1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 284 at pp. 314-5, 31 D.L.R. (4th) 569 at p.
579:

To state that any legislation which has an effect
on religion, no matter how minimal, violates the religious guarantee
"would radically restrict the operating latitude of the legislature":
Braunfeld v. Brown at p. 606. It is, of course, clearly arguable that under our
constitution this kind of concern should be dealt with under s. 1 of our

Charter
rather than
s. 2
. However, as I stated in Operation Dismantle Inc. et
al. v. The Queen et al. (1985), 18 D.L.R.

(4th) 481 at p. 517,
1985 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441 at p. 489, 59 N.R. 1:

"The rights under the
Charter
not being
absolute, their content or scope must be discerned quite apart from any
limitation sought to be imposed upon them by the government under
s. 1
."

In my view, the appellant has failed to show any
substantial impact of this legislation on his belief that God and not the state
is the true source of authority over the education of his children. While the
School Act makes no express reference to divine authority, it defers to
parental authority by allowing home instruction and instruction in private
schools, thereby accommodating the state purpose to the preferences of
individual parents. It defers, in other words, to beliefs such as the
appellant's. It recognizes the very values for which the appellant contends. If
the statutory machinery has any impact at all on the appellant's freedom of
conscience and religion which, for the reasons I have given, I doubt, it is an
extremely formalistic and technical one. I do not believe, therefore, that it
gives rise to a violation of
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

The appeal was dismissed.

In Edwards Books & Art Ltd. v. The Queen,
1986 CanLII 12 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 713, 35 D.L.R.
(4th) 1, 30 C.C.C. (3d) 385, several appeals raising a common issue concerning
the constitutional validity (in both a division of powers and
Charter
sense),
of the Retail Business Holidays Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 453, were heard together.
The consolidated appeals were from a decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal
sub nom. R. v. Videoflicks Ltd.,
1984 CanLII 44 (ON CA)
, 48 O.R. (2d) 395, 14 D.L.R. (4th) 10, 15
C.C.C. (3d) 353, in which Tarnopolsky J.A., on behalf of the court, discussed
the Charter guarantee of freedom of religion in the following language, at pp.
420-1 O.R., pp. 35-7 D.L.R.:

What follows is in no way to be taken as an exhaustive
definition of the fundamental freedom of religion embodied in
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
. In my view, while it would certainly include the rights enunciated by
Ritchie J. in Robertson and Rosetanni, supra, that definition is too
restrictive. Freedom of religion goes beyond the ability to hold certain
beliefs without coercion and restraint and entails more than the ability to
profess those beliefs openly. In my view, freedom of religion also includes the
right to observe the essential practices demanded by the tenets of one's
religion and, in determining what those essential practices are in any given
case, the analysis must proceed not from the majority's perspective of the
concept of religion but in terms of the role that the practices and beliefs assume
in the religion of the individual or group concerned.

In considering
s. 2
of the
Charter
one must keep
in mind that the fundamental freedoms therein guaranteed have been somewhat
more elaborately expressed than were the corresponding freedoms in the Canadian
Bill of Rights. Both a textual comparison and a review of the evidence before
the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and House of Commons on the
Constitution, 1981-82, confirm that the International Covenant on Civil and
Political Rights was an important source of the terms chosen. Since Canada
ratified that covenant in 1976, with the unanimous consent of the federal and
provincial governments, the covenant constitutes an obligation upon Canada
under international law, by
art. 2
thereof, to implement its provisions within
this country. Although our constitutional tradition is not that a ratified
treaty is self-executing within our territory, but must be implemented by the
domestic constitutional process (A.-G. Can. v. A.-G. Ont.,
1937 CanLII 362 (UK JCPC)
, [1937] 1 D.L.R. 673,
[1937] A.C. 326, [1937] 1 W.W.R. 299 (Labour Conventions Case)), nevertheless,
unless the domestic law is clearly to the contrary, it should be interpreted in
conformity with our international obligations. Therefore, art. 18 of the
covenant is pertinent to our consideration of the definition of freedom of
conscience and religion under the Charter.
Article 18
provides:

"(1) Everyone shall have the right to
freedom of thought, conscience and religion. This right shall include freedom
to have or to adopt a religion or belief of his choice, and freedom, either
individually or in community with others and in public or private, to manifest
his religion or belief in worship, observance, practice and teaching.

. . . . .

"(3) Freedom to manifest one's religion or
beliefs may be subject only to such limitations as are prescribed by law and
are necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals or the
fundamental rights and freedoms of others."

(Emphasis added.)

It will be noted that the right is defined as
including not only the right to have or adopt a religion or belief of one's
choice, but also to be able to "manifest" the religion or belief
"in worship, observance, practice and teaching". The pertinent part of
the definition of the word "manifest" in Webster's New World
Dictionary provides: "to make clear or evident; show plainly; reveal;
evince". The Oxford Dictionary definition is as follows: "To make
evident to the eye or to the mind; to show plainly; to display (a quality,
condition, feeling, etc.); to reveal the presence of, evince." It is
manifest, to use the term in another connotation, that all religions require
their adherents to observe the tenets of that religion by various practices
which would appear to others to have a purely secular significance, such as not
cutting one's hair and wearing turbans, or shaving one's head and wearing
saffron robes, such as not eating certain foods or eating them on certain days
and not others, such as not killing certain animals or consuming some and not
others and, above all, such as not working or buying or selling goods or
services on certain days specified as the sabbath. Such observations, when
practised as part of a religious observance, have to be considered within the
scope of one's religious freedom. This is so even though what is a religious
practice for people of one religion is secular for those of another and vice
versa.

In the Supreme Court of Canada the constitutional validity of the Retail
Business Holidays Act was upheld (Wilson J. dissenting, in part).

The judgment of Dickson C.J.C. and Chouinard and Le Dain JJ. was delivered
by the Chief Justice. For present purposes, it is only necessary to recall
those aspects of the reasons of the Chief Justice which concern the submission
that the legislation was constitutionally infirm because it denied the
appellants the freedom of religion guaranteed to them by
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
.

It was alleged by the appellants that the Act infringed freedom of religion
in that:

(i) indirectly, it made it more expensive for retailers and consumers who
observe a weekly day of rest other than Sunday to practise their religious
tenets, thereby, indirectly coercing such persons to forego the practice of a
religious belief, and

(ii) directly, it compelled non-believers to conform to majoritarian
religious dogma by requiring retailers to close their stores on Sunday.

In connection with the initial issue, whether indirect burdens on religious
practices are enjoined by the constitutional guarantee of freedom of religion,
the Chief Justice reasoned, at pp. 758-9 S.C.R., pp. 34-5 D.L.R.:

The first question is whether indirect burdens on
religious practice are prohibited by the constitutional guarantee of freedom of
religion. In my opinion, indirect coercion by the state is comprehended within
the evils from which
s. 2
(a) may afford protection. The court said as much in
the Big M Drug Mart case and any more restrictive interpretation would, in my
opinion, be inconsistent with the court's obligation under s. 27 to perserve
and enhance the multicultural heritage of Canadians. Although the court
apparently reached a different conclusion in Robertson and Rosetanni v. The
Queen in respect of the protection afforded under the Canadian Bill of Rights,
I would follow Big M Drug Mart in declining to be bound by jurisprudence
interpreting an instrument which purported only to reaffirm pre-existing rights
and freedoms. It matters not, I believe, whether a coercive burden is direct or
indirect, intentional or unintentional, foreseeable or unforeseeable. All
coercive burdens on the exercise of religious beliefs are potentially within
the ambit of
s. 2
(a).

This does not mean, however, that every burden on
religious practices is offensive to the constitutional guarantee of freedom of
religion. It means only that indirect or unintentional burdens will not be held
to be outside the scope of
Charter
protection on that account alone.
Section
2(a)
does not require the Legislatures to eliminate every miniscule
state-imposed cost associated with the practice of religion. Otherwise the
Charter would offer protection from innocuous secular legislation such as a
taxation act that imposed a modest sales tax extending to all products,
including those used in the course of religious worship. In my opinion, it is
unnecessary to turn to
s. 1
in order to justify legislation of that sort. The
purpose of
s. 2
(a) is to ensure that society does not interfere with profoundly
personal beliefs that govern one's perception of oneself, humankind, nature,
and, in some cases, a higher or different order of being. These beliefs, in
turn, govern one's conduct and practices. The Constitution shelters individuals
and groups only to the extent that religious beliefs or conduct might
reasonably or actually be threatened. For a state- imposed cost or burden to be
proscribed by
s. 2
(a) it must be capable of interfering with religious belief
or practice. In short, legislative or administrative action which increases the
cost of practising or otherwise manifesting religious beliefs is not prohibited
if the burden is trivial or insubstantial: see, on this point, Jones v. The
Queen

(1986),
1986 CanLII 32 (SCC)
, 28 C.C.C. (3d) 513, 31 D.L.R. (4th) 569, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 284, per
Wilson J. at 28 C.C.C. (3d) 513 at p. 522, 31 D.L.R. (4th) 569 at p. 578-9, 2
S.C.R. 284 at pp. 314-5.

The learned Chief Justice next considered the second form of religious
coercion said to arise under the Act, namely, that which involved the freedom
to abstain from the religious practices of others. He concluded on this issue,
at pp. 760-1 S.C.R., pp. 35-6 D.L.R.:

In Big M Drug Mart this court acknowledged that
freedom of conscience and religion included the freedom to express and manifest
religious non-belief and the freedom to refuse to participate in religious
practice: p. 425 C.C.C., p. 361 D.L.R., p. 346 S.C.R. These freedoms, which may
compendiously be referred to as the freedom from conformity to religious dogma,
are governed by somewhat different considerations than the freedom to manifest
one's own religious beliefs. Religious freedom is inevitably abridged by
legislation which has the effect of impeding conduct integral to the practice
of a person's religion. But it is not necessarily impaired by legislation which
requires conduct consistent with the religious beliefs of another person. One
is not being compelled to engage in religious practices merely because a
statutory obligation coincides with the dictates of a particular religion. I
cannot accept, for example, that a legislative prohibition of criminal conduct
such as theft and murder is a state-enforced compulsion to conform to religious
practices, merely because some religions enjoin their members not to steal or
kill. Reasonable citizens do not perceive the legislation as requiring them to
pay homage to religious doctrine. As Mr. Justice Tarnopolsky stated [at p. 380
C.C.C., p. 38 D.L.R.]:

"While freedom of conscience necessarily
includes the right not to have a religious basis for one's conduct, it does not
follow that one can rely upon the
Charter
protection of freedom of conscience
to object to an enforced holiday simply because it happens to coincide with
someone else's sabbath."

The majority judgment of the court in Big M Drug
Mart was careful, in defining the freedom from conformity to religious dogma,
to restrict its applicability to circumstances when the impugned legislation
was motivated by a religious purpose:

"What may appear good and true to a
majoritarian religious group, or the state acting at their behest, may not, for
religious reasons, be imposed upon citizens who take a contrary view. [p. 418
C.C.C., p. 354 D.L.R., p. 337 S.C.R.]

"If I am a Jew or a Sabbatarian or a Muslim,
the practice of my religion at least implies my right to work on a Sunday if I
wish. It seems to me that any law purely religious in purpose, which denies me
that right, must surely infringe my religious freedom. [p. 419 C.C.C., p. 355
D.L.R., p. 338 S.C.R.]

"For the present case it is sufficient in my
opinion to say that whatever else freedom of conscience and religion may mean,
it must at the very least mean this: government may not coerce individuals to
affirm a specific religious belief or to manifest a specific religious practice
for a sectarian purpose. [p. 426 C.C.C., p. 362 D.L.R., p. 347 S.C.R.]

"In my view the guarantee of freedom of
conscience and religion prevents the government from compelling individuals to
perform or abstain from performing otherwise harmless acts because of the
religious significance of those acts to others. [p. 428 C.C.C., p. 364 D.L.R.,
p. 350 S.C.R.]"

(Emphasis added.)

In my view, legislation with a secular
inspiration does not abridge the freedom from conformity to religious dogma
merely because statutory provisions coincide with the tenets of a religion. I
leave open the possibility, however, that such legislation might limit the
freedom of conscience and religion of persons whose conduct is governed by an
intention to express or manifest his or her non-conformity with religious
doctrine.

The majority held that the freedom of religion of Saturday- observing
retailers was infringed by s. 2 of the Retail Business Holidays Act, but that
such infringement fell within a reasonable limit which was demonstrably
justified in a free and democratic society and, accordingly, was justifiable
under
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

Beetz and McIntyre JJ. were of the view that the impugned legislation did
not violate the freedom of religion guarantee of
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and,
accordingly, was of full force and effect without the necessity of reference to
the justificatory criteria of
s. 1
.

La Forest J. agreed with the disposition proposed by the Chief Justice and
with most of his supporting reasons. In particular, La Forest J. stated, at p.
792 S.C.R., p. 65 D.L.R.:

... I fully agree with the Chief Justice that the
freedom of religion guaranteed by
s. 2
(a) not only serves to protect the
individual against direct legislative coercion but against indirect legislative
coercion as well.

It was the view of La Forest J. that the Act would be none the less valid
absent the Sabbatarian exemption found in s. 3(4).

Reference should finally be made to the decision of this court, differently
constituted, in Re Zylberberg and Director of Education of Sudbury Board of
Education (1986),
1986 CanLII 2631 (ON HCJ)
, 55 O.R. (2d) 749, 29 D.L.R. (4th) 709, 25 C.R.R. 193. The
several applicants there sought judicial review of the jurisdiction of the
Sudbury Board of Education to hold religious exercises in its schools and to
require the recitation of the Lord's Prayer in such exercises. The applicants
there sought a declaration that s. 28(1) of Reg. 262, as amended, was of no
force or effect upon the basis, inter alia, that it infringed the applicants'
freedom of religion guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
, in that it tended to
coerce public school pupils into religious exercises in which their individual
religious beliefs may dictate they should not participate.

A majority of the court (O'Leary and Anderson JJ.) held that the impugned
subsection of the regulation was constitutionally sustainable, either because
it did not, in purpose or effect, deny or infringe the applicants'
s. 2
(a)
freedom or, at all events, that any limitation thereby imposed fell within the
reach of
s. 1
of the
Charter
. O'Leary J., in reasons with which Anderson J. was
"not in disagreement", considered the nature of coercion which was
necessary to engage the operation of
s. 2(a)
of the Charter. He concluded, at
pp. 759-60 O.R., pp. 719-20 D.L.R.:

In attempting to determine the degree of pressure
to conform created by s. 28(1) and whether such pressure amounts to such
coercion as to infringe
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
, one must bear in mind that our
multicultural heritage is to be preserved and enhanced. Difference is the very
essence of a multicultural society. Difference is to be worn with pride not
hidden. It is obvious in speech, dress, personal appearance and mannerisms.
Being different from the majority, especially in the large metropolitan areas
of the province, is common-place.

If a child's culture is different to that of the
majority, quite apart from the issue of prayer or religious exercises, that
difference will quickly become apparent to his classmates. For a child whose
culture is different to that of the majority, the emotional stress of having to
disclose his religion is different to that of the majority, in most cases, must
be of little more consequence than disclosing any of the other differences that
identify the particular culture to which he belongs.

The child that differs from the majority only in
his religious beliefs might, if s. 28(1) did not exist, hide from his
classmates for some considerable time that his religious beliefs are different.
But it is almost inevitable that sooner or later, if he associates in a close
way with any of his classmates, it will become known that his religion is
different to the majority. If disclosing a difference in religion is an
embarrassment, it is nevertheless an embarrassment that will have to be faced
throughout life and not just during school years.

It must be noted that the parent or pupil does
not have to justify in any way his decision not to participate in the religious
exercises. The reason for the decision does not have to be disclosed. It can be
frivolous or even irrelevant.

The applicants' position amounts to this: The
very holding of religious exercises acceptable to most Christians, but not
acceptable to non-Christians, including non-believers, coerces non-Christians
to participate in those religious exercises since non-Christians may be
embarrassed to disclose those exercises are not acceptable to them. Such
coercion the applicants say violates their right to freedom of conscience and
religion.

The type of coercion complained of, is pressure
to conform rather than face the embarrassment of disclosing that a different
belief is held. If such coercion infringes the guarantee of freedom of
conscience and religion then such freedom is likewise infringed whenever prayer
is said at functions provided for by statute. For example, a religious exercise
or prayer in Parliament or the Legislature would infringe the right to freedom
of conscience and religion.

In my view, the pressure to conform complained
about here does not constitute coercion to such an extent as to infringe the
right of freedom of conscience and religion.

After a review of the decisions in Big M Drug Mart Ltd. and Videoflicks,
supra, and Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen,
1963 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, [1963] S.C.R. 651, 41 D.L.R.
(2d) 485, [1964] 1 C.C.C. 1, Anderson J. concluded, at pp. 779-80 O.R., pp.
739-40 D.L.R.:

Running throughout these judgments as offensive
interference with freedom of religion are the imperative concepts of
compulsion, coercion and constraint. Moreover, in the context in which the
cases were decided, the compulsion, coercion or constraint was one which was
capable of enforcement by penal sanction.

In my view, the attack on the constitutional
validity of the impugned regulation [R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262], based on
s. 2(a)

of the
Charter
, fails for the simple reason that it does not, either in purpose
or effect, compel, coerce or constrain anyone. It contains, in s. 28(10), a
complete and unconditional provision that no pupil shall be required to take
part in any religious exercise. In the face of such a right to be excused, I am
simply not prepared to hold that anyone is compelled, coerced or constrained to
religious exercises to which he or she objects.

Dickson J. says in Big M Drug that the protection
from compulsion or coercion in matters of religion and conscience must be
"within reason" and speaks of "the tyranny of the
majority". We are imperfect creatures in an imperfect world and it is not
"within reason" to expect to find perfect freedom and equality. In
society some constraints and some inequalities are inevitable, perhaps
particularly so in a multicultural society, and should not found an action to
strike down legislation. In a similar vein, it is difficult to see, in a
regulation which contains a full and unconditional right to abstain or be
absent from the exercises prescribed, anything which has about it the flavour
of tyranny.

The applicants and supporting intervenors argue,
as indeed they must, having no alternative, that the right to abstain from the
exercises or be absent from them, far from saving the regulation in fact
condemns it; that the mere provision of this right implies that the exercises
may be offensive to some, and that the need to have recourse to the right of
abstention or absence is in itself constraint, compulsion or coercion, or at least
a major inducement. Thus baldly stated, the argument, in my view, offends logic
and common sense. It is tantamount to saying that a right to refuse is a
compulsion to accept. Choice is of the essence of freedom and the decision as
to what choice is appropriate is often difficult. The difficulty is part of the
price of freedom.

Reid J. dissented. In his view, s. 28(1), in its purpose and effect,
interfered with the religious freedom of the applicants which
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
guaranteed. He further concluded that the limitation imposed by the
regulation was neither reasonable nor demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society and, accordingly, could not be salvaged under
s. 1
of the
Charter.

(c) Conclusion

The preceding discussion of the substance of the freedom of religion
guarantee enshrined in
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
shall suffice for present
purposes to designate the standard against which the constitutional validity of
the Regulation and curriculum of the respondent Board here impugned fall to be
adjudged.

(3) Equality rights

(a) Introduction

The second basis upon which it is said that the provisions of s. 28(4) to
(16) inclusive, of Reg. 262, as amended, are constitutionally infirm, is on
account of their alleged infringement of the applicants' rights to equality
before and under the law and their right to the equal protection and benefit of
the law without discrimination based on religion, as enshrined in
s. 15(1)
of
the
Charter
. The subsection, in its entirety, enacts, as follows:

15(1) Every individual is equal before and under
the law and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law
without discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on
race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or
physical disability.

The equality rights guaranteed to the extent provided in
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
, are not wholly without qualification or limitation. Although the
language in which the guarantee of equality rights is expressed is cast in most
expansive terms, encompassing not only substantive and procedural equality
before and under the law, but also, or further, its equal protection and
benefit without discrimination, it is none the less subject to the limitative
effect placed upon all rights and freedoms by
s. 1
. It is constitutionally
permissible for any law to limit an individual's equality rights in a manner
invidious to the plenary language of
s. 15(1)
, provided such limitation does
not exceed what is reasonable and can be demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society. Further, as was the case with the fundamental freedom of
religion which, by
s. 2
(a) is guaranteed to everyone, the equality rights
enshrined in
s. 15(1)
are expressly made subject to the override clause of
s.
33(1)
of the Charter. An expressed declaration by the enacting legislative body
that a particular statute or provision thereof shall operate notwithstanding an
enumerated Charter right or freedom guarantees such operation for renewable
periods of five years from the date of the declaration.

It is necessary to presently canvass a select few decisions in which the
application of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
has been considered, whereby to
ascertain, to some extent at least, the contours of the rights thereby given.

(b) The substance of the guarantee

The first expression of opinion by the Ontario Court of Appeal concerning
the reach of the equality rights provisions of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, so far
as I am able to determine, occurred in Re McDonald and The Queen (1985),
1985 CanLII 162 (ON CA)
, 51
O.R. (2d) 745, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 397, 21 C.C.C. (3d) 330, a case which considered
the bearing of the subsection upon certain provisions of the Young Offenders
Act, S.C. 1980-81-82-83, c. 110. Morden J.A., on behalf of the court (Dubin and
Grange JJ.A. concurring), observed, at p. 765 O.R., p. 417 D.L.R.:

It can reasonably be said, in broad terms, that
the purpose of
s. 15
is to require "that those who are similarly situated
be treated similarly": Tussman and tenBroek, "The Equal Protection of
the Laws", 37 Cal. L. Rev. 341 (1948), at p. 344.

Subsequently, in R. v. R.L. (1986),
1986 CanLII 4611 (ON CA)
, 26 C.C.C. (3d) 417, 52 C.R. (3d) 209, 27
C.R.R. 30, Morden J.A. expanded upon his earlier observations concerning the
"essentially relational nature of equality". At pp. 424-5 he held:

The basic nature of the right or rights conferred
by s. 15 requires some examination. The essentially relational nature of
equality has been described as follows. "The concept of equality is, by
definition, relational or comparative. A person can only be found to be equal
in relation to or in comparison with some other person who serves as a standard
or criterion." Monroe H. Freedman, "Equality in the Administration of
Criminal Justice", Nomos IX (1967) 250 at pp. 253-4. The concern for
equality is that those who are similarly situated with respect to the purpose
of the law be treated similarly: see Tussman and tenBroek, "The Equal
Protection of the Laws", 37 Cal.L.Rev. 341 (1948), and Re McDonald and The
Queen (1985),
1985 CanLII 162 (ON CA)
, 21 C.C.C. (3d) 330 at pp. 349-50, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 397, 51 O.R.
(2d) 745 at p. 765

(C.A.) referring to the Tussman and tenBroek article.

Similar views were expressed in Reference re Act to Amend Education Act
(1986),
1986 CanLII 2863 (ON CA)
, 53 O.R. (2d) 513 at pp. 554-5, 25 D.L.R. (4th) 1 at pp. 42-3, 23 C.R.R.
193, per Howland C.J.O. and Robins J.A. dissenting; Re Blainey and Ontario
Hockey Ass'n (1986),
1986 CanLII 145 (ON CA)
, 54 O.R. (2d) 513 at pp. 524-5, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 728 at

1986 CanLII 2485 (ON CA)
, 57
O.R. (2d) 409 at p. 411, 33 D.L.R. (4th) 477 at p. 479, 27 C.R.R. 25 (C.A.),
and R. v. Century 21 Ramos Realty Inc. and Ramos (1987),
1987 CanLII 171 (ON CA)
, 58 O.R. (2d) 737 at p.

released June 3, 1987 [since reported
1987 CanLII 183 (ON CA)
, 35 C.C.C. (3d) 398, 58 C.R. (3d) 252], it
was argued that
s. 507(3)
of the
Criminal Code
and its re-enactment by the
Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1985, S.C. 1985, c. 19, s. 115 (now s-ss. 507(b) and

rights. Lacourciere
J.A., on behalf of the court (Dubin and Blair JJ.A. concurring), emphasized the

Step one

In view of what Morden J.A. described as the
"essentially, relational nature of equality" in R. v. R.L. (1986),
1986 CanLII 4611 (ON CA)
, 26
C.C.C. (3d) 417 at pp. 424-5, 52 C.R. (3d) 209, 27 C.R.R. 30, it is necessary,
as a first step in the analysis of a
s. 15
challenge, to make comparisons and
to identify the class or classes of persons who are said to be treated
differently.

The second step in the analysis is described at pp. 33-4 of the reasons [pp.
419-20 C.C.C.]:

Step two

The following step in a s. 15 analysis, again
following Ramos, is to determine whether these classes are "similarly
situated", using the language adopted by Morden J.A. in Re McDonald and
The Queen (1985),
1985 CanLII 162 (ON CA)
, 21 C.C.C. (3d) 330 at p. 349, 21 D.L.R. (4th) 397, 51 O.R.
(2d) 745. The importance of the rule that "those who are similarly

1986 CanLII 2485 (ON CA)
, 33 D.L.R. (4th) 477, 57 O.R. (2d) 409, 27 C.R.R. 25], if the classes

. When proceeding with this analysis one must heed the

The third step to be followed is set out by Lacourciere J.A. at p. 35 of his
reasons [p. 420 C.C.C.], on behalf of the court:

Step three

It is unnecessary in this case, in view of the
analysis made in Ramos, to repeat the factors which influenced the court in
rejecting the so-called neutral approach to
s. 15
whereby every unequal
treatment would have to be justified by recourse to
s. 1
. Rather, the proper
approach to the words "without discrimination" in
s. 15
is what was
