discrimination". The initial question to be answered is whether or not
that person who is subject to a direct indictment, whether or not that person
had the benefit of a preliminary inquiry, is subject to an inherent
disadvantage. If so, is the distinction so unfair as to be discriminatory,
having regard to the purpose and effect of the legislation?

His Lordship next pointed out the necessity of ensuring that analysis under

s. 15
remain discrete from that required in the event of recourse to
s. 1
of
the
Charter
. He concluded upon this issue at pp. 36-8 [pp. 421-2]:

Where the analysis of the words "without
discrimination" takes place in the context of
s. 15
, the onus is on the
person alleging discrimination to demonstrate the unfairness or irrationality
of the differential treatment which is alleged to constitute an infringement.
In contrast, where the analysis focuses, on s. 1, the onus of proving that the
imposition of a limit or a restriction on a constitutionally guaranteed right
such as equality is reasonable and demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society is on the party seeking to uphold the limitation or
restriction. In both instances the standard of proof is the civil standard,
namely, proof by a preponderance of probability: see R. v. Oakes (1986),
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 24
C.C.C. (3d) 321 at p. 346, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 200, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103. Care must
also be taken to ensure that the determination of reasonableness and
justifiability, when applied to words qualifying a constitutional right, such
as the words "without discrimination", should remain analytically
distinct from the determination of whether an infringement can be justified
under
s. 1
(ibid., p. 344).

A narrow interpretation of Ramos may suggest that
the court found that there was no infringement of
s. 15
only because the
appellant has not suffered an inherent disadvantage. The court said at p. 37
[p. 378 C.C.C.]:

"To apply the pejorative or adverse test to
this case, we have to ask whether the different rights of appeal in a summary
conviction offence, as against those in an indictable offence, do pose an
inherent disadvantage."

[Emphasis added.]

However, I prefer to read the case as
establishing that factors such as fairness, rationality and justifiability
deserve some consideration in determining whether a particular distinction is
discriminatory, having regard to the purpose and effect of the impugned
legislation. These factors may, in a large number of cases such as the present,
make it unnecessary to resort to
s. 1
. However, I find nothing in Ramos which
would preclude the court from resorting to
s. 1
, particularly in cases where
the Crown is better equipped to lead evidence with respect to reasonableness,
as well as the purpose and effect of the legislation. In fact, the Ramos
decision recognizes that, where discrimination has been established, the court
is obliged to consider the applicability of
s. 1
. It may be that discrimination
based on some of the named grounds would more readily require recourse to
s. 1
.
In such cases, the
s. 1
analysis would constitute the fourth step in the
approach.

The impugned provisions were found constitutionally adequate and the appeal
dismissed.

After the conclusion of argument in the present application, the Court of
Appeal released its decision in Re McKinney and Board of Governors of the
University of Guelph unreported, released December 10, 1987 [since reported
1987 CanLII 179 (ON CA)
, 63
O.R. (2d) 1, 46 D.L.R. (4th) 193]. Seven professors and one librarian employed
by four Ontario universities, as well as one professor who sued in a
representative capacity, applied in separate applications for an order that the
mandatory retirement policies of the several universities were of no force and
effect, inter alia, on account of the provisions of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.
The applications were dismissed,
1986 CanLII 2832 (ON HCJ)
, 57 O.R. (2d) 1, 32 D.L.R. (4th) 65, 14
C.C.E.L. 1. The applicants appealed to the Court of Appeal. The appeals were
dismissed by a majority of the court (Howland C.J.O., Houlden, Thorson and
Finlayson JJ.A.). Blair J.A. dissented.

The proper interpretation of the word "discrimination" was
critical to a determination of the issue in the case. On the one hand, it was
argued by the appellants that discrimination should be read in a neutral sense,
that is to say, as meaning merely distinction or classification. The natural
consequence of such an interpretation would result in the universal application
of every law. It would follow that any law which drew a distinction between
individuals, on whatever ground or basis, would, prima facie, offend
s. 16
and
shift the issue to a consideration of
s. 1
and the onus to the party seeking to
uphold the limitation. On the other hand, the respondents submitted that
s.
15(1)
was not infringed absent unequal treatment resulting from discrimination
in the sense of invidious, unjustifiability, irrelevance or unreasonableness.
To put the matter otherwise, the position of the respondents would require a
prima facie showing of unreasonably imposed inequality before the analysis and
onus shifted to
s. 1
and the parties seeking to uphold the limitation.

The majority of the court, having expressed the view that in previous
decisions the court had never adopted the purely neutral approach of applying
the subsection (15(1)) simply because legislation created distinctions between
individuals and treated them differently, observed that it was unnecessary to
prove unreasonableness in order to establish discrimination under s. 15(1). At
pp. 54-5 [pp. 34-5 O.R., pp. 226-7 D.L.R.] of the majority reasons is the
following passage:

Equally significant is the fact that this court
in both the Education Act Reference and Blainey cases, did not adopt the view
that unreasonableness must be proved in order to establish discrimination under

s. 15(1)
. In Blainey, supra, Dubin J.A., after quoting the above passage with
approval, said at p. 525 O.R., p. 740 D.L.R.:

"Like Morden J.A. in Re McDonald and The
Queen, supra, Chief Justice Howland and Robins J.A. found it unnecessary to
pass upon the various approaches that have been suggested with respect to the
application of
s. 15(1)
, nor do I think it necessary to do so in this case. In
my opinion, by any of the various tests referred to above, s. 19(2) of the
Human Rights Code, 1981 is clearly inconsistent with
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter

and denies Miss Blainey the right to the equal protection and the equal benefit
of the law of this province as expressed in the Human Rights Code, 1981 by
reason of her sex."

In both cases the court avoided what, in our
opinion, is the false dichotomy between the neutral and Andrews interpretations
of "discrimination" by using the word in what is referred to as its
pejorative sense. The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary defines
"pejorative" as "tending to make worse; depreciatory"'.
This sense of "discrimination" contrasts with those denoting
refinement in taste or perception, or simply the act of distinguishing or differentiating.
One of the meanings ascribed to "discrimination" in the Oxford
English Dictionary (1961), is "to make an adverse distinction with regard
to; to distinguish unfavourably from others." Webster's New World
Dictionary of the American Language includes as one definition: "a showing
of partiality or prejudice in treatment; specific action or policies directed
against the welfare of minority groups". These dictionary definitions are
cited by Professor Tarnopolsky (as he then was) in his book Discrimination and
the Law (2nd ed., revised by William Pentney, 1985), c. 4, "Discrimination
and Affirmative Action", pp. 3-4, where he states:

"... the term 'discrimination', as used in
Canada, is intended to have the third of the three meanings suggested in
Webster's Dictionary, i.e., a specific act or a policy of partiality or
prejudice in treatment ..."

The description of "discrimination" in
these terms as treatment which, viewed objectively, is tangibly adverse,
unfavourable or prejudicial is consistent with the result in Blainey and the dissenting
judgments in the Education Act Reference. This concept of discrimination lies
between what we earlier described as the two extreme concepts of
discrimination. Because the question of definition was left open in both cases,
it is necessary to examine further whether treatment which is adverse or
prejudicial must also be unreasonable in order to constitute discrimination.

The majority next reviewed a number of decisions in which appellate courts
had considered whether it was necessary to demonstrate that treatment was not
only adverse or prejudicial, but also unreasonable in order to make a prima
facie showing of discrimination under s. 15(1). After making reference to the
decision in Ertel, supra, the majority concluded, at pp. 62-5 [pp. 39-40 O.R.,
pp. 230-2 D.L.R.]:

The court followed Ertel in R. v. Turpin,
Siddiqui and Clauzel, released August 20, 1987, unreported [since reported
1987 CanLII 6768 (ON CA)
, 36
C.C.C. (3d) 289, 60 C.R. (3d) 63]. In that case the three accused were charged
in Ontario with first degree murder. When they were charged the then
s. 430
of
the
Criminal Code
, enacted by S.O. 1953-54, c. 51, s. 417, allowed persons
charged with murder and certain other indictable offences in Alberta to elect
trial by judge alone. Sections 427 and 429 together required trial by judge and
jury for murder and other indictable offences in all other provinces. (
Section
430
was amended by the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1985, S.C. 1985, c. 19, s.
64, to permit persons charged anywhere in Canada with murder and other offences
listed in s. 427 to be tried by judge alone with their consent and that of the
Attorney-General.) The trial judge, invoking
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, allowed
the accused to elect trial by judge alone. One of the accused was acquitted and
the other two were convicted of second degree murder.

On appeal, the question was whether the
distinction created by
s. 430
violated
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
. The court in a
per curiam judgment found that the choice allowed to accused persons in Alberta
was a benefit, the absence of which in Ontario must be considered a
disadvantage. The disadvantage created by this geographically based difference
in criminal procedure was, however, not so unfair, invidious, or irrational as
to amount to discrimination under s. 15(1). In reaching this conclusion, the
court took into account the federal organization of Canadian society and the
history of differences in criminal procedure from province to province. The
court cited R. v. Hamilton; R. v. Asselin; R. v. McCullagh (1986),
1986 CanLII 4639 (ON CA)
, 57 O.R. (2d)
412, 30 C.C.C. (3d) 257, 54 C.R. (3d) 193 (C.A.) for the proposition that
Parliament may give special application, in terms of locality or otherwise, to
its enactments without necessarily attracting a successful challenge on
s. 15

grounds, and stated, at p. 20 [p. 301 C.C.C.], that "absolute uniformity
of criminal procedure as it applies throughout Canada, may be impossible or
undesirable ...". After giving examples, the court said at p. 21 [p. 302
C.C.C.]:

"If any of these variations were found to be
an advantage, would Parliament have had to extend them to every other province?
It seems unreasonable to so require. If it is unreasonable to so require, can
one conclude that there is such an 'invidious' or 'unfair' or 'irrational'
distinction with respect to the requirement for jury trials for charges of
murder in all provinces except Alberta as to amount to
"discrimination" for purposes of
s. 15
? It cannot be so. We would
have to conclude, therefore, that the limited option of a non-jury trial of a
murder charge in Alberta, whereas that option was not available in any of the
other provinces or the two Territories, did not amount to discrimination in the
sense of a denial of equal benefit of the law pursuant to
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
."

The Court decided that it was not necessary to
consider
s. 1
of the
Charter
but, nevertheless, observed at p. 22 [p. 302
C.C.C.] that:

"[I]f the conclusion had been reached in
this case that s. 15 was violated, then for the same reasons concerning
geographical distinction in a federal system, we would have held that whatever
disadvantage the respondents may have had in 1985, was the result of a
reasonable limitation which was demonstrably justified in a free, democratic
and Federally organized society."

Ertel and Turpin demonstrate the difficulty of
articulating the pejorative sense of the word "discrimination". In
these cases and others, various descriptions have been applied to legislation
which may discriminate against individuals under
s. 15(1)
, including
"invidious", "unfair", "irrational",
"adverse", and "prejudicial". These decisions,
nevertheless, make it clear that this court has not accepted the Andrews view
that the party impugning legislation must also prove that it is
"unreasonable".

In the present case there can be no doubt that s.
9(a) has a prejudicial and adverse impact on university staff over the age of
65 in comparison with others under that age. Because of these easily observable
prejudicial effects, the section discriminates against staff over the age of 65
and denies the equal treatment to which they are entitled under
s. 15(1)
. The
finding that s. 9(a) discriminates contrary to
s. 15(1)
is readily
distinguishable from the question whether it can be justified as a reasonable
limit on
s. 15(1)
rights under
s. 1
.

Reasonableness, then, is a matter to be
determined within the context of
s. 1
, where the rights of the person
challenging the legislation can be balanced against the interests of other
people and the societal values which the legislation may be claimed to assert
or uphold. With respect, we are of the view that to require proof of
unreasonableness for a finding of discrimination under
s. 15(1)
distorts the
operation of the
Charter
. The burden of proof which properly falls on the upholder
of the distinction under
s. 1
is shifted to the challenger. If in a given case
the requirement is not met, real discrimination could be defined out of
existence and the open discussion of competing rights and values, which
s. 1

requires, would be forestalled.

The majority concluded that s. 9(a) of the Human Rights Code, 1981, S.O.
1981, c. 53, which provides that "age" in s. 4(1) of the Code means
an age that is 18 years or more and less than 65 years, infringed the
appellant's equality rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, but not to such an
extent or degree that exceeded what was justifiable under
s. 1
of the Charter.
Section 4(1) of the Code, as is well known, provides a right to equal treatment
with respect to employment without discrimination because of age. The
"age" definition in s. 9(a) had the effect of permitting such
discrimination in employment based on age, at least in respect of putative
employees who are under 18 and over 65, hence the use of mandatory retirement
schemes like those in the respondent universities. In the result, the majority
held that s. 9(a) of the Code, in its application to Ontario universities,
constituted a reasonable limit upon the equality rights guaranteed by s. 15(1)
of the Charter that was demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society
under s. 1 of the Charter. The appeals were dismissed.

In dissent, Blair J.A. agreed that s. 9(a) of the Code was inconsistent with

s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, but concluded that it was not justifiable under
s. 1
.

by

of the

shall suffice for present purposes to designate the
