4. THE CONSTITUTIONALITY OF THE REGULATION

(1) Introduction: the enabling legislation

The constitutional attack in the present application, it will be recalled,
fastens not upon the integrity of the enabling statutory authority, ss. 50 and
10(1), para. 18 of the Education Act, but rather upon the regulations passed
thereunder, as well as the curriculum of the respondent Board, in accordance
with which instruction was given in religious education in the public elementary
schools of Elgin County. The absence of constitutional challenge to the
enabling legislation is plainly not dispositive of the constitutional issues
here raised, for it may be that in purpose or effect the regulations passed
thereunder have a constitutionally impermissible reach. It is, however, of
importance to here briefly assess the effect of the concession of
constitutionality of the enabling statutory authority.

Section 50 of the Act, entitled "Religious Instruction", enacts,
as follows:

50(1) Subject to the regulations, a pupil shall
be allowed to receive such religious instruction as his parent or guardian
desires or, where the pupil is an adult, as he desires.

(2) No pupil in a public school shall be required
to read or study in or from a religious book, or to join in an exercise of
devotion or religion, objected to by his parent or guardian, or by the pupil,
where he is an adult.

By s. 50 each pupil shall receive religious instruction only "as his
parent or guardian desires or, where the pupil is an adult, as he
desires". In no event is any pupil in a public school required to read or
study in or from a religious book, or to join in an exercise of devotion or
religion, to which objection is taken by the parent, guardian or pupil, if an
adult.

The position of the applicants would hold it constitutionally permissible
for the province to legislate, as in s. 50 of the Act, that a pupil in the
public elementary schools of the province shall receive, to the extent of
parental, or in some cases, pupil desires, religious instruction. The balance
of power in every event resides not in the board whose school the pupil
attends, but rather in the parent, guardian or adult pupil whose desires
determine, in the ultimate result, to what extent, if at all, the pupil shall
receive religious instruction. The provision, as well as receipt of religious
instruction, commensurate with parental or pupil desires is, ex concessis,
constitutionally permissible.

It would seem logically to follow that any determination as to whether or to
what extent a public elementary school pupil shall receive religious
instruction requires ascertainment of the desires of the parent, guardian or
pupil, as the case may be. By definition, the only person from whom such
knowledge or desires may be ascertained, is the parent, guardian or pupil.
There are, essentially, two methods of its ascertainment; namely,

(a) a request by the board directed to the parent, guardian or pupil seeking
disclosure of the relevant information, and,

(b) disclosure to the board by the parent, guardian or pupil of such
information without the necessity of request therefore by the board or on its
behalf.

In either event, the ultimate source of the information is one and the same.
It would equally appear that the ascertainment of such information concerning
the desires of the parent, guardian or pupil in respect of religious
instruction of the pupil is constitutionally permissible.

It may also be observed that s. 50(2) equally requires the communication of
information from the parent, guardian or adult pupil. It is not suggested that
the imposition of such a burden of disclosure is constitutionally
impermissible.

Section 50(1) of the Act assigns a prominent role to regulations in the
provision of a programme of religious instruction to be given in the public
schools of this province. Section 10(1), para. 18 of the Act expressly
authorizes regulations governing the provision of religious instruction in the
province's public schools. In equally express terms, the paragraph empowers the
making of regulations concerning the exemption of pupils, teachers and boards
from their respective roles or obligations in religious education. The conjoint
effect of the subsections would appear to be that a school board shall provide,
through its teachers who shall teach to its pupils who shall receive
instruction in religious education, but only to the extent that the parent,
guardian or adult pupil desires, and subject to the right of the pupil, teacher
and board to seek exemption therefrom. The position taken by the applicants
that neither s. 50 nor 10(1), para. 18 of the Act is constitutionally deficient
would seem necessarily to entail that it is not constitutionally impermissible
for the legislature to provide for instruction in religious education in the
public schools, nor to enact its provision in terms which imply that it shall
be given and received to the extent a parent, guardian or pupil desires, and
subject to exemption of any participant in the giving or receipt of such instruction.
In other words, it is not impermissible to legislate a scheme of provision to
the extent of desire subject to exemption. To put the matter in somewhat
different language, it is a valid exercise of provincial legislative authority,
not only to enact a programme of instruction in religious education in public
schools, but to do so in terms which make it mandatory, but subject to
exemption. Such a scheme or programme is not constitutionally invalid in either
purpose or effect according to the concession of the applicants.

In my respectful view, it follows from the position taken by the applicants
with respect to the constitutionality of the enabling legislation that it
cannot be the fact that the legislature has chosen a provision-exemption dichotomy
in which to provide for instruction in religious education in the public
schools that is constitutionally offensive, else the enabling legislation could
not itself withstand constitutional challenge. It should also be observed that
the very essence and nature of an exemption carries with it or connotes the
existence of a corresponding obligation or duty from which the person seeking
exemption wishes freedom or excusal. It is further, a commonplace that a party
who seeks an exemption from what would otherwise be a duty or obligation, bears
the onus of its assertion. Indeed, in many, if not most, instances, it is such
a party who is exclusively possessed of the wherewithal to assert it. A
concession that legislation in such form is constitutionally sustainable must
carry with it, in my respectful view, an acknowledgement that such a scheme is
not coercive to a constitutionally impermissible extent of those who may claim
exemption therefrom.

There are but two further preliminary observations that ought to be here
made in connection with the applicants' acknowledgement of the constitutional
validity of the enabling provisions of the Education Act. In the first place,
the enabling provisions contain no reference to the substance of the course of
instruction in religious education. To put it briefly, what is to be taught,
apart from "religious education", is not there specified. Secondly,
the constitutionality of the enabling legislation is not determinative of the
constitutionality of the regulations, nor of any what might be compendiously
designated "executive action" taken thereunder. An example drawn from
the criminal law will suffice to illustrate the point here being made. In R. v.
Finlay and Grellette (1985),
1985 CanLII 117 (ON CA)
, 52 O.R. (2d) 632, 23 D.L.R. (4th) 532, 23 C.C.C.
(3d) 48, 48 C.R. (3d) 341, the Court of Appeal upheld the constitutional
validity of that portion of Part IV.1 of the
Criminal Code
which empowered
judges of the District Court of Ontario and of the superior court of criminal
jurisdiction, upon satisfactory proof of certain conditions precedent, to issue
authorizations to intercept private communications as a means whereby the
commission of serious crime may be investigated. Notwithstanding the
constitutional validity of the legislation under which an authorization is
granted, the court expressly recognized that individual warrants, hence
interceptions, may none the less constitute an unreasonable search or seizure,
thereby offending against the guarantee of
s. 8
of the
Charter
. Martin J.A.
(Blair and Cory JJ.A. concurring) observed at p. 663 O.R., p. 563 D.L.R., p. 78
C.C.C.:

It is scarcely necessary to add that although the
legislative scheme of Part IV.1 is constitutional, the granting of a particular
authorization in the circumstances may be unreasonable and hence infringe s. 8.

(2) The Regulation and freedom of religion

(a) Introduction: The positions of the parties

(i) The position of the applicants

The position of the applicants, stated shortly, is that, in purpose as well as
effect, s. 28(4) to (16), inclusive, of the Regulation violate the freedom of
religion as guaranteed to the applicants under
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. In
essence, the applicants submit that the purpose and effect of the subsections
is the impermissible indoctrination of public elementary school pupils in the
religious beliefs and precepts of the Christian majority, rather than the
constitutionally permissible instruction in religious education.

In the first place, Mr. Sharpe invited consideration of the very nature or
essence of freedom, as a constituent element of the freedom of religion
guarantee enacted in
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. He submits that the recognition of
freedom in any society confers upon its individual members the liberty of free
choice, as well the power of self-determination, and imposes upon the state the
concomitant obligation to forebear or abstain from any action limitative of or
inimical to such unrestrained choice. Freedom of religion, it is urged,
mandates not only that the state not coerce any individual to form, hold or
manifest any particular religious belief, but also leave the extent, indeed the
very existence of religious belief, to the individual conscience and
self-determination of its members.

Mr. Sharpe next examined the purpose of the impugned subsections of the
Regulation. He submitted that, at the time relevant for a determination of
constitutionality, the time of enactment, the purpose which underlay their
proclamation was the constitutionally impermissible one of indoctrination of
the public elementary school pupils of the province in the religious beliefs of
the Christian majority. Mr. Sharpe asserted that such purpose plainly appears
in consequence of several factors, including:

(a) the objectives which underlay the passage of the legislation;

(b) the nature of the scheme for which provision is made in the Regulation,
and

(c) the option, available to a board under s. 28(7) and (8) of the
Regulation to permit a member of the clergy to give religious instruction in a
board school in lieu of a teacher or teachers.

The applicants identify the process of exemption as provided in the
legislative scheme, for all practical purposes, as determinative against its
constitutionality. The very existence of an exemption scheme whereby pupils,
teachers and boards may be relieved, upon request, of their respective
obligations to take, give or provide for instruction in religious education
demonstrates that it is religious indoctrination rather than education which
animated the enactment of the legislation. It is put simply that if religious
education were the purpose behind the legislation, no exemption would be
necessary. The existence of the exemption scheme constitutes a facial
demonstration of an overt religious purpose, indoctrination, which is not
constitutionally sustainable. The exemption, in other words, constitutes an
admission of a constitutionally impermissible purpose of indoctrination, not
education.

The applicants further submit that the effects of the Regulation are constitutionally
impermissible on account of their infringement of the applicants' freedom of
religion. It is said that, for all practical purposes, the provision- exemption
scheme of the Regulation determines or limits the alternatives available to
student participants, thereby coercing their participation in a programme which
compromises their own beliefs and enforces subscription to majoritarian
Christian precepts. The effect of the exemption scheme, it is added,
constitutes an unjustifiable infringement on the applicants' freedom of
religion in its requirement of public proclamation of disagreement with
prescribed religious observance.

(ii) The position of the respondents

The respondent Board and Minister take the position that in neither purpose
nor effect do the Regulations infringe the applicants' freedom of religion to
an impermissible extent.

On behalf of the respondent Board, it is the submission of Mr. Sopinka that
the guarantee of
s. 2
(a) is only infringed in the event that the Regulation, in
its purpose or effect:

(a) prevents individuals from entertaining religious beliefs, declaring them
openly or manifesting such beliefs by worship and practice;

(b) coerces individuals to affirm a specific religious belief or manifests a
specific religious practice for a sectarian purpose; or,

(c) imposes substantial, non-trivial costs or burdens which interfere with
religious beliefs or practices.

The Regulation, the argument continues, does not interfere with any person's
right to form, declare, manifest or decline individual religious beliefs, nor
coerce affirmation or manifestation of a particular religion. It imposes no
substantial non-trivial costs or burdens which interfere with religious beliefs
or practices. It follows, the submission runs, that there has been no
infringement of the applicants' freedom, a fortiori, of their constitutionally
guaranteed freedom of religion enumerated in
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

Mr. Sopinka further submits that the purpose which underlay the enactment of
s. 28 of the Regulation, at the time of its passage, was to instil in public
elementary school pupils in the province a sense of morality in preparation for
later and adult life. Instruction in religious education is but one aspect or
facet of such moral education. It is but one way of achieving such legitimate
secular purpose. The dissemination, even promotion, of Christian beliefs is not
the purpose of the legislation but, at all events, is not enjoined by the

Charter
guarantee, save to the extent that it inteferes with religious
self-determination and individual expression or coerces adherence to or
manifestation of particular religious beliefs. Neither the enabling legislation
or the Regulation, ex facie, mandate that instruction be given in a specific
religion nor require that it be sectarian in nature, hence indoctrination in
majoritarian Christian beliefs is not the purpose of the impugned sections.

Counsel for the respondent Board takes the further position that the
impugned sections of the Regulation, read in their entirety, in their effect
equally do not infringe the applicants' freedom of religion. The fact and
manner of exemption ensure that no individual is prevented from entertaining or
rejecting religious beliefs, openly declaring them or manifesting them by worship
and practice. No one is coerced to affirm a specific religious belief nor
manifest a specific religious practice for a sectarian purpose. Neither is
there imposed upon anyone a substantial non-trivial burden or cost which
interferes with religious beliefs or practices. Exemptions are given upon
request. Reasons are neither sought, nor, a fortiori, required. The subsections
are not coercive in their effect.

Mr. Wright, on behalf of the respondent Minister, not only adopted the
submissions of counsel for the respondent Board, but advanced further argument
in support of the constitutionality of the impugned subsections. It was his
submission that, far from infringing freedom of religion, the subsections and
enabling statute promote such freedom by offering the constituents a choice
concerning religious education. Choice, it is said, lies at the very root of
all freedom. Choice concerning religious education is talismanic of, not
antithetical to, religious freedom. There is neither coercion nor compulsion of
anyone to affirm any or specific religious beliefs, nor to participate in any
or specific religious practices. The complete and unconditional exempting
provision, s. 28(10), ensures the absence of coercion, compulsion or
constraint, hence the freedom of religion guaranteed under
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
.

Counsel for the Minister takes the further position that the embarrassment
felt by some pupils in the exercise of their right of exemption or withdrawal
from religious education classes under s. 28(10) is not a sufficient burden to
constitute an infringement of the
s. 2(a)

Charter
guarantee. It is argued that
the guarantee protects individuals or groups only to the extent that religious
beliefs might actually or reasonably be threatened or compromised, not in
respect of trivial or insubstantial burdens or costs.

Mr. Wright insists that the sole legislative purpose which underlay the
proclamation of the Regulation was a secular one, education. Instruction in
religious education is but a means or method whereby pupils in public
elementary schools may be introduced to moral and personal values, an essential
constituent of their education. Education, it is argued, comprehends not only
intellectual instruction, but equally, moral training. Instruction in religious
education introduces the youth of the public elementary schools to the
discussion and development of moral values, a critical part or aspect of their
over-all education. Its purpose is neither indoctrinal nor sectarian.

Counsel for the respondent Minister further contends that s. 28 of the
Regulation is not constitutionally admissible in its effect. Mr. Wright submits
that the effect of s. 28 of the Regulation, in its entirety, is to allow a
pupil to receive such religious education as the pupil, parent or guardian
desires. The exemption provision, enacted without qualification, gives a choice
to pupils. Choice is of the essence of freedom. A choice of whether to receive
or decline instruction in religious education constitutes the essence of
freedom of religion. The exemption provision serves to strengthen religious
freedom, not to weaken nor deny it. The effect of the provisions ensures
freedom of religion, not religion per se.

It is further the submission of Mr. Wright that the presence of a religious
element in the public school system in the province is not, per se, a
constitutional impropriety. The preamble to the
Charter
itself declares that:
"... Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy of God
...". The system of public education is but a reflection of society and,
hence, the permissibility of a religious element. The Constitution Acts,
1867-1982, it is argued, themselves contemplate a relationship between church
and state that is permissive rather than prohibitive of religious instruction
in the system of public education. Public education, it is conceded, cannot
coerce religious belief, a fortiori, particular religious belief, but values
education, founded in part upon our religious heritage, is constitutionally
permissible.

(b) The first test: legislative purpose

It is common ground that the initial test of constitutional validity
involves a consideration of the purpose of the legislation at the time of its
enactment: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra. A determination of legislative
purpose requires a critical examination of the aims and objectives of the
enacting authority. To be constitutional the legislative purpose thereby
ascertained must be consonant with, not inimical to, the guarantees enshrined
in the
Charter
. It has been well said that legislative purpose and effect are
closely connected, if not inseparable. The intended and actual effects of
legislation frequently inform an assessment of its objects, hence its validity:
R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra, at pp. 331-2 S.C.R., p. 350 D.L.R., per
Dickson J. It remains to ascertain the purpose or function of s. 28(4) to (16)
inclusive, of the Regulation, thereafter to ascertain its validity in length of
the guarantee of
s. 2
(a).

It is, in my respectful view, the purpose of s. 28 of the Regulation, most
especially when viewed in the context of its enabling authority, ss. 10(1),
para. 18 and 50 of the Education Act, to provide -- more accurately make
available -- for public elementary school pupils instruction in religious
education as part of the curriculum in such schools. Its provision is but part
of the wider or over-all purpose or function of the public school system,
namely, the systematic instruction or training of the young in preparation for
the work of life or, shortly put, education. It recognizes that education
encompasses more than intellectual instruction in language, mathematics, social
studies and science. Education has, equally, a moral aspect which requires the
introduction of moral and personal values into pupils in the public schools in
preparation for the work of life. Instruction in religious education is made
available to public elementary school pupils for the purpose of introducing or
instilling such a sense of morality in the constituents.

It may be observed that the
Charter
does not, in terms, enjoin instruction
in religious education in the public schools. Indeed, the individual applicants
concede that such instruction is at once constitutionally permissible and
positively desirable.
Section 2(a)
of the Charter does, however, provide the
constitutional standard against which statutory enactments such as the present
fall to be adjudged. The legislative purpose must not be to deny or infringe
freedom of religion. It must not, in other words, prevent public elementary
school pupils from entertaining religious beliefs, declaring them openly or
manifesting such beliefs by worship and practice. Neither must the purpose of
the subsection be to force pupils to affirm a specific religious belief or
manifest a specific religious practice for a sectarian purpose. It would be
equally impermissible if the purpose of the subsection were to impose
substantial non-trivial costs or burdens on pupils which interfered with their
individual religious beliefs or practices. It would seem self-evident that if
the subsection's purpose were to indoctrinate public elementary school pupils
in majoritarian Christian religious beliefs, it would not be constitutionally
permissible.

In my respectful view, a submission that the purpose of s. 28 of the
Regulation was enacted in order to indoctrinate public elementary school pupils
in majoritarian Christian religious beliefs cannot be sustained. I reach that
conclusion, notwithstanding the able submissions of Mr. Sharpe, for several
reasons.

In the first place, the applicants do not impugn the integrity of the
enabling authority contained in ss. 50 and 10(1), para. 18 of the Education
Act. They do not contend, for example, that the provisions of s. 50(1) whereby
"a pupil shall be allowed to receive such religious instruction as his
parent or guardian desires or, where the pupil is an adult, as he desires"
were enacted for the constitutionally impermissible purpose of indoctrinating
public elementary school pupils in majoritarian Christian religious beliefs.
Nor do they suggest that s. 10(1), para. 18 whereby, subject to the approval of
the Lieutenant-Governor in Council, the Minister may make regulations governing
the provision of religious education in public schools and providing for
exemption therefrom, is constitutionally inadmissible. It is further not said
that s. 28 of the Regulation is not authorized by s. 10(1), para. 18 of the
statute. It would seem to me logically to follow from such position that the
enabling legislation was enacted for a constitutionally admissible purpose,
viz., the secular purpose of introducing a moral element into the education of
public elementary school pupils whereby, together with intellectual
instruction, they may become adequately equipped to the task of the work of
life. There is nothing in the language of the enabling authority nor in the
provision-exemption dichotomy there enacted which evinces a sectarian purpose
of religious indoctrination in majoritarian Christian precepts. Neither the
structure nor language of the Regulation converts the constitutionally
permissible purpose which underlays the enabling authority to that which is
constitutionally infirm on account of
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

Secondly, the scheme for which provision is made in s. 28 of the Regulation
does not itself evidence a sectarian or other impermissible constitutional
purpose. The provision-exemption dichotomy simply tracks the pattern of the
enabling statute and provides the mechanics of its implementation. Apart
altogether from the failure to challenge the provision-exemption dichotomy in
the enabling legislation, the mere fact of exemption is quite antithetical to
the assertion of indoctrinal purpose. If the true purpose of the section were
indoctrinal, there would scarcely be provision made for exemption, a fortiori,
unqualified exemption. A purely indoctrinal purpose, as it seems to me, would
brook no excuse but would, rather, seek to imbue all constituents with the self-same
dogma. As earlier observed, the exemption process leaves the exempting
authority without the right of refusal. It requires, at least at the pupil and
teacher level, no articulation of reasons. Indeed, even the nature and extent
of the exemption is left to the self-determination of the requesting party.
Further, there is no sanction attached for non-attendance occasioned by
exemption. The mere fact of unqualified exemption is said to evidence the
inadmissible indoctrinal purpose of the section. In my respectful view, it is
more consonant with the legitimate educative purpose earlier described. The
exemption process equally acknowledges the somewhat unique nature of religious
education in the public elementary school curriculum. It is somewhat unique in
that it is a subject taught during regular class hours in respect of which
unqualified exemption may be given. No marks are apparently awarded to those
who undertake the instruction. Similar observations, I suspect, might be made
in respect of physical education, save that exemption therefrom probably
requires the demonstration of cause. It is unique in another sense, one that
may well account for the exemption procedure. Moral education is not a subject
indigenous to the public elementary school system. Intellectual instruction
upon subjects such as mathematics, science, history, geography and language is
given primarily at school. Although reasonable people may differ as to the
methods of instruction and their adequacy, no reasonable person eschews the primacy
of the public education system in this respect. Moral education, however, is
different. Its principal sources include the family and church. It is a subject
of extreme sensitivity with many persons. It is, in my respectful view, in
recognition of and response to such considerations that the legislature enacted
the enabling authority and the Minister, the Regulation, to ensure individual
self-determination in connection with religious education in the public
elementary schools.

Thirdly, the subject-matter of the instruction in religious education, as
required by the Regulation, is drained of sectarian content, hence
demonstrative of an educative, rather than indoctrinal, purpose at bottom of
the Regulation. Section 28(6) provides that "issues of controversial or
sectarian nature shall be avoided". Such provision, in my respectful view,
ensures that instruction in religious education remains educational, not
indoctrinal. Its inclusion underscores, rather than negates, the secular
purpose of the Regulation. There is nothing in the language used elsewhere in
the Regulation nor in the enabling statute reflective of a contrary legislative
purpose of indoctrination rather than education. The subject- matter of
instruction in religious education is not otherwise mentioned in any statutory
provision. It is, a fortiori, that there is no legislative requirement that the
precepts of any religious group or sect be disseminated to public elementary
school pupils.

In addition to the matter of instruction in religious education, there is
also the manner in which it is to be given. Under s. 28(6) of the Regulation,
it is, prima facie, a teacher who shall give instruction in religious
education. The prima facie rule may be ousted in at least three instances,
namely, where:

(a) the teacher applies for and is given an exemption from giving such
instruction;

(b) the board applies for and is given an exemption from providing such
instruction to a particular class-room or school, and

(c) the board, by resolution, selects a member of the clergy or lay person
selected by the clergy to give such instruction.

The existence of the exemptions of (a) and (b), does not detract from the
general rule that it is a teacher, rather than a member or designate of the
clergy, who shall generally give such instruction. Indeed, the prima facie rule
of teacher instruction, especially when coupled with the injunction against
sectarian content, would seem to be indicative of a secular purpose:
instruction in religious education is not only to be non-sectarian in content,
but is also to be given by a non-sectarian teacher, an employee of the public
school board in whose school the pupil is in attendance. The taking-up by the
board of its option (c), does not detract from the non- sectarian nature of the
instruction, although it creates the potential of a sectarian instructor. Such
potential, however, may rest unrealized and, at all events, does not diminish
the secular purpose which underlies the legislation. The potential presence of
a sectarian instructor is not indicative of a legislative purpose of
indoctrination as has been here suggested. The content limitation of s. 28(6)
remains.

It is, accordingly, my respectful view that the purpose of s. 28(4) to (16)
inclusive, of the Regulation, does not infringe or deny the applicants' freedom
of religion guaranteed by
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

(c) The second test: legislative effects

A finding that s. 28(4) to (16) inclusive, of the Regulation were enacted
for a constitutionally admissible purpose does not determine the present
inquiry, for purpose is but the initial test of constitutional validity. The
effects of legislation with a constitutionally integral purpose may, none the
less, render it infirm on account of infringement or denial of constitutionally
guaranteed rights or freedoms. This second test of constitutional validity
mandates study of the actual impact of the legislation, the impression it
produces, the results and consequences which ensue from its operation, whereby
to determine whether its operation and application vitiate, in the present
case, the constitutional guarantee of religious freedom. The acknowledged nexus
between the dual tests of constitutional validity, purpose and effects, of
necessity, entails some re-travel over already familiar ground in the
identification and assessment of the impacts of the subsections. The present
inquiry, in fine, looks to what happens when the subsections, enacted for a
constitutionally admissible purpose, are in practice applied to the instruction
of pupils in the public elementary schools of this province.

In practical terms, it is the application of the impugned subsections of s.
28 of the Regulation which determines the extent to which the statutory mandate
of s. 50 of the Education Act, is implemented. Instruction in religious
education is thereby made available to pupils in public elementary schools. Its
availability is not universal for, as has been earlier observed, a board may
seek and be given an exemption therefrom in respect of various class-rooms or
schools. If available, it will generally be offered by the school's teachers,
save to the extent that they are neither exempted nor otherwise replaced by
board resolution. At all events, the instruction shall avoid issues of a
controversial or sectarian nature. Instruction will be received by pupils only
to the extent, if at all, of the desires of their parents, guardians, or pupils
themselves, if adult. In no case is there a requirement of participation in an
exercise or instruction beyond the extent of the desires of the parents,
guardians or adult pupil.

At bottom, the operation of the subsections ensures that, where a board
makes available instruction in religious education to pupils in a public
elementary school class-room, each pupil will receive such instruction, if any,
as the pupil, parent or guardian desires. It is the self-determination of each
pupil, his or her parents or guardians, however, not the mere fact that
instruction in religious education is provided by the board, that is dispositive
of whether, a fortiori to what extent, the pupil shall receive such
instruction. Irrespective that instruction in religious education may be
provided by a board, hence available to a pupil, its provision in any case
shall not exceed the desires of the individual pupil, parents or guardians. The
basis upon which the self- determination of each pupil is founded remains
personal to the pupil. The board is entitled to and raises no voice in respect
of such decision. Objection guarantees exemption in commensurate degree with
the request. It is, however, incumbent upon the pupil, guardian or parent to
initiate the claim for exemption, else silence, at least where provision is
made for such instruction, be considered acceptance of and participation in the
instruction given. It remains to determine whether the scheme thereby provided
is obnoxious to the guarantee of religious freedom under
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
.

In the first place, the effects of the subsections do not prevent individual
pupils from entertaining religious beliefs, declaring them openly nor
manifesting such beliefs by worship and practice. The subsections, neither in
terms nor by necessary implication, enjoin pupils from entertaining individual
religious beliefs nor, indeed, even inquire of them as to the existence, nature
or state of any such belief. There is not, for example, any provision the
effect of which is to bar those who entertain any or specific religious beliefs
from such instruction nor, on the other hand, to erect any or specific
religious beliefs as conditions precedent to receipt of any such instruction.
The unqualified nature of the exemption provided would seem, rather, to
underscore that it is self-determination of religious beliefs that the
provisions seek to ensure rather than to stifle or eliminate. To provide for
instruction in religious education for a particular constituency, pupils in
public elementary school, and, at the same time, to guarantee unqualified
exemption therefrom is scarcely inimical to religious freedom. It permits the
constituents to work out for themselves, not only their own religious beliefs,
if any, but to what extent, if at all, they wish to declare them openly in the
context of instruction in religious education in the public elementary schools
which they attend, should it be there given.

Secondly, it is not, in my respectful view, the effect of the subsections to
coerce individuals to affirm a specific religious belief, nor to manifest a
specific religious practice for a sectarian purpose. In this respect, I take
coercion to include not only its more obvious forms, such as direct commands to
act or refrain from acting on pain of sanction, but, equally, indirect forms of
control whose effect is to determine or limit what would otherwise be alternative
courses of conduct available to others: see R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra,
per Dickson J. at pp. 336-7 S.C.R., p. 354 D.L.R. It is not the effect of the
subsections to force anyone to act in a way contrary to his beliefs or her
conscience. All are not bound to a sectarian Christian ideal. The dignity of
non- Christians is not impaired. The subsections do not proclaim the standards
of any faith, a fortiori, the precepts of Christian faith. They do not, as did
the Lord's Day Act in Big M Drug Mart Ltd., supra, take religious values rooted
in Christian morality and translate them into positive laws binding on
believers and non-believers alike. There is not enacted any prohibition whereby
non-Christians are enjoined, for religious reasons, from carrying out
activities which are otherwise lawful, moral and normal. There is not, by the
subsections, a protection of any religion and the concomitant non-protection of
others.

The legislation is strikingly silent in the proclamation of the standards of
any faith. It rather simply makes provision for instruction in religious
education to be offered in public elementary schools. It forces such
instruction upon no one. It positively eschews the affirmation of a specific
religious belief by its injunction against teachings of a sectarian or
controversial nature. It offers the programme, as well as the exemptions,
equally to Christians, non-Christians and non- believers. The exemptions are
unqualified and can be claimed with equivalent efficacy by Christians, non-Christians
and non- believers, alike. Observance of or adherence to the precepts of any
faith or religion is nowhere mentioned. The provisions, in my respectful view,
preserve and enhance the multicultural heritage of Canadians, rather than
impair religious freedom, an obvious component of it.

Thirdly, it is not the effects of the subsection to impose substantial,
non-trivial costs or burdens which interfere with religious beliefs or
practices. It has been authoritatively held that although the constitution shelters,
inter alia, the religious freedoms of individuals and groups, it does not do so
absolutely, but only to the extent that religious beliefs or conduct might
reasonably or actually be threatened by the impact of legislative activity. The
proscription of
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
only becomes engaged in the event that
the legislative action of the state imposes a cost or burden capable of
interfering with religious belief or practice. To interfere in a
constitutionally inadmissible manner the burden imposed must be more than
trivial or insubstantial.

In the case at bar, there is no legislative nor administrative action which,
in an economic sense, increases the costs of practising or otherwise
manifesting religious beliefs. At bottom, the costs are said to be the need to
claim exemption in order to avoid instruction in religious education in the
public elementary schools. It is said that the claim of exemption carries an
added cost in the form of psychological pressure upon the impressionable mind
of a child to conform, thereby rendering illusory the right to claim an
exemption.

It will be recalled that in Jones, supra, it had also been contended that a
provision in the School Act of the Province of Alberta, which excused a pupil
from attendance at a public school, inter alia, upon production of a
certificate of efficient instruction elsewhere infringed the appellant's
religious freedom. The appellant was there charged with three counts of truancy
on the part of his own children, who were neither attending public school nor
had been excused therefrom. Mr. Jones asserted that he had been authorized by
God to educate his children and that any legislative requirement, as in s.
143(1) of the School Act, that he obtain a certificate of efficient instruction
or secure approval as a private school, contravened his religious freedom. On
behalf of a majority of the court upon this issue, Wilson J. observed at pp.
313-14 S.C.R., p. 578 D.L.R.:

... not every effect of legislation on religious
beliefs or practices is offensive to the constitutional guarantee of freedom of
religion. Section 2(a) does not require the Legislature to refrain from
imposing any burdens on the practice of religion. Legislative or administrative
action whose effect on religion is trivial or insubstantial is not, in my view,
a breach of freedom of religion. I believe that this conclusion necessarily
follows from the adoption of an effects-based approach to the
Charter
.

In my respectful view, the excerpted passage is equally apposite to the
circumstances of the case at bar. The section, read as a whole, has no
substantial impact on religious freedom. It does not purport to force public
school children to take instruction in religious education. It allows pupils,
in the most unqualified of terms and free of sanction, to be absent from such
instruction. It defers to the individual beliefs and self-determination of the
pupils, their parents or guardians. Instruction in religious education is only
compulsory for those who desire it. Such instruction in no case shall exceed
their desires and, at all events, shall not contain any sectarian or
controversial matter. The impact of the statutory machinery constructed by the
section on the applicants' religious freedom is, at bottom, a formalistic and
technical one: an exemption must be sought by the applicants. It may be
observed that, once sought, the exemption is given without question or
qualification. There is, accordingly, in my respectful view, no
s. 2
(a)
infringement.

It will be recalled that in the case at bar there is evidence concerning the
impact of the provision-exemption process of s. 28 of the Regulation. There is,
first of all, direct evidence of the actual impact of specific instruction in
religious education upon Andrea Millington whilst she attended a public
elementary school administered by the respondent Board. The substance of that
evidence, earlier summarized, is not a matter of dispute. In addition, there is
the more general but conflicting evidence of expert opinion contained in the
affidavits of Dr. Freedman, on behalf of the applicants, and of Dr. Kennedy, on
behalf of the respondent Board. Each proffers an opinion as to the impact of
the exemption process on the students and describes the pressures associated
therewith.

It may well be argued that the evidence of the impact of a particular
curriculum of studies in religious education upon a single public elementary
school pupil at a given point in time lacks sufficient relevance to warrant its
reception and consideration on the issue of the constitutional validity of the
subsection of the Regulation which is here at issue. At all events, in my
respectful view, assuming relevance, its probative value upon such issue is, at
best, somewhat tenuous. As it would appear to me, at least, evidence of expert
opinion of the type here tendered is relevant to the issue of the effects of
the subsection, viz., the impact of the legislation, hence its
constitutionality. In the case at bar, however, the evidence of expert opinion
is not dispositive of the constitutional question for at least two reasons. In
the first place, the evidence of expert opinion is conflicting. The opinion of
Dr. Freedman, one of impressive academic qualifications, is controverted by the
opinion of Dr. Kennedy, whose practical experience is as impressive as the
academic background of Dr. Freedman. We are, quite simply, in no position to
make a factual determination of which view ought to prevail. It follows, in my
respectful view, that the applicants have simply failed to discharge the burden
of persuasion cast upon them to demonstrate constitutional infringement,
assuming that what is there disclosed would, in any case, rise to such extent:
compare R. v. Jetco Manufacturing Ltd. and Alexander (1987),
1987 CanLII 4436 (ON CA)
, 57 O.R. (2d) 776,
31 C.C.C. (3d) 171 (C.A.).

In addition, and assuming a view of the evidence most favourable to the
applicants, I am simply not persuaded, for the reasons earlier given, that the
effects of the section, viewed as a whole, are of such nature or extent as to
give rise to a violation of the applicants' religious freedom as guaranteed
under
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. At bottom, the essence of the applicants'
complaint is that the provision-exemption scheme of the Regulation has the
effect of coercing attendance in religious education classes, thereby
compromising religious beliefs and infringing religious freedom. It will be
recalled, however that the enabling legislation of ss. 50(1) and 10(1), para.
18 of the Education Act, is to the same effect. It is not, however, argued that
the enabling authority is constitutionally infirm. It is not suggested that s.
28 of the Regulation goes beyond what is authorized by the Act. Either the
effects of the provision-exemption scheme coerce attendance in classes of
instruction in religious education, thereby infringing religious freedom, or
they do not. It is conceded that the legislation does not have such effect.
Neither can it be said, in my respectful view, that the administrative scheme
put in place by s. 28 of the Regulation which not only implements and tracks
the statutory mandate, but which also provides for unqualified exemption
without specification of grounds, has such impermissible effect. The
unqualified nature of the exemption provisions, in my respectful view, is the
antithesis of constitutionally inadmissible coercion, not an exemplification of
it. I am, accordingly, not prepared to hold that the provisions of s. 28 of the
Regulation, viewed as a whole, offend the applicants' rights under s. 2(a) of
the Charter.

(d) Conclusion

It is, accordingly, my respectful view, for the reasons above given that, in
neither purpose nor effects, do s. 28(4) to (16), inclusive, of the Regulation
infringe or deny the applicants' freedom of religion as guaranteed under
s.
2(a)
of the
Charter
.

(3) The Regulation and equality rights

(a) Introduction

In addition to their impeachment of s. 28(4) to (16) inclusive, of the
Regulation as obnoxious to the freedom of religion guarantee of
s. 2(a)
of the

Charter
, the applicants assert constitutional infringement of their right to
equality before and under the law and their right to the equal protection and
benefit of the law without discrimination based on religion, as enshrined in
s.
15(1)
of the Charter.

A brief rehearsal of the positions of the parties will inform a
determination of the present issue.

(b) The position of the parties

(i) The position of the applicants

On behalf of the applicants, Mr. Sharpe takes the position that the
subsections, in purpose and effect, discriminate in favour of Christians and
against others, whether non-Christians or non-believers, thereby denying to
these latter groups the very equal protection and benefit of the law without
discrimination based on religion which they are guaranteed by
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
. The subsections confer a benefit upon one religion, Christianity,
which is withheld from others, namely, the teaching of its precepts in the
public elementary schools to the exclusion of the tenets of non-Christian
religions. Further, it is said the provision of instruction in religious
education to one group, those of Christian beliefs, but merely an exemption for
other groups, non-Christians and non-believers, denies this latter class of
persons, on religious grounds, the right to equal treatment under the law. It
is the submission of Mr. Sharpe that s. 28 of the Regulation is also
discriminatory in that it forces those who do not accept the particular
Christian beliefs of the teacher to take a positive, an application for
exemption, which is not required of adherents to the religion taught. Not only
is such requirement of exemption overtly discriminatory in distinguishing
between groups on religious grounds, but it also extracts a penalty from
religious minorities that adherents to the Christian majority do not pay.

(ii) The position of the respondents

Mr. Sopinka, on behalf of the respondent Board, submits that the provisions
of the subsections authorize religious education, but neither specify nor
require that instruction be in the precepts of any particular, a fortiori,
Christian, religion. Put shortly, the provisions do not have a facially
discriminatory purpose nor effect. He next takes the position that the
exemption provisions available without restriction to non-participants, in
purpose and effects, operate to ensure "equal protection of the law"
through a guarantee that no person, irrespective of the existence or nature of
his or her religious beliefs, need participate in a programme of instruction in
religious education to which he or she objects for reasons of conscience or
belief. It is finally said that the statutory exemption does not constitute a
discriminatory penalty against non-believers or non-Christians on account of
the presence of alternate activities, the lack of disciplinary sanction and the
wholly unexceptional nature of the exemption process in modern public
elementary school activities.

On behalf of the respondent Minister, Mr. Wright acknowledges that the
Regulation must not, in purpose or effects, impose greater burdens nor confer
greater benefits on adherents of one religion than those of others. He also
takes the position that the Regulation, read as a whole, is not facially
discriminatory between or amongst religions, but rather simply authorizes local
boards to provide instruction in religious education per se. Mr. Wright
contends that a declaration of invalidity ought not to be made on account of
the possibility that a local board might implement the Regulation in a manner
inimical to its obligations under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, and beyond the
prophylactic effect of
s. 1
. Counsel for the respondent Minister admits that,
possibly, in an individual case, local implementation of the Regulation might
demonstrate unequal or discriminatory treatment such as to engage the remedial
mechanism of s. 24(1), but such possibility, per se, does not render the
Regulation constitutionally inadmissible.

(c) The equality analysis

(i) Introduction

The applicants' submission of constitutional inadmissibility based upon an
allegation of infringement or denial of their
s. 15(1)

Charter
rights, requires
that the purpose and effects of s. 28 of the Regulation be next measured
against the substance or content of the guarantees of equality before and under
the law, as well as its equal protection and benefit. The constitutional
determination next to be made will be informed by a brief discussion of certain
aspects of the impugned subsections material to the substance of the equality
rights guaranteed by s. 15(1) of the Charter.

It may be recalled in the first place that the subsections make neither
express nor implied reference to any particular religion, its tenets or
precepts. There is not, for example, in any description of the subject-matter
of instruction in religious education, any mention that such instruction shall
consist, in whole or in part, of the teachings to the tenets or precepts of the
Christian faith. No such tenet or precept is itself part of the statutory
scheme, as for example was the case of Sunday observance under the Lord's Day
Act found to be constitutionally deficient on other grounds in Big M Drug Mart
Ltd., supra. There, equally, is no mention of any particular faith in
connection with the surrogate clergy who may instruct, by board resolution, in
lieu of the board's regular teachers. Sectarian and controversial issues are,
at all events, to be avoided.

Secondly, the only criterion or condition precedent to the receipt of
instruction is that the subject be a pupil in an Ontario public elementary
school whose school or class has not been awarded a ministerial exemption under
s. 28(15) of the Regulation. To put the matter somewhat differently, absent
school or class exemption, instruction in religious education is available to
all pupils in public elementary schools, irrespective of the existence or
nature of their religious beliefs. It is, in other words, not a condition
precedent to receipt of instruction in religious education by a public
elementary school pupil that such pupil, his parents or guardians, have any, a
fortiori particular, religious beliefs. The availability of such instruction is
to all who attend schools where it is offered.

Thirdly, the pupillary exemption of s. 28(10) is unqualified. It must be
extended to all who request it. The mandatory language there used makes no
reference to the existence, if any, a fortiori particular, religious beliefs as
a condition precedent to exemption. Application is dispositive of exemption.
The subsection requires no articulation of reasons or cause, a fortiori, any
founded upon the existence of state of religious beliefs of the pupils seeking
exemption. Upon application exemption must be given. In no case are reasons
required nor can exemption be refused.

Finally, it would appear clear from the whole of s. 28 that exemption from
instruction in religious education attracts no penalty nor sanction. Exemption
may, of course, entail the absence of a pupil from the class-room during the
period designated for instruction in religious education which, it will be
recalled, occurs during regular school hours. Whether absence even occurs, as
with the assertion of a claim for exemption, is wholly dependent upon the
desires of the parent, guardian or pupil, if an adult. It is expressly provided
by s. 28(13) that class-room absence on account of exemption does not
constitute a contravention of the rules of the school. It would seem
self-evident that, if failure of class-room attendance on account of exemption
does not contravene the rules of the school and thereby attracts no penalty,
exemption without concomitant absence mandates the same result. No other loss,
disadvantage or disability ensues to those who claim, therefore receive,
exemption.

(ii) The first step: identification of the class

It is first necessary in the case of any challenge founded upon
s. 15(1)
of
the
Charter
, to make comparisons, thereby to identify the class or classes of
persons who are said to be treated differently: see R. v. Ertel, supra.

Section 28 of the Regulation, in terms, has application to students in the
public elementary schools of Ontario. It is that class of persons to whom
instruction in religious education is made available and from whom it will be
withheld, upon and to the extent of the exercise of pupillary exemption. For
purposes of classification, however, the focus of the inquiry must be somewhat
narrower. Equality, as it has been said, is of an essentially relational nature
and invites comparison between or amongst classes of persons who, similarly
situated, are said to be treated differently by legislative enactment: see, R.
v. R.L., supra, per Morden J.A., at p. 424 C.C.C., and R. v. Ertel, supra, per
Lacourciere J.A., at p. 448 C.C.C., p. 271 C.R. It will be recalled, further,
that in a case under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, the issue is not whether those
who assert a violation of their equality rights have differences which exist
independently of the law said to be discriminatory, but rather whether the law
treats those persons differently: see R. v. Century 21 Realty Inc., supra, at
pp. 758-9 O.R., pp. 670-1 D.L.R., p. 374 C.C.C. The application of this
principle is exemplified by the decision of the Court of Appeal in Ertel,
supra. There, the challenge under
s. 15(1)
was to the provisions of
s. 507(3)

of the
Criminal Code
(now
s. 507
) which permitted the Attorney-General to
indict an accused in respect of an offence, notwithstanding that a preliminary
inquiry in relation to such an offence had either not been held or, if held,
had resulted in the discharge of the accused in relation to such offence. The
effect of the statutory provision, the constitutional validity of which was
impeached, was to create a separate or discrete class of accused persons,
namely, those who are subject to a direct indictment. Membership in such class
was determined either exclusively by the Attorney-General under whose authority
the prosecution was being conducted or by the conjoint effect of a discharge at
the preliminary inquiry and a decision of the Attorney-General to indict directly.
At all events, the accused had no choice in the matter. The court there held
that, for classification purposes, the two classes were:

(a) accused persons who are subject to direct indictment, and

(b) accused persons who are not subject to direct indictment.

It is the practical effect of s. 28 of the Regulation, read as a whole, that
of the class of public elementary school pupils in class-rooms where
instruction in religious education is offered, there are two separate
categories or classes, that is to say:

(c) pupils who receive instruction in religious education, and

(d) pupils who do not receive instruction in religious education.

It is the legislation that creates such classes. It is the
self-determination of the pupil that decides in which category or class he or
she will fall.

Discriminatory inequality in the case at bar is said to be grounded upon
religious belief. The applicants urge that Christians receive instruction in
religious education whereas non-Christians, including both non-believers and
those who entertain religious beliefs but not of the Christian majority,
receive exemption. Since it is the nature of the religious belief of the pupil
which is said to constitute the basis of the alleged discriminatory inequality,
I am prepared to consider, for classification purposes, the categories or
classes of public elementary school pupils as:

(e) pupils who entertain Christian religious beliefs, and

(f) pupils who do not entertain Christian religious beliefs.

It may be observed, however, that it is not s. 28 of the Regulation which
introduces the distinguishing characteristic which lies at the root of
categories (e) and (f). Distinctions amongst public elementary school pupils on
the basis of the existence or nature of religious belief exist independently of
s. 28. It is not, in other words, s. 28 which itself creates such distinction.
The existence or nature of the religious beliefs of public elementary school
pupils exist quite independently of s. 28. Accepting categories (e) and (f) as relevant,
however, for the purposes of classification, necessitates a determination of
whether s. 28 of the Regulation treats such persons differently.

(iii) The second step: are the classes similarly situated?

The second step in a
s. 15(1)

Charter
analysis requires a determination of
whether the classes above-described are "similarly situated" for, at
bottom of any equality rights, lies the obligation of the state to treat those
who are similarly situated similarly: see, Re McDonald and The Queen supra, p.
764 O.R., p. 416 D.L.R., p. 349 C.C.C., per Morden J.A.; R. v. Century 21
Realty Inc., supra and R. v. Ertel, supra, per Lacourciere J.A. at p. 419
C.C.C. It would seem self-evident, and has been authoritatively held, that if
the classes identified for classification purposes are not "similarly
situated", there is no constitutional obligation of equal or similar
treatment, hence no infringement nor breach of
s. 15(1)
: see, Bregman v. A.-G.
Can. (1986),
1986 CanLII 2485 (ON CA)
, 57 O.R. (2d) 409, 33 D.L.R. (4th) 477, 27 C.R.R. 25 (C.A.), and R.
v. Ertel, supra, per Lacourciere J.A. at pp. 419-20 C.C.C.

There can be little doubt that irrespective of whether one takes classes (c)
and (d), supra, or (e) and (f), supra, for purposes of the
s. 15(1)
analysis,
differences exist between the constitutents of each class. If the mere
existence of a difference between classes, per se, were dispositive of a
s.
15(1)
claim, as it would seem to me, the equality rights of the subsection
would sound a rather hollow ring. Few, if any, cases alleging a
s. 15(1)

infringement would proceed beyond this stage of analysis. There is, however, in
the present case, an overriding or controlling similarity, unity or nexus
between the classes: all the members of the classes are pupils in the public
elementary school system. It is, accordingly, necessary to proceed to the third
stage or level of the
s. 15(1)
analysis, thereby to determine whether the
differential treatment constitutes inadmissible inequality or discrimination
within the meaning of such provisions.

(iv) The third step: the nature of the treatment

The third step in an analysis of legislation under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter

involves a consideration of the nature of the differential treatment to
determine whether it infringes or denies the substance of the guarantees of the
subsection. It would seem clear that it is not every unequal treatment which
constitutes an infringement of
s. 15(1)
, thereby requiring consideration of
s.
1
to sustain constitutional vitality. At bottom, the applicants must
demonstrate that pupils who do not receive instruction in religious education
or pupils who do not entertain or hold Christian religious beliefs are at an
inherent disadvantage in comparison with those who do so. Further, the
distinction must be so unfair as to be discriminatory on the asserted basis,
having regard to the purpose and effect of the section: see, R. v. Ertel,
supra, per Lacourciere J.A. at p. 420 C.C.C. There must be some unfairness or
irrationality about the differential treatment to engage the application of s.
15(1) of the Charter.

In one and an obvious sense, a public elementary school pupil who is
exempted from instruction in religious education suffers a disadvantage
inherent in any process of exemption, namely, lack of that from which he or she
is exempt, in this case instruction in religious education. It is inherent in
any notion of advantage or benefit that those not entitled thereto are at a
disadvantage in comparison with those who are so entitled. There are, however,
no automatic exemptions in the sense that certain members of the wider class,
public elementary school pupils, are per se exempt from such instruction. He or
she who desires exemption must first seek it. It is, of course, true that it is
the legislation which permits, indeed in cases of application, requires
exemption. Application therefor, however, is required. Without it no pupillary
exemption can be given. The legislation provides the choice. The pupil makes
it. The disadvantage as above-described is one which the pupil chooses. It is
not one, as for example was the case in Ertel, supra, that arises solely on
acccount of a determination made by a third party to invoke a legislative
mechanism which is said to be discriminatory.

It is necessary to consider whether the applicants have demonstrated that
the differential treatment of exempt pupils said to constitute an infringement
of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, is unfair or irrational. When all is said and done,
the exemption mechanism is invoked by the very pupil who alleges it to be
discriminatory. The legislation provides the mechanism. The pupil engages it.
The loss of "advantage", instruction in religious education, is a
direct consequence of the self- determination of the pupil. It is difficult to
describe a treatment as irrational or unfair when it arises in consequence of
the very act of the pupil who asserts such irrationality or unfairness. The
exemption mechanism facilitates and fosters individual choice and
self-determination. It is an exemplification of fairness not its antithesis.

It may also be noticed that exemption from instruction in religious
education need not, in all cases, include physical absence of the exempt pupil
from the class-room in which such instruction is being given: see s. 28(12). At
all events, there is no contravention of school rules occasioned by such
absence.

An analysis of the issue from the point of view of the non- Christian pupil,
in my respectful view, compels the same result. Religious belief, a fortiori
Christian religious belief, is neither a condition precedent to the reception
of instruction in religious education nor statutorily relevant to exemption
therefrom. Instruction in religious education is available to all public
elementary school pupils, not only to such pupils who hold Christian religious
beliefs. Exemption from instruction in religious education is available upon
request to public elementary school pupils as equally to those who do not hold
Christian religious beliefs as to those who do. Neither reception nor exemption
is contingent upon the existence or nature of religious beliefs on the part of
the pupil. Christians are as free to claim exemption as non- Christians are to
attend. The right of self-determination is available equally to all. The
reasons which underlie its exercise lie in the breast of the pupil and need
never be disclosed. There is neither inherent disadvantage to the non-
Christian pupil nor unfair or irrational treatment of him or her based upon
religious belief.

(d) Conclusion

It is, accordingly, my respectful view for the reasons above given, that, in
neither purpose nor effects, do s. 28(4) to (16) inclusive, of the Regulation
infringe or deny the applicants' their right to equality before and under the
law nor their rights to the equal protection and benefit of the law without
discrimination based on religion as guaranteed by
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

(4)
Section 1
of the
Charter

As a result of my finding that the applicants have failed to establish an
infringement or denial of either their religious freedom under
s. 2
(a) or of
their equality rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, it becomes unnecessary to
consider whether, in the event of such infringement, s. 28 might, none the
less, be constitutionally sustainable under
s. 1
of the Charter.

5. THE CONSTITUTIONALITY OF THE CURRICULUM OF THE RESPONDENT BOARD

(1) Introduction

The applicants' assertions of constitutional invalidity, it may be recalled,
are not confined to the submission that s. 28(4) to (16), inclusive, of the
Regulation are infirm on account of their infringement of the applicants'
religious freedom and/or equality rights. A discrete attack is made upon the
constitutional integrity of the curriculum of the respondent Board in
accordance with which instruction in religious education is given to public
elementary school pupils in Elgin County. It is argued that such curriculum, in
purpose or effects, infringes or denies the applicants' religious freedom
and/or equality rights.

A consideration of the constitutional validity of the Board's curriculum
must await a determination of two preliminary issues, that is to say:

(a) whether the curriculum of the respondent Board is a "law"
within the meaning of
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, such that it may
be declared to be of no force or effect to the extent of its inconsistency with
the provisions of the Constitution, and

(b) if the answer to (a) is in the affirmative, what is the relevant
curriculum to be considered in determining the constitutional issue?

It is to those preliminary issues that I shall briefly turn.

(2) The curriculum as "law"

(a) Introduction

It may be recalled that the applicants seek judicial review, inter alia:

(b) to declare the curriculum of religious studies prescribed by respondent,
the Elgin County Board of Education, to be a denial of certain rights or
freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter
.

The declaration sought by the applicants seeks to engage the provisions of

s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, whereby any law that is inconsistent
with the provisions of the Constitution is to be declared, to the extent of
such inconsistency, of no force or effect. The subsection enacts, as follows:

52(1) The Constitution of Canada is the supreme
law of Canada, and any law that is inconsistent with the provisions of the
Constitution is, to the extent of the inconsistency, of no force or effect.

(Emphasis added.) The initial issue is whether the curriculum of the
respondent Board, in accordance with which instruction in religious education
is given in the public elementary schools of Elgin County under provincial
legislative mandate, falls within the term "any law" in
s. 52(1)
of
the
Constitution Act, 1982
.

(b) The positions of the parties

It is the position of the applicants, as I apprehend the submissions of Mr.
Sharpe, that the curriculum of the respondent Board falls within the reach of
the descriptive words "any law" in
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act,
1982
and, thereby, requires that the curriculum be declared of no force or
effect to the extent of its inconsistency with, inter alia, the provisions of
the Charter. Mr. Sharpe acknowledges that the curriculum of the respondent
Board is not "law" in the traditional sense of Acts or regulations
passed by the Federal Parliament or provincial legislature, but submits that,
since the executive action of the respondent Board is authorized by and
dependent upon provincial statute, it is subject to Charter review, including a
declaration of the nature envisaged by s. 52(1) of the Constitution Act, 1982.

On the other hand, Mr. Sopinka, on behalf of the respondent Board, takes the
position that the curriculum of the respondent Board in respect of instruction
in religious education is not "law" for the purposes of
s. 52(1)
of the

Constitution Act, 1982
. It is his submission that not all that is done by a
governmental agency is "law" within the meaning of the subsection. In
particular, the argument continues, the curriculum of the respondent Board is
not made binding by the force of the state and, accordingly, does not fall
within the compass of "any law" as that phrase appears in s. 52(1) of
the Constitution Act, 1982.

Mr. Wright, on behalf of the respondent Minister, takes no position with
respect to this preliminary question nor as to the constitutional validity of
the curriculum of the respondent Board. In para. 27 of his factum, however, in
addressing the applicants' submission that s. 28 of the Regulation is invalid
on account of its infringement of
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, counsel for the
respondent Minister conceded, as follows:

27. Regulation 262, R.R.O. 1980, s. 28 should not
be declared invalid on the ground that it is possible that a local board might
implement the regulation in a manner which conflicts with its obligations under
the
Charter
. It may be that on the facts of individual cases the established
inequality or discriminatory treatment could be such that the Courts should
intervene to provide a remedy under
s. 24(1)
of the Charter in that particular
case. However, the regulation itself cannot be held to be discriminatory
because it is possible for the curriculum of a local board to violate
s. 15(1)
.

(c) The authorities

It will be convenient to commence the present discussion by a recollection
of the application of the
Charter
. In s. 32(1), the Charter provides for its
application in the following terms:

32(1) This
Charter
applies

(a) to the Parliament and government of Canada in
respect of all matters within the authority of Parliament including all matters
relating to the Yukon Territory and Northwest Territories; and

(b) to the legislature and government of each
province in respect of all matters within the authority of the legislature of
each province.

The effect of
s. 32(1)
of the
Charter
was considered by the Supreme Court of
Canada in Retail, Wholesale & Department Store Union, Local 580 v. Dolphin
Delivery Ltd.,
1986 CanLII 5 (SCC)
, [1986] 2 S.C.R. 573, 33 D.L.R. (4th) 174, [1987] 1 W.W.R. 577.
The court had there to determine whether an individual could found a cause of action
or defence against another individual upon the basis of a breach of Charter
right. The court considered the scope of s. 32(1) in order to determine whether
the Charter had application to private litigation between purely private
parties in the absence of any exercise of or reliance upon governmental action
which would invoke the Charter. McIntyre J., with the apparent concurrence of
all other members of the court who heard the appeal, described the effect of s.
32 at pp. 598-9 S.C.R., p. 195 D.L.R.:

It is my view that
s. 32
of the
Charter
specifies
the actors to whom the Charter will apply. They are the legislative, executive
and administrative branches of government. It will apply to those branches of
government whether or not their action is invoked in public or private
litigation. It would seem that legislation is the only way in which a
legislature may infringe a guaranteed right or freedom. Action by the executive
or administrative branches of government will generally depend upon
legislation, that is, statutory authority. Such action may also depend,
however, on the common law, as in the case of the prerogative. To the extent
that it relies on statutory authority which constitutes or results in an
infringement of a guaranteed right or freedom, the Charter will apply and it
will be unconstitutional. The action will also be unconstitutional to the
extent that it relies for authority or justification on a rule of the common
law which constitutes or creates an infringement of a Charter right or freedom.
In this way the Charter will apply to the common law, whether in public or
private litigation. It will apply to the common law, however, only in so far as
the common law is the basis of some governmental action which, it is alleged,
infringes a guaranteed right or freedom.

After making reference to the decision of the Ontario Court of Appeal in Re
Blainey and Ontario Hockey Ass'n, supra, McIntyre J. continued, at pp. 602-3
S.C.R., pp. 197-8 D.L.R.:

... it is difficult and probably dangerous to
attempt to define with narrow precision that element of governmental
intervention which will suffice to permit reliance on the
Charter
by private
litigants in private litigation. Professor Hogg has dealt with this question,
at p. 677, supra, where he said:

"... the
Charter
would apply to a private
person exercising the power of arrest that is granted to 'any one' by the

Criminal Code
, and to a private railway company exercising the power to make
bylaws (and impose penalties for their breach) that is granted to a 'railway
company' by the Railway Act; all action taken in exercise of a statutory power
is covered by the Charter by virtue of the references to 'Parliament' and
'legislature' in
s. 32
. The Charter would also apply to the action of a
commercial corporation that was an agent of the Crown, by virtue of the
reference to 'government' in s. 32."

It would also seem that the
Charter
would apply
to many forms of delegated legislation, regulations, Orders in Council,
possibly municipal by-laws, and by-laws and regulations of other creatures of
Parliament and the legislatures. It is not suggested that this list is
exhaustive. Where such exercise of, or reliance upon, governmental action is
present and where one private party invokes or relies upon it to produce an infringement
of the Charter rights of another, the Charter will be applicable. Where,
however, private party "A" sues private party "B" relying
on the common law and where no act of government is relied upon to support the
action, the Charter will not apply. I should make it clear, however, that this
is a distinct issue from the question whether the judiciary ought to apply and
develop the principles of the common law in a manner consistent with the
fundamental values enshrined in the Constitution. The answer to this question
must be in the affirmative. In this sense, then, the Charter is far from
irrelevant to private litigations whose disputes fall to be decided at common
law. But this is different from the proposition that one private party owes a
constitutional duty to another, which proposition underlies the purported
assertion of Charter causes of action or Charter defences between individuals.

See also, Re Klein and Law Society of Upper Canada; Re Dvorak and Law
Society of Upper Canada (1985),
1985 CanLII 3086 (ON HCJDC)
, 50 O.R. (2d) 118 at p. 157, 16 D.L.R. (4th) 489
at p. 528, 13 C.R.R. 120, per Callaghan J. (Eberle J. concurring), and
Operation Dismantle Inc. v. The Queen,
1985 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 441, 18 D.L.R. (4th)
481, 13 C.R.R. 287.

In Re Ontario English Catholic Teachers Ass'n and Essex County Roman
Catholic School Board (1987),
1987 CanLII 4043 (ON HCJ)
, 58 O.R. (2d) 545, 36 D.L.R. (4th) 115, 18 O.A.C.
271, the applicants sought judicial review of the termination by the respondent
board of the employment of the applicant, Morowanec, as a teacher in accordance

Charter
review. A
majority of this court, differently constituted, held that the policy of the

s. 52(1)
of the Constitution Act, 1982,
and, accordingly, under
s. 32(1)
, the Charter had no application to the
termination. Anderson J. (McKinlay J. concurring) reasoned at pp. 562-3 O.R.,

The purpose of the
Charter
is to protect the
individual against certain acts or activities which impinge upon the acts or
activities of the individual, and which, because they have behind them the
power of the state, leave the individual unable to resist. An obvious example
is the use of the search warrant. The relationship involved is that of the
subject to the state.

The relationship of the applicant Mordowanec to
the respondent board is not that of the subject to the state; it is the
relationship of an employee to his employer. I do not consider it material that
the form of the contract is provided by the Act and the regulations thereunder,
or that the respondent board is controlled in certain respects concerning
termination of a teacher's employment by the provisions of the Act.

The real burden of Mordowanec's complaint is that
his employment was terminated for what he says was an improper

(discriminatory) cause. He has no contractual basis for this complaint, either

s.
15(1)
of the
Charter
cannot be invoked instead. I see nothing in the language

To designate as "law" the policy of the

He added, at p. 564 O.R., pp. 134-5 D.L.R., pp. 286-7 O.A.C.:

... the purpose of the
Charter
is to restrain the
exercise of the power of government in matters other than contract. I should

Craig J., dissenting, held that such policy was "law" under

of the

, and
