(d) The case at bar

In the case at bar, what is sought to be made the subject of
Charter

scrutiny is the curriculum of the respondent Board in accordance with which
instruction in religious education is given in the public elementary schools
under its administration.

The authority to provide instruction in religious education in the public
elementary schools of this province is furnished by s. 50 of the Education Act.
Section 10(1), para. 18 of the Act authorizes the making of regulations
governing the provision of religious education in such schools and providing
for pupil, teacher and Board exemptions therefrom. The Regulations, including s.
28, implement the statutory authority conferred by the Act. The Board, itself a
creature of the enabling Act, administers the Act and Regulations implementing
their provisions at the local level. The Board's authority to do so, in my
respectful view, derives wholly and exclusively from provincial legislative
enactment and subordinate legislation. Indeed, in the absence of such
legislation, the Board would have no existence, let alone authority. As it
appears to me, the respondent Board relies upon statutory authority to provide
the very instruction which the statute requires to be made available to pupils
in public elementary schools. Delegated to the local Board, for obvious good
reason, is the implementation of the statutory scheme of instruction in religious
education should the Board choose not to seek or be denied exemption. It is,
accordingly, my respectful view that, based upon the decision in Retail,
Wholesale & Department Store Union, Local 580 v. Dolphin Delivery Ltd.,
supra, the curriculum of the respondent Board in accordance with which
instruction in religious education is furnished under the legislative mandate
of the Education Act and Regulations is subject to
Charter
scrutiny.

The present application has about it some features analogous to situations
which not infrequently arise in the trial of criminal cases. The analogy may
shortly be exemplified. Let us suppose that a search warrant is issued in
accordance with the provisions of
s. 443(1)
of the
Criminal Code
. The warrant
is executed and articles seized. In a subsequent criminal prosecution, Crown
counsel tenders the articles seized as evidence to inculpate the accused in the
offence charged. Defending counsel objects to their admissibility upon the
basis that the search was unreasonable, hence in violation of
s. 8
of the

Charter
. It is not said that the enabling legislation, s. 443(1) of the
Criminal Code, nor the warrant itself offends against the Charter guarantee,
but rather that the execution of the warrant by investigating officers was unreasonable,
hence unconstitutional. In such a case, it would be for the trial judge to
determine whether, in the execution of the warrant, the accused applicant's s.
8 rights had been infringed. Thus, the administrative or executive action of
the state agency charged with the responsibility of implementing the authority
rooted in the statute is subject to curial review under the Charter. The remedy
sought would be exclusion of evidence under
s. 24(2)
of the Charter. The action
to be reviewed is not the enabling law or the order made pursuant thereto, but
rather the manner of its execution by agents of the state. Indeed, to hold
otherwise would be to immunize such action against Charter scrutiny: see,
generally, Re Zevallos and The Queen (1987),
1987 CanLII 169 (ON CA)
, 37 C.C.C. (3d) 79, 59 C.R. (3d)
153 (Ont.C.A.); Collins v. The Queen,
1987 CanLII 84 (SCC)
, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 265, 38 D.L.R. (4th) 508,
33 C.C.C. (3d) 1, and R. v. Finlay and Grellette, supra, leave to appeal to the
Supreme Court of Canada refused February 28,
1986, 54 O.R. (2d) 509
n,
65 N.R.
159
fn.

(e) Conclusion

It is, accordingly, my respectful view, for the reasons above given, that
the applicants are not disentitled to invoke the
Charter
to impeach the
curriculum of the respondent Board as inconsistent with the rights and freedoms
thereby guaranteed.

(3) The curriculum to be reviewed

(a) Introduction

It may be recalled that the curriculum of instruction in religious education
of the respondent Board has been the subject of ongoing review, change and
consultation with members of the community. It is unnecessary for present
purposes to here repeat what has earlier been said about the substance of the
curriculum. It will suffice, rather, to record that both in content and
instructor the curriculum has made changes in recent years. In earlier times,
almost exclusively Christian precepts were disseminated by fundamentalists,
designates of the Elgin County Bible Club, not otherwise connected with the
system of public education in Elgin County or elsewhere in Ontario. The most
recent curricula, actual as well as proposed, adopt a more cosmopolitan and
educative approach. Instruction is to be given by teachers. The fundamentalist
surrogate approach has been abandoned by the respondent Board.

(b) The positions of counsel

The submissions of the applicants invite consideration of the
constitutionality of the past as well as proposed curriculum. The court was
invited to strike down the former and enjoin the latter. Each was said to be in
violation of the applicants' freedom and equality rights.

Mr. Sopinka, on the other hand, reminded us of the inadvisability, indeed
inefficacy, of passing upon the constitutionality of that which is no longer in
existence and will not be revivified. He further took the position that, at all
events, no constitutional infringements were involved in the proposed
curriculum in respect of which the Board ought to be allowed to proceed.

(c) The case at bar

It will be recalled that the relief which the applicants seek in the present
proceedings is, inter alia:

(b) to declare the curriculum of religious studies prescribed by respondent,
the Elgin County Board of Education, to be a denial of certain rights or
freedoms guaranteed by the
Charter
, and

(c) to enjoin the respondent, the Elgin County Board of Education, from
continuing to require or permit its curriculum of religious studies to be
offered in its schools.

Such relief is said to be available upon proof that the applicants'
religious freedom under
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and equality rights under
s.
15(1)
of the Charter have been infringed by the curriculum of instruction in
religious education of the respondent Board. The remedies sought are said to
arise in consequence of the conjoint operation of
s. 52(1)
of the Constitution
Act, 1982, and
s. 24(1)
of the Charter. The relief sought is principally,
though not exclusively, declaratory in nature.

In my respectful view, it is neither necessary nor desirable, in consequence
of the nature of the relief here sought, to pronounce upon the
constitutionality of a curriculum of instruction in religious education which
is no longer followed in the public elementary schools administered by the
respondent Board. What is past is but prologue to that which shall be offered
in the schools of the respondent Board. As it appears to me, no useful purpose
would be achieved by disserting upon the constitutional vitality of a course of
instruction in religious education, since deceased, and in accordance with
which no public elementary school pupil in Elgin County will hereafter be instructed.
In some instances, to be certain, the mere fact of statutory repeal or a
termination or alteration in a course of action followed by the administrative
or executive branches of government under statutory authority will not
determine or truncate the inquiry into constitutional validity. The relief
sought in such cases as a result of what is said to have been constitutional
infringement is not, however, declaratory in nature. The relief is, rather,
specific to the asserted infringement, as for example, where the remedy claimed
as appropriate and just in the circumstances under
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
is
damages on account of constitutional infringement or, in a criminal
prosecution, where the relief sought under
s. 24(2)
of the Charter is the exclusion
of evidence tendered against one whose guaranteed right or freedom is said to
have been infringed or denied. In neither case can it be said that the claim is
moot. In each, there is a tangible effect of infringement. There is none in the
case at bar.

On the other hand, it might be said with equivalent authority that it is
premature to pass upon the constitutional integrity of a curriculum of
instruction in religious education that has yet to be given by teachers of the
respondent Board. One ought not assume that a statutory body will act in an
unconstitutional manner any more than it may be presumed that a court will act
in excess of its jurisdiction, thereby giving rise to relief by way of
extraordinary remedy in anticipation of jurisdictional error: see, for example,
Jorgenson v. Pool (1959),
1959 CanLII 454 (BC CA)
, 124 C.C.C. 39, 30 C.R. 333 sub nom. Jorgenson v.
North Vancouver Magistrates (B.C.C.A.), and R. ex rel. Fraser v. Meisner
(1955),
1955 CanLII 477 (NS SC)
, 113 C.C.C. 394, 37 M.P.R. 330 (N.S.S.C.).

There is, however, in my respectful view, some necessity for a determination
of the constitutional validity of the proposed curriculum, lest pupils in the
public elementary schools administered by the respondent Board who do not claim
exemption be required to undertake a course of instruction in religious
education that is not constitutionally permissible. It is that curriculum,
accordingly, which must be examined to determine whether what is proposed is
constitutionally sustainable under
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Charter
.

(4) The curriculum and freedom of religion

(a) Introduction

It is unnecessary to here repeat the description earlier given of the
curriculum nor at any length the submissions of counsel as to its
constitutional integrity.

(b) The positions of the parties

It will further suffice to observe that for essentially the reasons advanced
against the constitutionality of the enabling Regulation, Mr. Sharpe submits
that the curriculum is constitutionally inadmissible.

On the other hand, it is the position of Mr. Sopinka that the curriculum, in
comformity with the enabling Regulation, fosters rather than denies religious
freedom.

Mr. Wright took no position with respect to the constitutionality of the
curriculum of the respondent Board, but rather confined his submissions to the
applicants' assertion that the enabling Regulation was itself constitutionally
deficient.

(c) The case at bar

As has been earlier observed, the constitutionality of the underlying
statutory mandate is not dispositive of the self- same issue in respect of any
and all action taken by the executive and administrative branches of government
thereunder. Such action may, on the one hand, be fully in accordance with the
statutory mandate and evince no scent of constitutional infringement. On the
other hand, such action may be so at odds with the statutory mandate, as well
as constitutional principle, as to infringe or deny the very or other rights or
freedoms which the enabling authority itself does not offend, hence demand
remedial action under
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, or
s. 24
of the
Charter. Each case, as it is so often said, will depend upon its own facts and,
in particular, upon the nature of the administrative and executive action as it
falls to be adjudged against constitutionally guaranteed rights and freedoms.

In the case at bar, I am respectfully of the view that the curriculum of
instruction in religious education by means of which the respondent Board
proposes to discharge its statutory mandate is constitutionally sustainable. I
reach that conclusion for several reasons, many reminiscent of the basis upon
which I have earlier found the enabling authority to be constitutionally
adequate upon challenges under
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

In the first place, I am satisfied that, in neither purpose nor effect, does
the proposed curriculum of the respondent Board prevent individuals from
entertaining religious beliefs, declaring them openly or manifesting such
beliefs by worship and practice. Pupils are not enjoined from entertaining any
or particular religious beliefs. No inquiry is addressed to them as to the
existence, nature or state of any such beliefs. The holding of any or
particular religious beliefs is a condition precedent to neither the reception
of nor exemption from instruction in religious education. Pupils, their parents
and guardians, are fully informed of the exemption process. Exemptions are
granted upon request. No reasons need be advanced therefor.

Secondly, in my respectful view, it is neither the purpose nor the effects
of the proposed curriculum to coerce individuals to affirm a specific religious
belief or to manifest a specific religious practice for a sectarian purpose.
The mere fact that discussion of Christian religious beliefs predominates the
curriculum, thereby reproducing a mirror image of the county in which such
instruction is given, is not for the purpose nor does it have the effect of
forcing pupils to act in a way contrary to individual beliefs or conscience.
All are not, thereby, bound to a sectarian Christian ideal. They are not, for
example, graded upon such knowledge and only passed in the event of a
demonstration of adequate knowledge of and adherence to such beliefs. The
dignity of non-Christians is not impaired or otherwise compromised.

A review of the proposed curriculum and the consultative process applied by
the respondent Board satisfies me that the injunction against teachings of a
sectarian or controversial nature is being obeyed. Further, the programme is
offered, equally, to Christians, non-Christians and non-believers. The
exemptions, as earlier observed, are, as the legislation requires, unqualified
and may be claimed with equivalent efficacy by Christians, non-Christians and
non-believers. There is nowhere mention, a fortiori requirement, of observance
of or adherence to the precepts of any faith or religion.

Additionally, the effects of the proposed curriculum do not impose
substantial, non-trivial costs or burdens which interfere with religious
beliefs or practices. The burden, if any, imposed by the proposed curriculum
does not rise above the level earlier found not to be constitutionally infirm
in respect of the enabling legislation.

As it appears to me, the applicants' complaint concerning the proposed
curriculum of the respondent Board is more effects- based than founded upon a
constitutionally impermissible purpose. It is, none the less, desirable to
consider whether the proposed curriculum is animated by a purpose inimical to
the
Charter
guarantee of religious freedom. In essence, the complaint is that
the curriculum of the respondent Board is so weighted in favour of Christian
religious beliefs as to be demonstrative of a constitutionally impermissible
purpose, namely, to indoctrinate pupils in such beliefs, thereby infringing on
their religious freedom guaranteed under
s. 2(a)
of the Charter.

It is, no doubt, true that the teachings of Christian religious beliefs
predominate the proposed curriculum of instruction in religious education. They
equally predominate in the County of Elgin and, I venture to say, in Canada as
a whole. The
Charter
guarantees religious freedom. It does not guarantee that
where instruction is offered in religious education, equal time must be
afforded to the precepts of each and every of the world's religions,
irrespective of the number or location of its adherents. It may be that in some
cases it could be said that such an imbalance is demonstrative of a
constitutionally impermissible purpose of indoctrination. I am satisfied,
however, that for several reasons such a conclusion is not sustainable in the
premises.

In the first place, it will be recalled that in consequence of the
consultative processes of the Board, the curriculum of instruction in religious
education will include a discussion of the precepts of religion other than
Christianity. The Board solicited, received and proposes to have discussed
information concerning the beliefs of other of the world's religions. There is
nothing to suggest that the Board has been unfair or unreasonable in its
selections.

Secondly, as is statutorily required, the right of unqualified exemption
remains. There is nothing different about the procedural exemption as it
applies in Elgin County than in its application elsewhere in the province in
accordance with the statutory mandate. Reasons are not required. Application
therefor is dispositive of exemption. No sanction is attached or non-attendance
on account of exemption. Exemption is not dependent upon the existence nor
nature of the applicant's religious beliefs.

Thirdly, the instruction is to be offered through the Board's teachers,
rather than clergy-nominated surrogates whose self- interest and fervour may
tend to colour the nature or content of their instruction.

Finally, there is no warrant in the premises for a submission that the
Board, in its proposed curriculum, is doing otherwise than following the
legislative injunction against teachings of sectarian or controversial issues.

(d) Conclusion

It is, accordingly, my respectful view that, for the reasons above-given,
the proposed curriculum of the respondent Board does not, in purpose or effect,
infringe the applicants' religious freedom under
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

(5) The curriculum and equality rights

(a) Introduction

The final basis upon which it is said that the curriculum of the respondent
Board is constitutionally impermissible is that it denies the applicants their
rights to equality guaranteed by
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

(b) The position of the parties

The applicants and respondent Board here take essentially the same position
in respect of the curriculum as had earlier been taken by each in connection
with the submission of constitutional invalidity of s. 28 of the Regulation on
the self-same grounds. It is, accordingly, neither necessary nor desirable to
repeat such submissions in the present context.

(c) The case at bar

The unconstitutionality of the curriculum of the respondent Board on account
of its infringement of the equality rights of the applicants, is said to arise
as a result of the conferral of a benefit upon one religion, Christianity,
namely the teaching of its precepts in the public elementary schools of the
respondent Board, to the exclusion or virtual exclusion of the tenets of
non-Christian religions. Constitutional infirmity is said further to arise
because of the provision of instruction in religious education to one group,
pupils of Christian beliefs, but merely an exemption for other groups,
non-Christians and non-believers, thereby denying the latter groups, on religious
grounds, the right to equal treatment or benefit under the law.

A review of the proposed curriculum of the respondent Board satisfies me
that, in neither purpose nor effects, is there a teaching of the precepts of
Christian religions to the exclusion of the tenets of non-Christian religions.
It is true, as has earlier been observed, that discussion of Christian
religious beliefs dominates the curriculum of instruction in religious
education. The curriculum, however, reflects cognizance of our multicultural
heritage and encompasses discussion of other systems of religious beliefs.
Equal time for all is not a requisite of
s. 15(1)
, provided the treatment is
not unfair or unreasonable. It is not so here. Public meetings have solicited
the views of constituents. There is no evidence that the respondent Board has
failed to include materials on any religion upon request therefor. Whatever may
have been the case in respect of earlier curricula, in my respectful view, it
cannot be said of that which is proposed that discriminatory inequality arises
on account of the composition of the proposed curriculum.

It has further not been established, in my respectful view, that the purpose
or effect of the proposed curriculum is to provide instruction in religious
education to pupils of Christian religious beliefs and exemption to pupils who
do not hold such or any beliefs, thereby to deny to such latter groups, on
religious grounds, their right to equal treatment or benefit under the law.

In the first place, the statutory exemption mechanism is accorded its full
amplitude under the proposed curriculum. It may be engaged by the Christian,
the non-Christian and the non- believer on equivalent grounds and with
identical results. The existence or nature of religious beliefs is immaterial
to the operation of the exemption. It is equally immaterial to the provision of
instruction.

It is, further, rather to overstate the case to say that Christians get
instruction in religious education, whereas non- Christians and non-believers
receive exemption. One receives instruction where it is provided and no
exemption is sought. The holding of Christian religious beliefs neither
enhances nor detracts from pupillary entitlement to receive instruction. The
absence of such beliefs operates likewise. The absence of Christian religious
beliefs, per se, does not give nor enhance entitlement to exemption. It is
equally so with the holding of such beliefs. It is, in all cases,
self-determination that is dispositive. The religious beliefs or otherwise of a
pupil will, no doubt, be a factor of significance in the individual decision
whether to take instruction or apply for exemption. They are, however, no more
than a factor.

(d) Conclusion

It is, accordingly, my respectful view, for the reasons above-given, that,
in neither purpose nor effects, does the proposed curriculum of the respondent
Board infringe or deny the applicants their right to equality before and under
the law nor the rights to the equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination
based on religion as guaranteed by
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

(
6
)
Section 1
of the
Charter

As a result of my finding that the applicants have failed to establish an
infringement or denial of either their religious freedom under
s. 2
(a) or of their
equality rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
, it becomes unnecessary to
consider whether, in the event of such infringement, the curriculum of the
respondent Board might, none the less, be constitutionally sustainable under
s.
1
of the Charter.

IV DISPOSITION

In my respectful view, the application should be dismissed. The issue of
costs may be spoken to at a date to be fixed by the registrar.

28(1) A public school shall be opened or closed
each school day with religious exercises consisting of the reading of the

(7) to give religious instruction in the same school, the principal of the

This application was launched by the Corporation of the Canadian Civil
Liberties Association (the C.C.L.A.), in April, 1986. It was brought because of
the concern the association has had since its creation in 1964 regarding
programmes of religious instruction in the public schools. The association's
concern was that the promotion of knowledge about various religious ideologies
would be commendable, but the programme in use from time to time was
inappropriate as it appeared designed to promote a belief in a particular
ideology.

The association has taken an active role in promoting and advocating the
position that respect for basic civil liberties values requires that religious
exercises and religious instruction be eliminated from the public school
system. On March 14, 1985, in contemplation of the coming into force of
s. 15

of the
Charter
in April, 1985, the association wrote to the then Minister of
Education to renew its complaint; specific reference was made to the material
being used in Elgin County, in Norfolk, in Frontenac County and in the Port
Hope area. The basic complaint was that the material being taught was almost
exclusively Christian and offensive not only to non-Christians but to many
denominations of Christians as well. The association urged the Minister that as
Ontario was even more religiously and culturally heterogeneous than it had ever
been, religious instruction in the public schools should be terminated at the
earliest possible moment.

When that approach failed, the association brought this application. At this
point, the Millingtons had no connection with the association. It is necessary
to go back in time to see how they fit in.

In 1983, Mr. and Mrs. Millington lived in the Town of St. Thomas, in the
County of Elgin. Mr. Millington was the director of nursing for the Elgin
County Homes for Senior Citizens. Mr. and Mrs. Millington had three children:
Jared, then age two, Alison, then age four and Andrea, then age seven. In the
fall of 1983, Andrea was in Grade II at Forest Park Elementary School operated
by the Elgin County Board of Education. During that fall, Andrea experienced
recurring nightmares to the effect that the "devil" was after her and
that she was "burning in hell". On these occasions, she would wake up
in the night and be very distraught and in tears. Mr. and Mrs. Millington
discussed these dreams with Andrea and learned from her for the first time that
she was being taught religion at school.

Mr. and Mrs. Millington are members of the Baha'i faith and were raising
their children in that faith. The Baha'i religion is based upon principles of
tolerance and respect for other religions. As a member of that faith, Mr. and
Mrs. Millington wanted their children to learn about various religions and
their moral teachings and precepts.

Following this discovery, Mr. and Mrs. Millington made some inquiries. They
found that classes in religious instruction were given at Forest Park School by
Brian Plum, a member of the Elgin County Bible Association and that no other
religious instruction was either offered or available at Forest Park School.
They also discovered that during the religion classes, no regular teacher or
representative of the school or the school board was in the class-room.

Mr. Millington took up the matter with Andrea's teacher, Mrs. Flintoff. Mrs.
Flintoff showed Mr. Millington the religious instruction curriculum. He
concluded that it contained exclusively Christian teachings.

He then met with Mr. Plum and expressed some concern that since all the
children in the class were not Christian, and that even the Christians came
from different denominations, it was inappropriate to teach about only one
belief. He described Mr. Plum as "unreceptive and unsympathetic to my
suggestions". He said that Mr. Plum refused to consider altering his
course in any way because he said his way was "the truth". He said
that Mr. Plum said that if told by the board that he had to change his approach
to teach about other religions, he would resign. Mr. Plum said he was a
"born again Christian". Although he had no teaching qualifications,
he had a sincere interest in teaching children about Jesus.

Mr. Millington then met with Mr. Moore, then the principal of Forest Park
School. Mr. Moore seemed surprised at what Mr. Millington had to say and
appeared to be unaware of the nature of the instruction that was being offered.
Mr. Moore agreed to look into the situation. As far as Mr. Millington could
tell, no changes were made during the balance of that year.

In the fall of 1984, Andrea entered Grade III at Forest Park School and
advised her father that Mr. Plum was again teaching the religion classes and
that she was being taught lessons similar to those given her in Grade II.

Mr. Millington then arranged to meet with the new principal of the school,
Mr. Lovelock. He repeated his concerns to Mr. Lovelock who appeared to be
sympathetic. Mr. Lovelock agreed to sit in on one of Mr. Plum's classes and
also suggested that the Millingtons consider withdrawing Andrea from the class
during this particular period.

Mr. and Mrs. Millington say they considered this option very carefully and
they discussed it with Andrea. She was already very sensitive about the fact
that her religion was different from that of her teacher and her classmates and
they feared that excluding her in the manner suggested would ostracize and
embarrass her. Andrea could not accept this as a real choice. She was worried
about being teased by her peers and became upset at the suggestion. She said: "Please
don't make me sit in the hall." Accordingly, they decided that it was in
her better interest not to have her exempted from the classes.

Two weeks after their initial meeting, Mr. Millington met again with Mr.
Lovelock. The latter indicated that he had sat in on one of Mr. Plum's classes
and that during that class, Mr. Plum had not placed any emphasis upon the Devil
and had only discussed the concept of the Devil occasionally. Mr. Millington
pointed out that children seemed very interested in magical concepts such as
beasts with horned tails and pitchforks and that even though this concept was
talked about only occasionally, it had a great impact on the children. Mr.
Lovelock did not appear to disapprove of Mr. Plum's teaching and gave no
indication that anything would change.

The Millingtons then decided that they should bring the matter to the
attention of the Elgin County School Board and did so by letter.

The following year Andrea was in Grade IV at Forest Park School and was
again being taught religion by Mr. Plum. In the meantime, Alison had started
school and was in Grade I at Wellington Street Public School. Mr. Millington
met with Mr. VanPatter, the principal of that school, in May, 1986, and
expressed his concern about the fact that only Christianity was being taught in
the religious education class. Mr. VanPatter indicated that the curriculum was
under review and Mr. Millington indicated his willingness to participate in
such a review.

About the same, Mr. Millington met with Mrs. Gough, the religion teacher for
that school. She was also a member of the Elgin County Bible Association. He
looked at her lesson plans and she agreed with Mr. Millington's comments that
they were exclusively Christian teachings. She also advised Mr. Millington that
the curriculum was under review by an inter- denominational group; it turned
out that these were all Christian denominations.

During the school year 1986-1987, all three Millington children attended
Forest Park School in St. Thomas until they moved to the Town of Lincoln in the
Niagara North Judicial District in March, 1987. All three children were taught
religion by Mr. Plum. On the basis of the accounts given by his children, it
was clear to Mr. Millington that there was no significant change from the teaching
offered by Mr. Plum in previous years with the exception that he did two
lessons with Andrea's class on Hanukkah and Yom Kippur. None of the Millington
children received any instruction relating to any other non-Christian faith.

It is apparent from the other material filed on the application by the board
that the population of the county is overwhelmingly Christian, and of that,
largely Protestant. It also appears that the complaints of the Millingtons came
as a surprise to the teachers and to the board. It is also apparent that as a
result of these complaints some changes were initiated and that further changes
are contemplated for the teaching year 1987-1988. The changes made for the
teaching year 1986-1987 reflected some concern with respect to other faiths but
by and large, the teaching of the Elgin area was still by the Elgin County
Bible Association and largely from a fundamentalist Christian perspective. What
changes, if any, will be made for the 1987-1988 remain to be seen, apart from
the fact that it is intended that the teaching will be done by the staff rather
than by the members of the Elgin County Bible Association.

When the Millingtons failed to persuade the board to move, or to move

virtue of the order of the Honourable Mr. Justice Griffiths dated September 15,
1986.

The respondents neither consented to nor opposed their being added as

s. 24
of the
