they can legitimately claim
status as applicants in this matter. Their standing is therefore confirmed.

Counsel on behalf of the Minister took the position that there was a
conflict of interest as between the C.C.L.A. and the other applicants. The
other applicants he said want to have some religion to be taught in the schools
whereas the C.C.L.A. wants no religion to be taught in the schools. As I
understood the material and the position of the parties, there was no real
conflict. No party opposes the dissemination of religious knowledge in the
schools. What is opposed -- and by all applicants -- is religious
indoctrination. The position of the C.C.L.A. is that the regulations have since
at least 1944 permitted religious indoctrination through the mandatory
programme and that many boards have used that opportunity to indoctrinate
students in a particular religious faith, the Elgin Board amongst them.

Overview

As stated earlier, the applicants' complaint is that s. 28(4) of the
regulation is being used for the indocrination of public school children with a
particular religious viewpoint, namely, Christianity and that this offends the

Charter
's guarantees of freedom of religion and equality of religion.

The position of the Minister is that:

1. The object is education not indoctrination.

2. The regulation does not coerce anyone to affirm specific religious
beliefs or to participate in specific religious practices.

3. The exemption section provides a complete answer to any suggestion of
coercion.

4.
Section 15
of the
Charter
guarantees equality of religion. There is no
inequality on the face of the regulation. The regulation is not invalid if some
board chooses to implement it in a discriminatory manner.

The position of the board is that:

1. It responded to the Millingtons and the 1986-1987 programme contained
references to other faiths.

2. Further changes are in process for 1987-1988, amongst them the exclusion
of non-teachers.

3. The court should not interfere while changes are being made.

4. The board must respond to the strong desire of the vast majority of the
residents in Elgin County that the programme continue to include instruction
based on Christian principles.

5. In any event, the exemption section provides a complete answer to any suggestion
of coercion.

Approach

The Supreme Court of Canada has indicated that in assessing the
constitutional validity of legislation, both its purpose and effect are
relevant. If the purpose is found to offend the
Charter
and it is not saved by

s. 1
, then that is the end of the inquiry. But if the purpose is not offensive,
its effects may still be fatal: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 2 S.C.R.
295, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321, 18 C.C.C. (3d) 385.

What then is the purpose of Reg. 262, s. 28? I should say at the outset that
although the application as framed attacked the whole of s. 28, it was only
those parts which deal with religious education in the class-room which were
addressed and I shall confine my remarks to them.

In my view, it is necessary to go back to at least 1944 in order to
understand the purpose of s. 28(4). Up to that time, there had been religious
instruction in the schools but at least in recent years not during regular
school hours. In February, 1944, the new Premier and Minister of Education, the
Honourable George Drew, announced in the Speech from the Throne that,
"Religious education will be offered in public and secondary
schools." This was implemented by O. Reg. 30/44, Religious Exercises and
Religious Education in the Public Schools, which except in two respects was
virtually identical to the s. 28 of today. One of those respects had to do with
s. 28(1) which is not attacked in this application; the other I will deal with
in due course.

Ontario Regulation 30/44 implemented three significant changes:

1. It brought religious education within school hours, thereby making it
mandatory.

2. It provided that, "Religious Education shall be given by the teacher
in accordance with the course of study authorized for that purpose by the
Department ...".

3. It provided for exemptions -- of a pupil, of a class and of a school.

To implement the second of these changes, guides were produced by the
department for Grades I to III in 1944, and for Grades IV to VI the next year.
A brochure entitled "Religious Education in the Public Schools of
Ontario" was produced by a group called the "Inter-Church
Committee" and in 1946 a joint advisory committee was set up comprising
representatives from the Department of Education and from the Inter-Church
Committee.

There was a good deal of opposition to the new programme both from political
parties and from religious groups. This led to a review of the subject by the
Royal Commission on Education in Ontario (the Hope Commission). In its report
in 1950, the Commission in discussing the aims of education made the following
statements:

There are two virtues about which there can be no
question -- honesty and Christian love [p. 27].

. . . . .

For the preservation of our society, the school
must teach honesty and Christian love [p. 28].

. . . . .

Honesty and Christian love are the absolutes of a
Christian society. They may therefore be taught by the strongest means at the
school's command -- an explicit acceptance that they are right. If this be
indoctrination, we accept the stricture [p. 29].

. . . . .

Without proclaiming any creed or doctrine, we
know that in our democracy the Christian ideals as personified and exemplified
by Jesus have an appeal to all persons of goodwill, and are the surest common
ground for an educational programme related to the pupil as a person. The
attitude of Jesus toward children, His understanding of human nature and
behaviour, His charity and loving kindness toward all men form a perfect model
for true democracy in the classroom, the community and the nation [pp. 36-37].

In its chapter on social, spiritual and other aspects of education and under
the heading "Religious Education", the Commission report notes at p.
126 that:

The Bible is the only text book for the subject
of religious education. There are strong reasons for valuing the authorized
version, based on tradition and literary appreciation, but it is written in
sixteenth century English and the language is a serious obstacle to
understanding on the part of pupils in the elementary school.

The report recommended the continuation of the existing course of religious
education in elementary schools. It noted that: "No provision is made in
the present Regulations for religious education in secondary schools as a
subject of study within school hours" (p. 129).

While it may not be directly relevant to the question now before the court,
one could fairly conclude on the basis of the information set out above that in
so far as the purpose can be gained from the programme, that purpose was
indoctrination in the Christian faith.

There was continuing opposition to the programme. In 1966, the then Minister
of Education, Mr.W. G. Davis, made a report which had the following recitals:

Whereas a program of religious education in the
Public Schools of Ontario was established in 1944; AND WHEREAS there has (sic)
been from time to time representations made for changes in the program; AND
WHEREAS there is a need for evaluation of this program in the light of the
experience with it and the requirements of the present day;

This report led to the appointment of a special committee entitled "The
Committee on Religious Education in the Public Schools of the Province of
Ontario" under the chairmanship of the late J. Keiller Mackay.

The Mackay Committee made a thorough examination of the matter of the
teaching of religion in the public schools of Ontario during the following
three years and issued its report in 1969. The report traced the history of
religious education in the public schools in Ontario from 1816 until 1969. The
opening paragraph of the historical section begins with these words:

It is possible to say with some truth that
religious instruction has always been present in the public schools of Ontario
and also that it had not been present until 1944. So ambiguous has the
situation been that any statement about it depends on definition of terms and
on the speaker's angle of vision. To one shade of opinion, the schools may
appear always to have been steeped in religious feeling and to another to have
been unswervingly secular throughout their history.

At p. 21 of the report, the Committee refers to the requirements of the 1960
regulations and goes on to say, "the approved text books are the
Scriptures and Bible Readings for schools" issued by the Department of
Education and the course of study is outlined in the "Programme for
Religious Education in the Public Schools of Ontario" and the
"Teachers Guides to Religious Education, Grades I to VIII". Neither
the programme nor the guides was amongst the material filed on this
application. However, the letter of March 14, 1985, to the then Minister of
Education, referred to earlier, purports to quote from the programme as
follows:

They [the Scriptural interpretations] will be confined
to those expressions of the Christian faith upon which all Christian
denominations are in substantial agreement ...

. . . . .

... Jesus Christ is more than a hero to be
admired; He is the Revelation of God in history and an abiding power in the lives
of men; He is "the Way, the Truth and the Life".

The same letter quoted from the departmental guides as follows: "...
nor is there any dispute as to the ultimate aim of the instruction, which is
the acceptance of the historic Christian Faith."

The Mackay Report described them in the following language:

This material, much of which is definitely
Christian and Protestant in content, is in our opinion a vehicle leading to
religious commitment rather than to true education. The Regulations and
Programme clearly states that "the schools of Ontario exist for the
purpose of preparing children to live in a democratic society which bases its
way of life upon the Christian ideal" and further, that "the school
must seek to lead the child to choose and accept as his own, those ideals of
conduct and endeavour which a Christian and democratic society approves".
The teacher is then counselled "to bring home to pupils as far as their
capacity allows, the fundamental principles of Christianity and their bearing
on human life and thought" [pp. 21-22].

From its perspective, the Mackay Committee assessed the situation in 1969 as
follows:

In accordance with these instructions, the
children of Ontario are exposed to Christian indoctrination throughout the
elementary grades. This indoctrination begins in the kindergarten where the
teacher finds readily available Bible stories, hymns and busy-work materials
adapted to young children and it continues with more or less intensity into the
higher grades. The pressure becomes stronger at the Christmas and Easter
seasons, sometimes resulting in serious conflict in the minds of children. The
views expressed in their homes on religious matter may differ from those stated
by the teacher. To the youthful mind, the authority of the teacher is usually
beyond question. Where does this leave the authority of the parents? Confusion
and distress is thus created in the minds of young children loyal to both
teacher and parents.

Christian doctrines are not only inculcated by
the present course, but it is implied that these truths are exclusive to
Christianity. The introduction to the program of studies for Grades I to VI
states "Religious teaching cannot be confined to separate periods on the
timetable. It will affect the teaching of all subjects, and the wise teacher
will be anxious, in the various departments of school activity, to bring home
to the pupils, as far as their capacity allows, the fundamental truths of
Christianity and their bearing on human life and thought."

Accordingly, pupils may be taught that all of the
high principles of morals and ethics on which our society is founded are
exclusive to Christianity. It is quite conceivable, therefore, that children
might leave Grade VIII with the impression that the Ten Commandments and the
Golden Rule, for example, are solely Christian doctrines. This misapprehension
will not be discouraged in those schools where the classes are conducted by
some Protestant clergymen or by teachers employed through Christian Bible
clubs.

Organized religions other than Christian are made
to appear alien and inferior in our present course of studies [p. 22].

The report went on to note as follows:

We do, of course, recognize that a general
knowledge of religion is necessary to form a well-educated person. This,
however, does not mean that religious indoctrination should take place in the
public schools. We must distinguish between religion as a subject for study and
religion as a manifestation of faith. As a subject for study, it will be
encountered naturally in all areas of the curriculum. When taught in a period
specifically set aside to achieve the aims of the present course, it is much
too likely to become an exercise in religious commitment [pp. 23-24].

The report of the Mackay Committee concluded "that the present course
of study in religious education in the elementary schools of Ontario should be
discontinued, and that aims as set out in related legislation, programs of
studies, regulations, and guide books, should be abandoned" (p. 27). In
arriving at that conclusion, the committee had this to say:

Our view that the present course of studies in
religious education is unsuitable takes into consideration the fact that the
Ontario community has changed greatly in the last 24 years. From a
predominantly Anglo-Saxon Christian society, it has become a pluralistic one.
In Ontario now flourish many religious denominations and sects related to
ethnic groups which have come to this province from all parts of the world. To
disregard this fact would be to discriminate against large segments of the
population. Further, in this contracting world, Canadians are daily coming into
close contact with people of other countries. It is important that they adopt a
broad religious outlook that will enable them to regard world movements
sympathetically. The principles of human and civil rights which are being
passionately restated all over the world must certainly be applied in the
public schools of this enlightened province. We ought not to continue to be one
of the few non-sectarian school systems in North America which provide for
religious instruction within school hours by the classroom teacher; we have an
obligation to join the mainstream. Among the many problems facing modern
society are the avoidance of war, the improvement of education, and the
adjustment of humanity to a mechanized world. The present course in religious
education in Ontario contributes nothing to the understanding of these dynamic
problems; instead, it exacerbates them [pp. 24-25].

The Mackay Committee also considered a number of alternatives.

Can the present course of instruction be modified
to meet the standards required of modern education? It has been suggested that
its emphasis on Christianity is justified by the fact that in addition to being
the faith of a majority of the population of Ontario, Christianity has so
greatly influenced the history and literature of western civilization. Thus, it
is said, the course, after modification to include less intensive study of
other major religions, could then be updated by introducing more real life
situations. Discrimination and intolerance, it was claimed, would decrease if
this modified course were presented by better trained teachers ... We have
given careful consideration to this proposal. It is our opinion that a
satisfactory modification of the present course cannot be achieved. This course
is supported by the fact that various briefs have expressed views that the
present course is too superficial, too dogmatic, too emotional, too bland, too
elementary, too abstract. We find much evidence to support all these views,
conflicting though they are. ... The fact remains that, after 24 years, the
manuals, although revised, are still objectionable to many; the teachers,
although better informed, are still inadequately prepared; and the course
itself is still only haphazardly integrated into the curriculum. At many levels
and in many areas it has fallen into disuse or has become the cause of friction
in the community. The course invades the integrity of public education and is,
therefore, basically wrong. There must be a totally new approach to the problem
[pp. 25-26].

The recommendations of the Mackay Report were not adopted by the provincial
government. Instead in 1978, by O. Reg. 704/78, the regulation was amended by
deleting the words "in accordance with the course of study authorized by
the Department of Education" from what is now s-s. (6). According to the
submissions of counsel for the Minister of Education, this change would
accommodate local autonomy. Each board could develop a programme or curriculum
to suit its own individual needs, which would vary according to the religious
make-up of its population.

Board material

In so far as the material used by the Elgin Board up to and including 1986
is concerned, no serious attempt was made to defend it. A review of it reveals
it to be exclusively Christian, Protestant, fundamentalist and evangelical. As
such, it would be offensive to some non-Christians and to a good many
Christians as well. From the content and from the layout of the material, it is
a fair inference that it was used or to be used for indoctrination rather than
education.

Indeed it is not necessary to draw inferences; in February, 1986, the
teachers' guide for Grade VII stated that: "The objective of the religious
education program in the schools of Elgin County would be to provide pupils
with a religious context, primarily Christian, in which to develop appropriate
responses to life's situations."

It was apparent from the changes made from the teaching year 1986-1987 that
part of Mr. Millington's message got through. The curriculum material did
contain references to other faiths, specifically Judaism, the Mennonites,
"Native Peoples'', the Mormons, Jehovah's Witnesses, Islam and Baha'i. It appears
to me however that the material continued to be taught exclusively from the
Christian point of view, not from the point of view of a person of one or other
of the other faiths. Again the content and the layout of the material suggests
strongly that the purpose was indoctrination rather than education in the
ordinary sense.

While Elgin was the only board whose material was before us, reference was
made to a number of other municipalities. Mention has already been made of a
letter dated March 14, 1985, from the C.C.L.A. to the then Minister of
Education. In that letter, the association stated that in Norfolk, the Board of
Education had acquired for its religious education programme, the assistance of
Christian Service Centres of Canada. It was stated that in the words of the
material produced by this group, the primary aim of the curriculum is "to
help the pupil gain a clearer understanding of God the Father, His Son, Jesus
Christ, and the Holy Spirit". The letter went on to say that the material
counsels the teacher to help the student "realize that a Heavenly Home is
being prepared for all who believe and trust Jesus as Saviour" and that
the material explicitly states that one of the learning objectives is
"that the student will desire to share with others the fact that Jesus
died, arose, ascended into Heaven and will return".

The association went on in the same letter to state that in Frontenac County
the Board of Education has permitted representatives of the Kingston and
District Bible Movement to teach the programme in a number of its schools. It
said that Ron Axford, president of the group, explained to the Kingston
Whig-Standard that the reason for going into the schools "is to offer
pupils an opportunity to ... learn about what God says to them through the
Bible about himself and about Jesus Christ".

The C.C.L.A. made reference in the same letter to "a recent controversy
in the Port Hope area [which] has served to reveal something of the nature of
what has been taught under the jurisdiction of the Northumberland and Newcastle
Board of Education". Responding to a board decision to consider the
teaching of comparative religion, Reverend Alexander Young expressed his
objection in a letter to a local newspaper. He was critical of the possibility
that the world's religions could be presented "on a par qualitatively with
Christianity".

The boards of these other municipalities were not made parties to this
application nor was any effort made to contradict these allegations of the
association which support the inference that the situation in Elgin is not
unique.

The legislation

Although no direct attack was made on the legislative foundation of the
regulation, it may be helpful to look at that foundation before dealing with the
regulation itself. That foundation is in ss. 50 and s. 10(1), para. 18 of the
Education Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 129. The texts of those sections are as follows:

50(1) Subject to the regulations, a pupil shall
be allowed to receive such religious instruction as his parent or guardian
desires or, where the pupil is an adult, as he desires.

(2) No pupil in a public school shall be required
to read or study in or from a religious book, or to join in an exercise of
devotion or religion, objected to by his parent or guardian or by the pupil,
where he is an adult.

. . . . .

10(1) Subject to the approval of the Lieutenant
Governor in Council, the Minister may make regulations in respect of schools or
classes established under this Act, or any predecessor of this Act, and with
respect to all other schools supported in whole or in part by public money,

. . . . .

18. governing the provision of religious
exercises and religious education in public and secondary schools and providing
for the exemption of pupils from participating in such exercises and education
and of a teacher from teaching, and a public school board or a secondary school
board from providing, religious education in any school or class;

Unlike any other subject, a pupil is only to be allowed to receive such
religious instruction as his parent or guardian desires and he is not to be
required to read or study in or from a religious book or to join in an exercise
of devotion or religion, objected to by his parent (emphasis added). As far as
I have been able to determine, this provision is unique in its language,
demonstrating as it does, extreme sensitivity to the subject-matter. The use of
the phrase "an exercise of devotion or religion" of course strongly
suggests something other than pure education. This section in and of itself
would support the inference that the purpose is indoctrination rather than
teaching in the ordinary sense.

Section 10(1), para. 18 refers to "religious exercises and religious
education". Again the use of the expression "religious
exercises" suggests something other than teaching in the ordinary sense of
that expression. The section goes on to deal with the exemption of pupils from
participating in such exercises and education. Again, if all that was involved
in "religious education" was teaching in the ordinary sense, it is
difficult to understand why any provision should be made for the exempting of
students. The section then goes on to deal with exempting teachers from
teaching this subject and again it is difficult to imagine, unless the object
is indoctrination, why teachers should be exempted from teaching this
particular subject. Finally, the section goes on to provide an exemption for
either a whole class or a whole school. This exemption is "from providing
religious education". There is no indication as to why a distinction is
drawn, if such is the case, between religious exercises and religious
education. Again, it is difficult to imagine why there is to be a provision for
exemption of a class or a school unless the object of the legislation is
something other than education in the ordinary sense. Counsel were not able to
give the court any other examples of such exemptions.

The regulation

Section 28 of the regulation provides for and deals with two separate
matters -- religious exercises at the opening or closing of school and
religious education. The latter is dealt with in s. 28(4) to (15) inclusive and
some guidance is to be had from reviewing those subsections.

Section 28(4) is the basic subsection. It requires that two periods per week
of one-half hour each be devoted to religious education. There is nothing on
the face of this subsection which gives any offence.

Section 28(6) provides that "Instruction in religious education shall
be given by the teacher and issues of controversial or sectarian nature shall
be avoided". Until 1978, this read:

41(7) Instruction in religious education shall be
given by the teacher in accordance with the course of study authorized for that
purpose by the Department, and issues of a controversial or sectarian nature
shall be avoided [R.R.O. 1970, c. 191].

Again it must be admitted that on its face this language is inoffensive, yet
as has been seen from the review set out above, the material produced by the
department for use in the schools was clearly intended for indoctrination.
Counsel for the Attorney-General relied upon the latter part of this provision
as a clear indication that the purpose of the regulation was not
indoctrination. In his reply argument, counsel for the C.C.L.A. argued that
what was contemplated when this regulation was drawn was Christian sectarian
teaching, that is, the object was to avoid interdenominational friction amongst
various sects, all of the Christian faith. What was not in the minds of the
persons writing the regulation, counsel suggested, was that there would be an
even hand in teaching the principles of Christianity, Hinduism, Buddhism,
Islam, Baha'i, etc. Counsel for the C.C.L.A. relies for this interpretation in
part on the date this part of the regulation became law, 1944, and the
overwhelming Christian affiliation of the population at that time. As he put
it, it might have been fine in its day; it is now offensive, both by reason of
increasing multi- culturalism and because of the existence of the
Charter
. In
the C.C.L.A.'s letter to the Minister of Education in 1985 this interpretation
is attributed to "certain education officials". The Minister's
response, if any, was not before the court.

Section 28(7) provides that:

28(7) By resolution of a board, a clergyman or
clergymen of any denomination, or a lay person or lay persons selected by the
clergyman or clergymen, may give religious instruction in a school of the board
in lieu of a teacher or teachers.

This is really a continuation, in a new form, of the practice which
prevailed prior to 1944. A clergyman had the right to ask to give religious
instruction in the schoolhouse before or after school hours "to pupils of
his own denomination". On its face this provision supports the proposition
that the purpose of the regulation is indoctrination. It is difficult to think
why else a member of the clergy would be invited into the school to provide
instruction. Counsel for the Minister was unable to provide any other example
where "outsiders" are authorized by the regulations to assume the
responsibility for part of the school programme except possibly the recent
heritage language programme. In the absence of any evidence that clergymen are
any better equipped to teach comparative religions or religious knowledge (as
opposed to being skilled at indoctrination), this part of the regulation would
seem to suggest that the purpose of the regulation generally is indoctrination
rather than education in the normal sense.

Section 28(8) provides that:

28(8) Where two or more clergymen of different
denominations, or lay persons selected by the clergymen, upon written
application to the board, secure permission under subsection (7) to give
religious instruction in the same school, the principal of the school, by resolution
of the board, shall arrange for such accommodation within the school and such
times within the periods referred to in subsection

(5) as are agreeable to both the principal and the clergymen or the lay persons
selected by the clergymen.

While no argument was addressed to this specific subsection, the use of the
word "denominations" rather than "religions" or
"faiths" would provide some basis for the argument that the draftsmen
of the regulation had in mind the Christian faith rather than many faiths. This
would seem to tie in with the interpretation of s-s. (6) set out above and with
the reference to "all Christian denominations" in the letter to the
Minister in 1985.

Section 28(9) reads as follows:

28(9) Where the number of rooms in a public school
is insufficient to meet the needs of the groups organized for religious
instruction under subsection (7) or (8), the principal of the school, by
resolution of the board, may arrange for additional accommodation elsewhere.

Read with s-ss. (6) and (8), this is compatible with the idea of
indoctrination rather than education in the normal sense. If the idea behind
the regulation was the teaching of comparative religions, it is difficult to
imagine that the facilities of the school would not be sufficient. On the other
hand, if a number of "competing" denominations of the Christian faith
are represented amongst the population, it is not at all difficult to imagine
or understand why separate rooms would be necessary and why the school itself
might not be of sufficient size to accommodate the number of rooms necessary.

Section 28(10) (as amended) reads as follows:

28(10) No pupil shall be required to take part in
any religious exercise or be subject to any instruction in religious education
where a parent of the pupil, or the pupil where the pupil is an adult, applies
to the principal of the school that the pupil attends for exemption of the
pupil therefrom.

Again counsel for the Minister was unable to provide any other example of a
student being entitled to an exemption from a particular form of teaching.
Again, if the object of the regulation was the teaching of comparative
religions, it is difficult to imagine a parent wanting his or her child
exempted and it is even more difficult to imagine the Ministry acceding to such
request. If ignorance is the basis of intolerance, then clearly learning or
education is the remedy, not exemption.

Section 28(11) provides that:

28(11) In public schools without suitable waiting
rooms or other similar accommodation, if the parent of a pupil or, where the
pupil is an adult, the pupil applies to the principal of the school for the
exemption of the pupil from attendance while religious exercises are being held
or religious education given, such request shall be granted.

This seems to suggest the pupil granted exemption from either the religious
exercise at the opening of school or the religious education contemplated by
s-s. (4), will not be in the class-room or perhaps even in the school at all
but will "wait" elsewhere. In 1983 at least, Andrea Millington had it
in mind that if she was exempted, she would "sit in the hall". Mrs.
Sebestyen said that that was the situation in 1984. It appears from the
material filed by Elgin that it is no longer so and that exempted pupils, of
whom there were 124 in 1986, are constructively engaged elsewhere. The
specifics of those alternative arrangements were not detailed.

Section 28(12) provides that:

28(12) Where a parent of a pupil, or the pupil
where the pupil is an adult, objects to the pupil taking part in religious
exercises or being subject to instruction in religious education, but requests
that the pupil remain in the classroom during the time devoted to religious
exercises or instruction in religious education, the principal of the school
that the pupil attends shall permit the pupil to do so, if the pupil maintains
decorous behaviour.

This does not appear to throw any particular light on the purpose of s.
28(4).

Section 28(14):

28(14) A teacher claiming exemption from the
teaching of religious education as prescribed by this section shall notify the
board to that effect in writing, and the board shall make such other provision
as is necessary to implement this section with respect to the teaching of
religious education.

Again, counsel were unable to provide any other instance of a teacher being
exempted from the class-room or from teaching. If the regulation was designed
to promote the teaching of comparative religions, it is difficult to imagine a
teacher who would want to be exempted from doing so and even more difficult to
imagine the Ministry permitting an exemption on that basis. Again, the language
of the subsection is consistent with the proposition that the object of the
regulation is indoctrination.

Section 28(15) reads as follows:

28(15) The Minister may grant to a board
exemption from the teaching of religious education in any classroom or school
if the board requests in writing the exemption and submits reasons for its
request.

Again, counsel for the Minister was unable to provide any other instance of
a similar provision. If the object of the regulation was the teaching of
comparative religions, it is difficult to imagine why an exemption would be
provided. If on the other hand, the underlying object of the regulation was
religious indoctrination, it is perfectly understandable that in some sections
of the province this would produce problems. It appears from the report in Re
Zylberberg and Director of Education of Sudbury Board of Education (1986),
1986 CanLII 2631 (ON HCJ)
, 55
O.R. (2d) 749, 29 D.L.R. (4th) 709, 25 C.R.R. 193, that an exemption has been
granted to the City of Toronto. Having regard to its very mixed racial and
religious make-up, an exemption is understandable -- if the object of the regulation
is religious indoctrination.

Two other aspects of the programme should be noted although neither is
apparent from the language of the regulation. One is that pupils are not marked
on this course; the other is that it does not appear on their report cards.
Both of these points suggest that there is something "different"
about religious education as it is taught in Ontario.

On all of the evidence, historical and present day, I do not think I have
any alternative but to conclude that s. 28(4) of Reg. 262 was calculated to
permit the indoctrination of schoolchildren in Ontario in the Christian faith
and that it is being used for that purpose at the present time.

Exemption

Both respondents relied on the exemption provisions as a complete answer to any
suggestion of coercion. The applicants say: "No, exemption is not a
complete answer. There is still some coercion; there is still inequality."

There was conflicting evidence as to the impact, if any, of exemption upon
pupils. The applicants filed the affidavit of Jonathon Lewis Freedman, a
professor in the Department of Psychology at the University of Toronto. His
evidence was to the effect that there are at least two kinds of pressure to
remain in the class-room during the giving of religious instruction. One is the
pressure from the authority of the teacher and the school system and the other,
the more powerful pressure, from the rest of the class. He was of the view that
where the religion taught is that of the majority, those of a minority, even if
offered the formal right to claim an exemption, do not feel free to do so. He
said that while there may be some children strong enough to resist that
pressure, many will not be able to do so. As a result, he said that those
children may suffer considerable conflict and stress. If they do not
participate, they risk offending the teacher and the school and are seen to be
"different" by the rest of the class. On the other hand if they do
participate, they offend either their own beliefs or those of their parents. He
also suggested that if they do decide to participate, they are especially
likely to be influenced by what they hear.

The Elgin Board filed the affidavit of Donald Robert Kennedy, a psychologist
in private practice in the Metropolitan Toronto area. Mr. Kennedy had a wealth
of experience in the field of education and disagreed with Mr. Freedman's view
as to the pressure on children to remain in the class-room. According to Mr.
Kennedy, it is common practice for children to be excused from a class-room for
many reasons during the course of a day, e.g., French immersion, enrichment,
heritage language programmes. Accordingly, in his view, children in Ontario
schools do not perceive the choices of remaining or leaving in the way that
Freedman suggested. Kennedy said that there was little pressure to conform. He
indicated that within individual children there could be some feelings of
conflict around participation in religious instruction classes just as there
could be in connection with the many other school activities in which they
either do or do not participate. In other children there would be no conflict
at all. Kennedy also disagreed that peer pressure was a normal or usual result
of exemption from any school activity. He was also of the view that peer
pressure or conflict should not be considered harmful except in very extreme
situations. Moderate levels of "pressure to conform" and
"conflict" he regarded as part of the normal developmental process in
children as well as in adults. He concluded by stating that he had never
encountered a child with serious problems arising from an exemption relating to
religious exercises or religious instruction in the schools.

In the present case, there was also the evidence of the Millingtons about
the experiences of and discussions with their children referred to earlier.
Mrs. Millington said that she tried to encourage Andrea to speak out in class
and to share her own ideas with the class on various topics related to religion
but Andrea was very concerned that Mr. Plum would become angry if she did that
and that the children in the class would tease her. Andrea's sensitivity about
the fact that her religious background was different from that of her teacher
and her classmates and her fear of being teased or singled out led Mrs.
Millington to the conclusion that it was not in Andrea's better interest to be
excluded from the classes despite Mrs. Millington's very serious misgivings
about the nature of the material being taught in those classes.

Mrs. Millington testified that at one point when Andrea was in Grade III,
she came home and seemed very upset and confused about what had been discussed
that day. Andrea told her that either her father and her mother were lying to
her or Mr. Plum was. Mrs. Millington said it was very hard for Andrea to
understand and accept her parents' explanation that even though their beliefs
were different from Mr. Plum's beliefs, they still had to respect his right to
believe what he wished. These discussions with Andrea caused Mrs. Millington to
be concerned about the fact that the attitudes of tolerance and respect for
others and other religions that they were attempting to teach her were being
undermined by a very intolerant and narrow approach being taken in the school.

Because Mr. Plum was her "teacher", Mrs. Millington said that
Andrea definitely saw him in the role of an authority figure and found it very
hard to doubt the truth of what he was saying. This led to confusion in her
mind because on the other hand, she found it just as difficult to doubt her
parents. Mrs. Millington said that while the nightmares were the most dramatic
demonstration of the effects of the religious classes on Andrea, Andrea had
been constantly confronted with the fact that at school someone was attempting
to make her believe in things her family did not accept and that she had to
deal with this dilemma and confusion for three years.

In her letter of March 30, 1985, to the Religious Education Committee of the
St. Thomas Board of Education, Mrs. Millington said that:

In our case, we became concerned over one year
ago when our daughter, then in Grade 2, began having nightmares due to the
discussions in the religion classes about the Devil and burning in hell-fire
for one's sins. She was terrified of these concepts. Many times she would come
home and tell us what they had discussed and we simply felt that some of the
things she was learning were not in accordance with our views on Christianity.

Later in the same letter, she stated that:

Several days ago our daughter came home and
seemed rather upset. She announced that she was not one of God's chosen people.
When we asked what she meant, she said that the religion teacher had said that
Christians were God's chosen people. Another thing that upset her was the statement
that if we didn't believe that Jesus was our only Saviour, we wouldn't go to
heaven.

The Millingtons filed three affidavits. There was no cross- examination on
any of these affidavits nor was any attempt made to minimize this evidence.
Whatever may be the views of Messrs. Kennedy and Freedman, there is no doubt
that teachings of Mr. Plum had a pronounced effect on Andrea Millington.

As indicated above, two applicants were added at the time of the hearing of
this application. They were Edith Louise Hough and Elizabeth C. Sebestyen. Mrs.
Hough had the advantage of not only having two children ages 12 and 13 in the
public school system in Elgin County but herself having attended public school
in Elgin County and having been "subjected to the fundamentalist
evangelical teaching of Mrs. Houghton, a member of the Elgin County Bible
Club". Mrs. Hough said that she strongly objected to the type of religious
teaching offered in the schools of Elgin County and in particular in the school
which her children attended (Port Stanley Public School, in the Township of
Southwold) and as a result asked that they be exempted. She said that she had
voiced her objections to the religious education programme to Mr. Gordon
Houghton, the local school trustee, but that Mr. Houghton was completely
unreceptive to her views and when she explained to him that she too had been
subjected to religious indoctrination when she attended public school, he
suggested that she was out for revenge. She referred to the teaching in Elgin
County as "fundamentalist and evangelical Christian teaching". She
indicated that it demonstrated little or no tolerance for thinking on religion
that does not reflect its own convictions and beliefs. In Mrs. Hough's letter
to Mrs. Westaway of the Elgin Board she said that "In my family alone,
three generations have been taught by Mrs. Alma Houghton, a very evangelical
Baptist lady with very little tolerance for any other thinking no matter how
noble or old the belief". She also said that:

Our concept of acceptable religious training
includes the appreciation of all religions and beliefs that our children may
encounter in their formative years. To exclusively teach or show preference for
one particular religion or church is to reinforce prejudice and misunderstanding.
The only way to fight discrimination is with knowledge, and knowledge is what
education is all about.

Mrs. Sebestyen has two children in the Elgin County public school system
ages five and seven. She too objects strongly to the religious classes as presently
taught at her children's school, Aldborough Public School, in Rodney, Ontario.
Mrs. Sebestyen said that she first became aware of the issue of religious
education in Elgin County during the spring of 1984 when she attended the
school to register her oldest child for kindergarten. The religious education
class was being taught in the kindergarten room at the time and she observed
two small boys sitting on a bench outside the class-room. She said that she
assumed that these children had misbehaved and were being punished but when she
inquired, she was informed that the children were Jehovah's Witnesses whose
parents had requested exemption from the religion classes because of their
religious views. Mrs. Sebestyen said that it immediately became apparent to her
that if she opposed the type of religious education offered, she had two
completely unacceptable options -- to either allow her children to stay in the
class, although she objected to them being subjected to the religious
instruction being offered -- or to ask that they be excused, in which case her
children would sit on a bench outside the class-room. Mrs. Sebestyen said that
she also found the option of requesting an exemption unacceptable because she
feared that her children would be socially ostracized by their classmates. She
pointed out that they live in a small rural community and the children have few
opportunities outside the school to establish social relationships. She said
she believed that in the primary grades in particular there should be an
opportunity for children to learn to get along with one another and to feel
comfortable with their peers. She also said that she felt a stigma was attached
to being sent out of the class-room to sit in the hall as this usually denotes
punishment. She said that despite her misgivings, she decided to allow her son
to attend the classes, while explaining her own personal religious beliefs,
teaching morals and describing the basic teachings of the other world religions
at home.

Mrs. Sebestyen said that she had reviewed the material brought home from
school by her son from the religion class and had discussed the classes with
him. On the basis of this information, she objects strongly to the type of
material he is given and the type of instruction offered. She expressed her
view as being that of an attempt by a special interest religious group to
indoctrinate easily influenced and naive children into the Christian faith.

Mrs. Sebestyen expressed the view that children will generally believe and
trust the voice of authority, particularly their teachers at school and it is
particularly dangerous that they be taught one view of religion by an adult at
the school as the ultimate truth. In her view, this is what is happening at
Aldborough Public School. She finds that she is losing control of her children
and their religious upbringing.

In April, 1987, she sat in on a regularly scheduled half-hour Grade VI
religious education class taught by a Mrs. Fodor. On the basis of her
observations and her prior discussion with Mrs. Fodor, Mrs. Sebestyen concluded
that Mrs. Fodor regarded religious instruction as her mission and that her
intention was to teach children about the Bible with a view to having them
believe it without doubt. Mrs. Sebestyen said that for Mrs. Fodor religious
instruction was not an objective study but rather it is a means and opportunity
of spreading her own personal religious beliefs, beliefs to which Mrs.
Sebestyen takes strong objection. It was because of this strong objection and
her conviction that the board could not and would not change its ways that Mrs.
Sebestyen sought to be added as a party to these proceedings.

There are really three kinds of evidence before the court. There is the
direct evidence of the Millingtons with respect to Andrea, there is the
indirect evidence of Messrs. Freedman and Kennedy and there is the direct
evidence of the parents, of Mr. and Mrs. Millington, Mrs. Hough and Mrs.
Sebestyen. This latter evidence consists of the fact that some parents,
although they found the classes objectionable, chose to leave their children in
rather than have them exempted. The same course was taken by Mr. and Mrs.
Gregg, Mr.and Mrs. Wyers and Mr. Inver in the Zylberberg case, referred to
earlier. I cannot find that their concerns are groundless. As Reid J. said in
Zylberberg [at p. 769 O.R., p. 729 D.L.R.]: "No one has suggested that the
feelings expressed by the applicants are not real, or that they do not run
deep." I believe I must find that there is an appreciable degree of coercion
or pressure on the personal applicants in this case. There is an inequality of
situation by virtue of the nature of this programme. Accordingly, I am unable
to agree with counsel for the board and for the Minister that the exempting
provisions constitute a complete answer to any suggestion of inequality or
coercion.

Zylberberg

The decision in Re Zylberberg and Director of Education, supra, was relied
upon by counsel for Elgin and for the Minister as being a complete answer to this
application. In that matter, the religious exercise at the opening of school
was under attack. A majority of the Divisional Court panel hearing the matter
dismissed the application. Mr. Justice O'Leary held that s. 28(1) does not
require anyone to participate in or be present at religious exercises and that
there was no evidence that the pressure to participate was substantial. He held
that whatever pressure or coercion there was to conform was not sufficient to
infringe
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
and even if it could be said that it did, it
was such an infringement as could be demonstrably justified in a free and
democratic society. He held that the most obvious way to teach morality is to
associate it with God and that while some pupils may feel pressure to
participate to avoid embarrassment, that was at most a minor infringement of
their freedom of conscience and religion and must not be allowed to stand in
the way of the obligation of the schools to teach morality in the most
effective and least offensive way they knew how, namely, by holding religious
exercises.

He also held that s. 28(1) does not discriminate against non- Christians in
a manner offensive to
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
. Accepting that the Scriptures
and the Lord's Prayer are solely Christian forms of devotion, the "other
suitable readings" or "other suitable prayers" referred to in s.
28(1) do not have to be. The religious exercises required by s. 28(1) do not
have to be Christian and can be adapted by the school board and teachers as
suits the particular make-up of any class-room. Section 28(1) does not require
or encourage religious discrimination so far as believers are concerned.
Non-believers may argue that the mere holding of religious exercises gives
believers an opportunity to reinforce their beliefs that is not afforded
non-believers. If this constitutes religious discrimination, then it
constitutes a reasonable limit or infringement under
s. 1
of the Charter. Where
a country is founded on the principle of the supremacy of God, there is no
obligation on the schools to spend the same effort reinforcing the belief of
non-believers that God does not exist as in teaching believers about the nature
of God.

Mr. Justice Anderson held that the exemption section provides a complete and
unconditional answer to the application. He found that to suggest otherwise
offended logic and common sense. He said it was tantamount to saying that a
right to refuse is a compulsion to accept. He found that choice is of the
essence of freedom and the decision as to what choice is appropriate is often
difficult; that difficulty is part of the price of freedom.

Mr. Justice Reid dissented. He found that s. 28(1) was mandatory and held
that a law that requires performance of religious exercises is a restriction on
freedom of religion. This would be so even if the exercise be of a person's own
religion. Turning to the exemption, he found that if a truly free choice were
offered, i.e., everyone was free to either attend or not attend the opening
exercise, then there would be no compulsion, no coercion. There is a difference
between imposing a rule and providing for exceptions on the one hand and
providing truly alternative choices on the other. Had the object been to
provide real freedom of choice, it could easily have been achieved. All that
was required was to provide that there would be a time during the day when
those who wished could take part in religious exercises and those who did not,
need not. While such a provision might possibly be effected in some schools so
as to make those who wished not to participate feel "different" or
"left out" in the hope that they would join the participating group,
the provision on its face would not be objectionable under the
Charter
. As it
was, however, the regulation disclosed a purpose contrary to the Charter, a
purpose to interfere with religious freedom.

As to the regulation's effect, there was evidence that some parents and
students felt compelled to refrain from asserting their right to exemption.
This did not stem from fear of penal sanctions but penal sanctions are not
necessary to the existence of compulsion. Compulsion may take many forms. It
may be that a control or a limitation indirectly imposed is not readily
appreciable to those who are not affected by it. It may be difficult for
members of a majoritarian religious group to appreciate the feelings of member
of minority religions. It may be difficult for religious people to appreciate
the feelings of agnostics and atheists. Nevertheless those feelings exist. He
found the effect of s. 28(1) to be contrary to both
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the

Charter
.

Section 28(1) cannot be saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
. It is not a reasonable
limitation on religious freedom. No governmental concern had been demonstrated so
pressing as to justify the obvious interference with religious freedoms sought
by and caused by the regulation. In addition,
s. 1
was not intended to be
applied so as to justify an interference with the religious freedom of some but
not of others. That would make the Charter contradict itself. If any
interference may be justified by
s. 1
, it must be an interference not with the
right of some to religious freedom but with the right of all.

In my view, a clear distinction can be drawn between s. 28(1) and (4).
Section 28(1) deals with the opening exercises and makes specific reference to
"the Scriptures or other suitable readings and the Lord's Prayer or other
suitable prayers" (emphasis added). Section 28(4) prescribes "two
periods per week of one-half hour each, in addition to the time assigned to
religious exercises at the opening or closing of a public school, to be devoted
to religious education". Whatever may have been the evidence in
Zylberberg, there is in my view clear evidence that in Elgin County at least,
s. 28(4) is used for the purpose of religious indoctrination of a
fundamentalist evangelical Christian nature. In Zylberberg, Mr. Justice O'Leary
referred to the decision of Mr. Justice Dickson in the Big M case, supra, and
went on to say [at p. 757 O.R., p. 717 D.L.R.]:

It must be remembered that these words were
written while the Court was considering a statutory requirement that under pain
of penal consequences Sunday was to be observed as the day of rest by all no
matter what their religious view as to the day to be so sanctified. Section
28(1) does not, of course, require anyone to participate in or be present at
religious exercises. In my view, the words of Dickson J. just quoted do not
support the proposition that any amount of pressure, no matter how slight,
tending to influence a pupil to participate in religious exercises against the
dictates of his conscience, violates
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

He then went on to say: "There is no evidence before us to suggest that
the pressure to participate in the religious exercises created by s. 28(1) is
substantial." In that case he had, as in the present case, the evidence of
Donald Robert Kennedy. In addition, he had a conflicting affidavit from Dr.
Edward Bassis. He concluded that: "The pressure to conform complained
about here does not constitute coercion to such an extent as to infringe the
right of freedom of conscience and religion."

One must remember that Mr. Justice O'Leary was referring to conditions in
Sudbury, Ontario, a relatively large multicultural community. Without dealing
with Mr. Justice O'Leary's finding that "the words of Dickson J. just
quoted do not support the proposition that any amount of pressure, no matter
how slight, tending to influence a pupil to participate in religious exercises
against the dictates of his conscience, violates
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
",
I find that there was in the present case, sufficient coercion to accomplish
that end, i.e., to violate the Charter. Specifically, I refer to the evidence
of the Millingtons with respect to the experiences of their daughter, of the
effect of those experiences on their daughter and on themselves. In my view,
there is in the present case, evidence of real coercion. In the Canada of 1987
or 1988, such coercion should not exist.

As a matter of interest, the Mackay Committee also looked at opening
exercises and supported their retention although with the deletion of the
reading of passages from the Bible.

As a further matter of interest, the example given by Reid J. in Zylberberg
as a truly free choice, that is a time during the day when those who wished
could take part in religious exercises and those who did not, need not, was the
situation existing up until 1944 with respect to religious education. In so far
as there were periods of religious instruction, these occurred either before or
after regular school hours and could be attended or not as the students, or
their parents, saw fit.

I find therefore that s. 28(4) constitutes an appreciable interference with
freedom of religion and an inequality within the meaning of
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)

of the
Charter
.

Section 1
of the
Charter

The respondents argue that such interference and inequality are
"reasonable limitations" for the purposes of
s. 1
of the
Charter
.
Assuming, without deciding, that recourse may be had to s. 1, R. v. Oakes,

1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103 at pp. 138-9, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 200 at p. 227, 24 C.C.C. (3d)
321, lays down the appropriate tests:

1. The objective must be of sufficient importance to warrant overriding a
constitutionally protected right or freedom;

2. The means must be reasonable and demonstrably justified; that is

(a) The measures adopted must be carefully
designed to achieve the objective in question and must be rationally connected
to the objective;

(b) The means must impair the right as little as
possible;

(c) There must be a proportionality between the
effects of the measures adopted and the objective for which they were adopted.

In applying these tests, the onus is on the respondents and the standard of proof
is the civil standard, namely, a preponderance of probability.

The objectives put forward by the respondents as warranting the overriding
of constitutionally protected rights were the teaching of religion to those
pupils whose parents wanted such instruction and the teaching of moral values.

Dealing with the first of these, the respondents' position, in a nutshell,
is that interference with the religious rights of the minority is justifiable
in order to satisfy the religious requirements of the majority. In my view,
that position is simply untenable. It purports to amend the
Charter
itself.
"What may appear good and true to a majoritarian religious group, or the
state acting at their behest, may not, for religious reasons, be imposed upon
citizens who take a contrary view. The Charter safeguards religious minorities
from the threat of the 'tyranny of the majority' ": R. v. Big M Drug Mart
Ltd., per Dickson J. at p. 337 S.C.R., p. 354 D.L.R.

I adopt, if I may, the reasoning of Reid J. in Zylberberg, supra, at p. 770
O.R., p. 730 D.L.R.: "To divide us into two groups; those who have to put
up with restriction of their religious freedom and those who do not, is to deny
the freedom of religion that the
Charter
guarantees."

As to the second objective, namely, the teaching of moral values, the most
useful evidence was the Mackay Report which examined that question thoroughly
and concluded that schools could and should teach moral values and could do so
without attempting religious indoctrination. The report provided a good deal of
constructive advice on such a programme.

Accordingly, I find that the respondents have not satisfied the tests to
show that Reg. 262, s. 28(4) is saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

The curriculum

Having found s. 28(4) offensive to the
Charter
, programmes and curricula
purporting to be set up under it will fall. I should however deal with the
possibility that another court will find s. 28(4) valid. In those
circumstances, can the Elgin curriculum stand?

Counsel for the board argued that the curriculum was not "law" and
that therefore the
Charter
had no application. He relied on Re Ontario English
Catholic Teachers Ass'n and Essex County Roman Catholic School Board (1987),
1987 CanLII 4043 (ON HCJ)
, 58
O.R. (2d) 545, 36 D.L.R. (4th) 115, 18 O.A.C. 271. A board of education
terminated a teacher's contract in accordance with its policy of mandatory
retirement at age 65. The teacher and his association applied for judicial
review. The case was decided by Craig, Anderson and McKinlay JJ., and all
agreed that it should be dismissed. Counsel for the board in the present case
relied upon the decision of Anderson J. with whom McKinlay J. concurred, to the
effect that the board's policy was not law and hence not subject to the
Charter. In my view, that decision does not assist the Elgin Board. Anderson J.
based his finding on the proposition that the relationship between the teacher
and the board was not one of subject to state but one of employee to employer.
In the present case, the relationship is one of subject to state, the state in
this instance being the board.

In Essex, Craig J. held that the board's retirement policy was
"law" within the meaning of the
Charter
.

In Re Klein and Law Society of Upper Canada (1985),
1985 CanLII 3086 (ON HCJDC)
, 50 O.R. (2d) 118, 16
D.L.R. (4th) 489, 13 C.R.R. 120, this court, differently constituted, held that
the rules and commentaries respecting fee advertising in the Law Society's Code
of Professional Conduct fell within the ambit of the
Charter
.

Section 32(1)(b)
of the
Charter
provides that the Charter "applies ...
to the legislature and government of each province in respect of all matters
within the authority of the legislature of each province". Until 1978, the
legislature exercised that authority directly by providing programme and
curricula. Now it is "delegated" in a sense to local boards. None the
less, the content of board programmes and curricula remain within the authority
of the legislature and, accordingly, I conclude that the Elgin curriculum is
"law" within the meaning of the Charter.

As that law undoubtedly offends
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Charter
, it must
fall.

The Education Act, sections 10 and 50

No attack was made on s. 10(1), para. 18 or on s. 50 of the Education Act. These
are the statutory foundation of Reg. 262, s. 28. It was argued that as neither
of these sections had been attacked, anything done under or pursuant to them
must be valid. This does not follow.

As ss. 10(1), para. 18 and 50 stand, there is nothing inherently offensive
about either of them. What is attacked and has been dealt with above is Reg.
262, s. 28(4) and the Elgin curriculum. As no attack was made on either s.
10(1), para. (18) or s. 50, it is not appropriate to make any further comment
on them or to make any order which would affect them.

Other matters

Counsel for the Minister drew the attention of the court to Donald v. Board
of Education for City of Hamilton,
1945 CanLII 117 (ON CA)
, [1945] O.R. 518, [1945] 3 D.L.R. 424. In
that case, two secondary school children of parents who were Jehovah's
Witnesses sought exemption from the opening exercise which involved saluting
the flag and singing the National Anthem. The court found that the applicant
believed that saluting the flag and joining in the singing of the National
Anthem were both contrary to and forbidden by the command of Scripture -- the
former because they considered the flag an "image" within the literal
meaning of Exodus, c. 20, verses 4 and 5 and the latter because, while they
respected the King and the state, the prayer voiced in this anthem was not
compatible with the belief and hope which they hold in the early coming of the
new world in the government of which present temporal states can have no part.
Counsel advised the court that since that decision, Jehovah's Witnesses have
been exempted from opening exercises and he predicted some difficulty with that
group in the event that s. 28(4) was struck down.

The application as brought attacks the whole of Reg. 262, s. 28. The
evidence and argument however were directed entirely at s. 28(4), the
class-room time, if I may call it that, and to the parts of s. 28 that are
necessary to give effect to 28(4). These do not include s. 28(1) which deals
with opening exercises. Accordingly, the concern raised by counsel for the
Minister appears to me to be unwarranted.

(14), (15), and those parts of s-ss. (10), (11), (12) and (13), pertaining to
class-room instruction. In my view they are inconsistent with
